items.title: SGLang's +75% sampler speedup skips Qwen3 chat requests
items.summary: SGLang v0.5.20's release notes credit a nine-line change in the sampler with "Qwen3.5-2B decode +75% at batch 1 and +23% at batch 32". The nine lines are real, they are in the published wheel, and they do less work on the host than the line they replace. What the note leaves out is the predicate they sit behind: if a single request in the decode batch asks for top_k, top_p or min_p, your tokens never reach them. Serve a Qwen3 model through /v1/chat/completions with SGLang's own defaults and none of your traffic does, because the model's generation_config.json sets top_k and top_p for you. This is the first of our claim checks: one published number, a test plan written before anything runs, hardware anyone can get, and a plain account of which parts hold. Nobody paid for this one. Nine lines, and exactly one call site PR #38117 landed on 6 September 2026 and shipped in v0.5.20 (tag commit 94602c9c , 18 September; v0.5.19 is 0bcd8223 ). Inside sampling_from_probs_torch in python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py , v0.5.19 drew the next token like this: sampled_index = torch . multinomial ( probs , num_samples = 1 ) v0.5.20 keeps that line as a fallback and puts the new rule in front of it, behind an environment switch that defaults to on: if envs . SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE . get (): q = torch . empty_like ( probs , dtype = torch . float32 ). exponential_ ( 1.0 ) q . clamp_min_ ( torch . finfo ( torch . float32 ). tiny ) sampled_index = ( probs . float () / q ). argmax ( dim =- 1 , keepdim = True ) else : sampled_index = torch . multinomial ( probs , num_samples = 1 ) Dividing the probabilities by an Exp(1) draw and taking the argmax is the Gumbel-max trick, and it picks tokens from the same distribution as a categorical draw. The code comment is specific about where the time goes: torch.multinomial keeps CPU-side philox offset bookkeeping and runs a distribution-validity assert, both on the decode critical path. That work is on the host, between kernel launches, which is why the note's number is large at batch 1 and smaller at batch 32, and why your CPU decides how much you get. SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE is declared EnvBool(True) in python/sglang/srt/environ.py and accepts 0 , false , no or n . That switch is the honest way to A/B this on your own hardware: same wheel, same weights, one environment variable. One request with top_p takes the whole batch off the fast path In v0.5.20 that function has one caller, Sampler._sample_from_probs , under if simple_sampling_case . The flags come from SamplingBatchInfo.from_schedule_batch , with any() over the requests: need_top_p_sampling is any top_p != 1.0 , need_top_k_sampling is any top_k != TOP_K_ALL ( 1 << 30 ), need_min_p_sampling is any min_p > 0 . Before that, is_all_greedy (every request with top_k <= 1 ) sends the batch to the greedy path, and --enable-deterministic-inference sends it to the seeded path. So there are four outcomes, and only one of them is the new code: Batch Path in v0.5.20 Every request plain temperature sampling Gumbel-max, the new code Every request greedy (temperature 0) greedy argmax, untouched Any request with top_k, top_p or min_p the filtered path, untouched Server with deterministic inference seeded multinomial, untouched The third row is the one that bites. A greedy request has top_k = 1 after normalization, and 1 != 1 << 30 , so one temperature: 0 request sharing a decode batch moves everyone onto the filtered path. It also lasts longer than the request that caused it. The flags are computed when requests are prefilled, and merge_batch ORs them into the running decode batch when new requests join. When a request finishes, filter_batch drops its rows and leaves every flag as it was. So one top_p request keeps the whole running batch on the filtered path after it has finished, until the running batch empties completely and the next prefill batch starts it fresh. On a server that's never idle, that can be a long time. This port of SGLang's own arithmetic tells you which row a batch is in: TOP_K_ALL = 1 << 30 # sampling_params.py: top_k = -1 ("whole vocabulary") becomes this SAMPLING_EPS = 1e-6 # sampling_params.py: _SAMPLING_EPS def normalize ( params ): """ SamplingParams.normalize(): temperature below _SAMPLING_EPS means greedy (top_k = 1). """ p = dict ( params ) if 0 <= p [ " temperature " ] < SAMPLING_EPS : p [ " temperature " ] = 1.0 p [ " top_k " ] = 1 if p [ " top_k " ] == - 1 : p [ " top_k " ] = TOP_K_ALL return p def path_for_batch ( requests , enable_deterministic = False ): """ The sampler path for one decode batch. `requests` are normalized parameter dicts. Returns " greedy " , " gumbel " (the v0.5.20 fast path), " deterministic " or " filtered " . """ if not requests : raise ValueError ( " a batch needs at least one request " ) is_all_greedy = all ( r [ " top_k " ] <= 1 for r in requests ) need_top_p = any ( r [ " top_p " ] != 1.0 for r in requests ) need_top_k = any ( r [ " top_k " ] != TOP_K_ALL for r in requests ) need_min_p = any ( r [ " min_p " ] > 0 for r in requests ) if is_all_greedy : return " greedy " if not ( need_top_p or need_top_k or need_min_p ): # simple_sampling_case return " deterministic " if enable_deterministic else " gumbel " return " filtered " Your model's generation_config decides, and only on the chat endpoint SGLang's --sampling-defaults defaults to model : the server reads temperature , top_k , top_p , min_p and repetition_penalty out of the model's generation_config.json ( ModelConfig.get_default_sampling_params ). They're applied in OpenAIServingChat , whose request conversion documents the order as user value, then model generation_config , then OpenAI defaults. /v1/responses is served by a subclass of it and takes the model's temperature and top_p too. /v1/completions and /generate never read the file, so they keep top_p = 1.0 and top_k = -1 and stay on the fast path, unless you started the server with --preferred-sampling-params , which the tokenizer manager merges into every request on every endpoint. Here is that merge for the chat endpoint, from the same port: # ChatCompletionRequest._DEFAULT_SAMPLING_PARAMS; /v1/completions and /generate use the same # numbers from their own defaults, but never read the model's generation_config. OPENAI_DEFAULTS = { " temperature " : 1.0 , " top_p " : 1.0 , " top_k " : - 1 , " min_p " : 0.0 } MERGED_KEYS = ( " temperature " , " top_k " , " top_p " , " min_p " ) # model_config.get_default_sampling_params() def effective ( request , endpoint = " chat " , generation_config = None , sampling_defaults = " model " ): """ The sampling parameters the scheduler will see, before normalization. endpoint: " chat " for /v1/chat/completions, " generate " for /generate and /v1/completions. sampling_defaults: the server ' s --sampling-defaults ( " model " is the default). """ from_model = {} if endpoint == " chat " and sampling_defaults == " model " and generation_config : from_model = { k : generation_config [ k ] for k in MERGED_KEYS if generation_config . get ( k ) is not None } out = {} for key in MERGED_KEYS : if request . get ( key ) is not None : out [ key ] = request [ key ] elif key in from_model : out [ key ] = from_model [ key ] else : out [ key ] = OPENAI_DEFAULTS [ key ] return out Pass a request body's sampling fields (missing ones as None ) through effective , then normalize , then put the results in a list for path_for_batch . Qwen's documentation recommends Temperature 0.6, TopP 0.95, TopK 20 and MinP 0 for thinking mode and calls those "the default setting in generation_config.json ". Serve a Qwen3 model that ships that file, send a plain chat completion, and need_top_k_sampling is true before your request reaches the scheduler. The model in the release note is the exception, but only half of one: Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B had no generation_config.json when we checked on 26 October, so plain chat requests to it do land on the new path. Its model card, though, recommends four sampling configurations, and every one of them sets top_k=20 . Clients that follow the card are on the filtered path anyway. To see what your own server merged, grep its startup log for "Using default chat sampling params from model generation config", which OpenAIServingChat logs once with the dictionary. No line, no merge. What a free T4 can and cannot tell you The plan, written before the run: time both versions' rules on the same probability tensors at batch 1, 8, 32 and 64 and at vocabulary 32,768 and 151,936, once measuring the host-side call alone and once synchronizing the GPU, 200 calls a cell after 30 warm-ups, as medians with their interquartile spread; download both wheels to confirm the timed lines are the published code; compare the two rules' distributions over 200,000 draws; then install v0.5.20 and run a decode benchmark with the switch on and off. The session gave us a Tesla T4 (sm_75, 15,360 MiB, driver 580.178.04), four vCPUs and torch 2.11.0+cu128. Both wheels still carry the lines printed above, so these numbers come from published code. The new rule landed 0.0023 from the target distribution in total-variation distance, and SGLang's two spellings of the trick picked the same token in 100% of 1,024 rows on shared randomness. Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B answered 404 for generation_config.json , which checks the paragraph above. At Qwen3.5-2B's vocabulary of 151,936 tokens, per sampler call, median of 200 calls with every interquartile spread under 25%: Batch v0.5.19 multinomial v0.5.20 Gumbel-max Saved per call 1, host-side only 143.2 µs 45.1 µs 98.1 µs 1, GPU synchronized 170.6 µs 61.9 µs 108.7 µs 32, host-side only 693.5 µs 46.1 µs 647.4 µs 32, GPU synchronized 725.4 µs 628.1 µs 97.3 µs Three separate sessions produced the same table within 10%. The host-side column is the mechanism the patch targets, and it behaves as the code comment says: the new rule's host cost stays near 46 µs at every batch size, while multinomial's climbs. That's what you'd expect if its validity check makes the host wait for the device: at batch 32 its host-side time (693.5 µs) is almost all of its synchronized time (725.4 µs). The synchronized column is what a decode step pays, and there the saving is about 0.1 ms a step at both batch sizes. That is where the claim and our measurement part company. A 0.109 ms saving becomes +75% decode throughput only if the old step cost about 0.25 ms (0.109 × 1.75 ÷ 0.75), near 4,000 tokens a second on one stream. We measured no step: pip install sglang==0.5.20 would not build in the session, because outlines_core has no wheel for its Python 3.13. So the verdict is narrow on purpose. The mechanism holds and is worth about 0.1 ms a decode step here; the +75% as worded is unverified rather than disproved, and a saving in host work scales with the host, which on Kaggle is four vCPUs and not the authors' machine. Nothing here speaks to Hopper, Blackwell or multi-GPU setups. Gotchas Benchmark with temperature 0 and you measure nothing. SGLang's own one-batch benchmark defaults --temperature to 0.0 , which normalizes to greedy, which never calls the changed function. Qwen's docs separately tell you not to use greedy decoding with their models. Comparing wheels is not comparing the patch. Between the two tags sampler.py alone gained 288 insertions across five commits, sampling-mask capture among them. To measure this change, flip SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE inside one install. Expect different tokens, not different quality. The two rules draw from the same distribution but consume randomness differently, so a test that pinned exact token IDs will diff after the upgrade. If you need reproducibility, --enable-deterministic-inference moves you to the seeded path, which also forces the pytorch sampling backend and skips this change. Do this today Run the port above against your real request bodies and your model's generation_config.json , and include the other traffic that shares your server: one request with top_k, top_p, min_p or temperature 0 in the running batch is enough. If it prints filtered , this release note isn't about your server. If it prints gumbel , measure your own gain: start the same build twice, once with SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE=0 , and compare decode tokens/s. To get the fast path on the chat endpoint, send top_p: 1.0 and top_k: -1 explicitly, or start the server with --sampling-defaults openai and drop the model author's recommended settings. Then serve greedy and filtered traffic from another instance, because one such request holds the whole running batch off the fast path until it drains. We also timed both rules at batch 8 and 64, and at a 32,768-token vocabulary next to Qwen3.5-2B's own 151,936, in the same run. Ask in the comments and we will post that table with its spreads. Which vendor performance claim would you like checked next, and on what hardware? Checked against SGLang v0.5.19 ( 0bcd8223 ), v0.5.20 ( 94602c9c ), the v0.5.20 release notes and PR #38117's commit be00a543 . InferPrice ran the sampler rules, the distribution checks and the wheel comparison on a free Kaggle Tesla T4 on 26 October 2026. We ran no SGLang server anywhere, so no end-to-end decode throughput here is ours, and we measured no Hopper, Blackwell or multi-GPU path. Sources SGLang v0.5.20 release notes: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.20 The change itself, commit be00a543 (PR #38117), and python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py at tags v0.5.19 and v0.5.20: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE in python/sglang/srt/environ.py , the predicate in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_batch_info.py , and the defaults in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_params.py , all at v0.5.20 filter_batch and merge_batch in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_batch_info.py , and the running-batch merge in python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py , at v0.5.20 OpenAIServingResponses in python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_responses.py , and --preferred-sampling-params in python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py , at v0.5.20 --sampling-defaults in python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/serving.py , ModelConfig.get_default_sampling_params in python/sglang/srt/configs/model_config.py , and the merge order in python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/protocol.py --temperature default in python/sglang/benchmark/one_batch_server.py at v0.5.20 Qwen's recommended sampling parameters: https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/quickstart.html The Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B model card's recommended sampling parameters: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B The Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B file list, checked 26 October 2026: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B/tree/main Originally published at inferprice.pages.dev .

if envs.SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE.get():
    q = torch.empty_like(probs, dtype=torch.float32).exponential_(1.0)
    q.clamp_min_(torch.finfo(torch.float32).tiny)
    sampled_index = (probs.float() / q).argmax(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
else:
    sampled_index = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1)

Dividing the probabilities by an Exp(1) draw and taking the argmax is the Gumbel-max trick, and it picks tokens from the same distribution as a categorical draw. The code comment is specific about where the time goes: torch.multinomial keeps CPU-side philox offset bookkeeping and runs a distribution-validity assert, both on the decode critical path. That work is on the host, between kernel launches, which is why the note's number is large at batch 1 and smaller at batch 32, and why your CPU decides how much you get.

SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE is declared EnvBool(True) in python/sglang/srt/environ.py and accepts 0, false, no or n. That switch is the honest way to A/B this on your own hardware: same wheel, same weights, one environment variable.

In v0.5.20 that function has one caller, Sampler._sample_from_probs, under if simple_sampling_case. The flags come from SamplingBatchInfo.from_schedule_batch, with any() over the requests: need_top_p_sampling is any top_p != 1.0, need_top_k_sampling is any top_k != TOP_K_ALL (1 << 30), need_min_p_sampling is any min_p > 0. Before that, is_all_greedy (every request with top_k <= 1) sends the batch to the greedy path, and --enable-deterministic-inference sends it to the seeded path.

So there are four outcomes, and only one of them is the new code:

Batch Path in v0.5.20 Every request plain temperature sampling Gumbel-max, the new code Every request greedy (temperature 0) greedy argmax, untouched Any request with top_k, top_p or min_p the filtered path, untouched Server with deterministic inference seeded multinomial, untouched

The third row is the one that bites. A greedy request has top_k = 1 after normalization, and 1 != 1 << 30, so one temperature: 0 request sharing a decode batch moves everyone onto the filtered path.

It also lasts longer than the request that caused it. The flags are computed when requests are prefilled, and merge_batch ORs them into the running decode batch when new requests join. When a request finishes, filter_batch drops its rows and leaves every flag as it was. So one top_p request keeps the whole running batch on the filtered path after it has finished, until the running batch empties completely and the next prefill batch starts it fresh. On a server that's never idle, that can be a long time.

This port of SGLang's own arithmetic tells you which row a batch is in:

TOP_K_ALL = 1 << 30  # sampling_params.py: top_k = -1 ("whole vocabulary") becomes this
SAMPLING_EPS = 1e-6  # sampling_params.py: _SAMPLING_EPS


def normalize(params):
    """SamplingParams.normalize(): temperature below _SAMPLING_EPS means greedy (top_k = 1)."""
    p = dict(params)
    if 0 <= p["temperature"] < SAMPLING_EPS:
        p["temperature"] = 1.0
        p["top_k"] = 1
    if p["top_k"] == -1:
        p["top_k"] = TOP_K_ALL
    return p


def path_for_batch(requests, enable_deterministic=False):
    """The sampler path for one decode batch. `requests` are normalized parameter dicts.

    Returns "greedy", "gumbel" (the v0.5.20 fast path), "deterministic" or "filtered".
    """
    if not requests:
        raise ValueError("a batch needs at least one request")
    is_all_greedy = all(r["top_k"] <= 1 for r in requests)
    need_top_p = any(r["top_p"] != 1.0 for r in requests)
    need_top_k = any(r["top_k"] != TOP_K_ALL for r in requests)
    need_min_p = any(r["min_p"] > 0 for r in requests)
    if is_all_greedy:
        return "greedy"
    if not (need_top_p or need_top_k or need_min_p):  # simple_sampling_case
        return "deterministic" if enable_deterministic else "gumbel"
    return "filtered"
Your model's generation_config decides, and only on the chat endpoint

SGLang's --sampling-defaults defaults to model: the server reads temperature, top_k, top_p, min_p and repetition_penalty out of the model's generation_config.json (ModelConfig.get_default_sampling_params). They're applied in OpenAIServingChat, whose request conversion documents the order as user value, then model generation_config, then OpenAI defaults. /v1/responses is served by a subclass of it and takes the model's temperature and top_p too. /v1/completions and /generate never read the file, so they keep top_p = 1.0 and top_k = -1 and stay on the fast path, unless you started the server with --preferred-sampling-params, which the tokenizer manager merges into every request on every endpoint.

Here is that merge for the chat endpoint, from the same port:

# ChatCompletionRequest._DEFAULT_SAMPLING_PARAMS; /v1/completions and /generate use the same
# numbers from their own defaults, but never read the model's generation_config.
OPENAI_DEFAULTS = {"temperature": 1.0, "top_p": 1.0, "top_k": -1, "min_p": 0.0}
MERGED_KEYS = ("temperature", "top_k", "top_p", "min_p")  # model_config.get_default_sampling_params()


def effective(request, endpoint="chat", generation_config=None, sampling_defaults="model"):
    """The sampling parameters the scheduler will see, before normalization.

    endpoint: "chat" for /v1/chat/completions, "generate" for /generate and /v1/completions.
    sampling_defaults: the server's --sampling-defaults ("model" is the default).
    """
    from_model = {}
    if endpoint == "chat" and sampling_defaults == "model" and generation_config:
        from_model = {k: generation_config[k] for k in MERGED_KEYS if generation_config.get(k) is not None}
    out = {}
    for key in MERGED_KEYS:
        if request.get(key) is not None:
            out[key] = request[key]
        elif key in from_model:
            out[key] = from_model[key]
        else:
            out[key] = OPENAI_DEFAULTS[key]
    return out

Pass a request body's sampling fields (missing ones as None) through effective, then normalize, then put the results in a list for path_for_batch.

Qwen's documentation recommends Temperature 0.6, TopP 0.95, TopK 20 and MinP 0 for thinking mode and calls those "the default setting in generation_config.json". Serve a Qwen3 model that ships that file, send a plain chat completion, and need_top_k_sampling is true before your request reaches the scheduler. The model in the release note is the exception, but only half of one: Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B had no generation_config.json when we checked on 26 October, so plain chat requests to it do land on the new path. Its model card, though, recommends four sampling configurations, and every one of them sets top_k=20. Clients that follow the card are on the filtered path anyway.

To see what your own server merged, grep its startup log for "Using default chat sampling params from model generation config", which OpenAIServingChat logs once with the dictionary. No line, no merge.

What a free T4 can and cannot tell you

The plan, written before the run: time both versions' rules on the same probability tensors at batch 1, 8, 32 and 64 and at vocabulary 32,768 and 151,936, once measuring the host-side call alone and once synchronizing the GPU, 200 calls a cell after 30 warm-ups, as medians with their interquartile spread; download both wheels to confirm the timed lines are the published code; compare the two rules' distributions over 200,000 draws; then install v0.5.20 and run a decode benchmark with the switch on and off.

The session gave us a Tesla T4 (sm_75, 15,360 MiB, driver 580.178.04), four vCPUs and torch 2.11.0+cu128. Both wheels still carry the lines printed above, so these numbers come from published code. The new rule landed 0.0023 from the target distribution in total-variation distance, and SGLang's two spellings of the trick picked the same token in 100% of 1,024 rows on shared randomness. Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B answered 404 for generation_config.json, which checks the paragraph above.

At Qwen3.5-2B's vocabulary of 151,936 tokens, per sampler call, median of 200 calls with every interquartile spread under 25%:

Batch v0.5.19 multinomial v0.5.20 Gumbel-max Saved per call 1, host-side only 143.2 µs 45.1 µs 98.1 µs 1, GPU synchronized 170.6 µs 61.9 µs 108.7 µs 32, host-side only 693.5 µs 46.1 µs 647.4 µs 32, GPU synchronized 725.4 µs 628.1 µs 97.3 µs

Three separate sessions produced the same table within 10%.

The host-side column is the mechanism the patch targets, and it behaves as the code comment says: the new rule's host cost stays near 46 µs at every batch size, while multinomial's climbs. That's what you'd expect if its validity check makes the host wait for the device: at batch 32 its host-side time (693.5 µs) is almost all of its synchronized time (725.4 µs). The synchronized column is what a decode step pays, and there the saving is about 0.1 ms a step at both batch sizes.

That is where the claim and our measurement part company. A 0.109 ms saving becomes +75% decode throughput only if the old step cost about 0.25 ms (0.109 × 1.75 ÷ 0.75), near 4,000 tokens a second on one stream. We measured no step: pip install sglang==0.5.20 would not build in the session, because outlines_core has no wheel for its Python 3.13. So the verdict is narrow on purpose. The mechanism holds and is worth about 0.1 ms a decode step here; the +75% as worded is unverified rather than disproved, and a saving in host work scales with the host, which on Kaggle is four vCPUs and not the authors' machine. Nothing here speaks to Hopper, Blackwell or multi-GPU setups.

Gotchas

Benchmark with temperature 0 and you measure nothing. SGLang's own one-batch benchmark defaults --temperature to 0.0, which normalizes to greedy, which never calls the changed function. Qwen's docs separately tell you not to use greedy decoding with their models.

Comparing wheels is not comparing the patch. Between the two tags sampler.py alone gained 288 insertions across five commits, sampling-mask capture among them. To measure this change, flip SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE inside one install.

Expect different tokens, not different quality. The two rules draw from the same distribution but consume randomness differently, so a test that pinned exact token IDs will diff after the upgrade. If you need reproducibility, --enable-deterministic-inference moves you to the seeded path, which also forces the pytorch sampling backend and skips this change.

Do this today
  1. Run the port above against your real request bodies and your model's generation_config.json, and include the other traffic that shares your server: one request with top_k, top_p, min_p or temperature 0 in the running batch is enough. If it prints filtered, this release note isn't about your server.
  2. If it prints gumbel, measure your own gain: start the same build twice, once with SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE=0, and compare decode tokens/s.
  3. To get the fast path on the chat endpoint, send top_p: 1.0 and top_k: -1 explicitly, or start the server with --sampling-defaults openai and drop the model author's recommended settings. Then serve greedy and filtered traffic from another instance, because one such request holds the whole running batch off the fast path until it drains.

We also timed both rules at batch 8 and 64, and at a 32,768-token vocabulary next to Qwen3.5-2B's own 151,936, in the same run. Ask in the comments and we will post that table with its spreads.

Which vendor performance claim would you like checked next, and on what hardware?

Checked against SGLang v0.5.19 (0bcd8223), v0.5.20 (94602c9c), the v0.5.20 release notes and PR #38117's commit be00a543. InferPrice ran the sampler rules, the distribution checks and the wheel comparison on a free Kaggle Tesla T4 on 26 October 2026. We ran no SGLang server anywhere, so no end-to-end decode throughput here is ours, and we measured no Hopper, Blackwell or multi-GPU path.

Sources
  • SGLang v0.5.20 release notes: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/releases/tag/v0.5.20
  • The change itself, commit be00a543 (PR #38117), and python/sglang/srt/layers/sampler.py at tags v0.5.19 and v0.5.20: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang
  • SGLANG_OPT_USE_GUMBEL_SAMPLE in python/sglang/srt/environ.py, the predicate in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_batch_info.py, and the defaults in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_params.py, all at v0.5.20
  • filter_batch and merge_batch in python/sglang/srt/sampling/sampling_batch_info.py, and the running-batch merge in python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py, at v0.5.20
  • OpenAIServingResponses in python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/serving_responses.py, and --preferred-sampling-params in python/sglang/srt/managers/tokenizer_manager.py, at v0.5.20
  • --sampling-defaults in python/sglang/srt/arg_groups/fields/serving.py, ModelConfig.get_default_sampling_params in python/sglang/srt/configs/model_config.py, and the merge order in python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/openai/protocol.py
  • --temperature default in python/sglang/benchmark/one_batch_server.py at v0.5.20
  • Qwen's recommended sampling parameters: https://qwen.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started/quickstart.html
  • The Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B model card's recommended sampling parameters: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B
  • The Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B file list, checked 26 October 2026: https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B/tree/main

items.title: A Private Evidence Checklist for Tech Workers Sponsoring a Common-Law Partner in Canada
items.summary: A remote developer can move cities, work from a partner's home and keep most records in cloud services. That can make a Canadian common-law sponsorship file harder to reconstruct later. IRCC's current rule requires at least 12 consecutive months of living together in a conjugal relationship; short temporary absences may be compatible, but long separations need careful assessment. Treat the timeline as a data-integrity problem Before collecting files, write a simple chronology of addresses, move dates and temporary travel. Then check that leases, household bills, government letters and the forms agree. Never edit metadata, backdate records or create evidence that did not exist. If a bill is in one partner's name, record the real reason and use other genuine documents where available. Build a private evidence index A useful folder structure is one folder per quarter, with an index listing document date, address, owner and why it is relevant. Keep original copies and a version used for submission. Avoid uploading complete bank statements, identity scans or passwords to public repositories or AI chat tools. Limit access to the people preparing the application and follow the current IRCC checklist for the documents actually required. Do not confuse the PR file with work authorization An application or acknowledgement of receipt does not itself authorize work. Separate open-work-permit rules may apply to eligible sponsored partners living in Canada. Check the current rule and existing status before any employment decision. The application should also declare required family members, including non-accompanying children. Official IRCC sources (checked 26 October 2026): who you can sponsor , complete application guide , and open work permits for sponsored partners in Canada . For individual advice, contact Titanium Law Professional Corporation or call +1 778-683-8110. General information, not legal advice. Individual eligibility varies. Prepared with AI assistance and checked against linked IRCC guidance.

items.title: The first LLM router metric I check is the missing-row count
items.summary: A router can choose a model for every prompt and still leave you with a very incomplete evaluation. Those are different achievements. I want to see both before I trust the quality chart. 🔎 AutoBench's new router audit makes that distinction unusually easy to inspect: it publishes the decisions as well as the scores. The author reports that none of the commercial settings in its headline comparison beats a particular static model on quality and cost together. That is the author's result, not a fresh model test from me. [1] My contribution here is smaller and reproducible: read the released decision ledger, count which decisions have scores, and check whether a supposedly adaptive policy mostly picks the same model. Original chart computed from the pinned AutoBench decision export. Unscored means unavailable for scoring in this ledger; it does not establish a failed request. A missing score needs its own denominator In the exported azure_cost pass, all 252 decisions name a model, but only 35 have scored=True . Its top model receives 149 decisions. In orca_constrained_quality , the corresponding counts are 245 scored and 252 top-model selections, again out of 252 decisions. [2] The first pass raises a coverage question. The second raises a routing question. A single quality percentage hides that distinction. Imagine printing a restaurant review after tasting only the starters. The score may describe the starters perfectly. It still needs a label. 🍽️ For a benchmark, I would keep a decision count, a scored count and a missing-cell explanation next to every quality number. A score calculated over available cells is a conditional result. It should not silently become a statement about the entire workload. That does not mean every unavailable cell is a bad answer. The provider may have selected a model outside the stored score matrix. Penalizing every such cell as a miss is another evaluation choice, not an automatic repair. Print the ledger before the leaderboard 🧪 Save the following as audit.py and run python3 audit.py with Python 3.10 or newer and internet access. It uses the standard library, pins the dataset revision and checks the downloaded file's digest before parsing it. import csv import hashlib import io from collections import Counter , defaultdict from urllib.request import urlopen revision = ' 43755180be7d8097068982d7a3f37fc04cd15379 ' url = f ' https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutoBench/router-benchmark-2026-10/resolve/ { revision } /decisions.csv ' raw = urlopen ( url ). read () assert hashlib . sha256 ( raw ). hexdigest () == ' d000e5310744ae15f9c9d572ee1f88f84858fc0ba01fb54eef1e6a73a505d540 ' passes = defaultdict ( list ) for row in csv . DictReader ( io . StringIO ( raw . decode ())): passes [ row [ ' pass ' ]]. append ( row ) assert sum ( map ( len , passes . values ())) == 7046 assert len ( passes ) == 28 collapsed = 0 for rows in passes . values (): assert len ({ r [ ' prompt_id ' ] for r in rows }) == len ( rows ) top = Counter ( r [ ' selected_model ' ] for r in rows ). most_common ( 1 )[ 0 ][ 1 ] collapsed += 10 * top >= 9 * len ( rows ) print ( ' exported passes: ' , len ( passes ), ' | collapsed: ' , collapsed ) for name in [ ' orca_constrained_quality ' , ' azure_cost ' , ' nd_subset_k0 ' , ' or_auto ' ]: rows = passes [ name ] top = Counter ( r [ ' selected_model ' ] for r in rows ). most_common ( 1 )[ 0 ][ 1 ] scored = sum ( r [ ' scored ' ] == ' True ' for r in rows ) print ( f ' { name } : scored { scored } / { len ( rows ) } , top-model picks { top } / { len ( rows ) } ' ) The output is: exported passes: 28 | collapsed: 9 orca_constrained_quality: scored 245/252, top-model picks 252/252 azure_cost: scored 35/252, top-model picks 149/252 nd_subset_k0: scored 248/252, top-model picks 252/252 or_auto: scored 245/252, top-model picks 248/252 ✅ Here, nine of the 28 exported passes send at least 90% of decisions to one model. The threshold uses integer arithmetic, so a floating-point boundary cannot change the classification. There is an easy trap here: the export's 28 passes are not the blog's 17 headline settings . The dump also contains secondary and reference passes. My count describes the whole exported ledger; it does not correct or contradict the author's narrower count. [2] A constant can be a good policy A concentrated policy is not automatically useless. If one model is suitable for the workload, consistently choosing it may be sensible. Reliability requirements, contractual constraints and availability can also narrow a usable pool. What concentration changes is the comparison I want. If a policy nearly always selects model A, compare it with always selecting A. Then ask what the remaining decisions contribute. Merely showing that it beats random selection does not isolate the value of adapting to the prompt. 💡 I would also compare routers on the same scored prompt set before interpreting a quality difference. Otherwise a router evaluated on difficult questions and another evaluated on an easier subset can trade places without either improving. Keep the missing rows visible, and report the full workload separately from that matched subset. What this check does—and doesn't—establish This is an offline audit of published decisions, not another round of router or model calls. I did not reproduce AutoBench's judges, bootstrap procedure or cost ranking. The source says its router calls predate this release; the ledger is not a guarantee about current vendor behavior. [2] The useful habit survives those limits: print coverage and concentration before celebrating a quality score. A routing graph gets much more interesting once you know which decisions it actually describes. References [1] Peter Kruger, Do LLM Routers Actually Route? . [2] AutoBench, router benchmark dataset and methodology notes . Counts and original chart derived from its CC BY 4.0 decision table. The script pins the exact revision. AI disclosure AI was used to draft the article.
items.summary_html:
A router can choose a model for every prompt and still leave you with a very incomplete evaluation. Those are different achievements. I want to see both before I trust the quality chart. 🔎

AutoBench's new router audit makes that distinction unusually easy to inspect: it publishes the decisions as well as the scores. The author reports that none of the commercial settings in its headline comparison beats a particular static model on quality and cost together. That is the author's result, not a fresh model test from me. [1]

My contribution here is smaller and reproducible: read the released decision ledger, count which decisions have scores, and check whether a supposedly adaptive policy mostly picks the same model.

Original chart computed from the pinned AutoBench decision export. Unscored means unavailable for scoring in this ledger; it does not establish a failed request.

A missing score needs its own denominator

In the exported azure_cost pass, all 252 decisions name a model, but only 35 have scored=True. Its top model receives 149 decisions. In orca_constrained_quality, the corresponding counts are 245 scored and 252 top-model selections, again out of 252 decisions. [2]

The first pass raises a coverage question. The second raises a routing question. A single quality percentage hides that distinction.

Imagine printing a restaurant review after tasting only the starters. The score may describe the starters perfectly. It still needs a label. 🍽️

For a benchmark, I would keep a decision count, a scored count and a missing-cell explanation next to every quality number. A score calculated over available cells is a conditional result. It should not silently become a statement about the entire workload.

That does not mean every unavailable cell is a bad answer. The provider may have selected a model outside the stored score matrix. Penalizing every such cell as a miss is another evaluation choice, not an automatic repair.

Print the ledger before the leaderboard 🧪

Save the following as audit.py and run python3 audit.py with Python 3.10 or newer and internet access. It uses the standard library, pins the dataset revision and checks the downloaded file's digest before parsing it.

import csv
import hashlib
import io
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from urllib.request import urlopen
revision = '43755180be7d8097068982d7a3f37fc04cd15379'
url = f'https://huggingface.co/datasets/AutoBench/router-benchmark-2026-10/resolve/{revision}/decisions.csv'
raw = urlopen(url).read()
assert hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest() == 'd000e5310744ae15f9c9d572ee1f88f84858fc0ba01fb54eef1e6a73a505d540'
passes = defaultdict(list)
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw.decode())):
    passes[row['pass']].append(row)
assert sum(map(len, passes.values())) == 7046
assert len(passes) == 28
collapsed = 0
for rows in passes.values():
    assert len({r['prompt_id'] for r in rows}) == len(rows)
    top = Counter(r['selected_model'] for r in rows).most_common(1)[0][1]
    collapsed += 10 * top >= 9 * len(rows)
print('exported passes:', len(passes), '| collapsed:', collapsed)
for name in ['orca_constrained_quality', 'azure_cost', 'nd_subset_k0', 'or_auto']:
    rows = passes[name]
    top = Counter(r['selected_model'] for r in rows).most_common(1)[0][1]
    scored = sum(r['scored'] == 'True' for r in rows)
    print(f'{name}: scored {scored}/{len(rows)}, top-model picks {top}/{len(rows)}')

The output is:

exported passes: 28 | collapsed: 9
orca_constrained_quality: scored 245/252, top-model picks 252/252
azure_cost: scored 35/252, top-model picks 149/252
nd_subset_k0: scored 248/252, top-model picks 252/252
or_auto: scored 245/252, top-model picks 248/252

✅ Here, nine of the 28 exported passes send at least 90% of decisions to one model. The threshold uses integer arithmetic, so a floating-point boundary cannot change the classification.

There is an easy trap here: the export's 28 passes are not the blog's 17 headline settings. The dump also contains secondary and reference passes. My count describes the whole exported ledger; it does not correct or contradict the author's narrower count. [2]

A constant can be a good policy

A concentrated policy is not automatically useless. If one model is suitable for the workload, consistently choosing it may be sensible. Reliability requirements, contractual constraints and availability can also narrow a usable pool.

What concentration changes is the comparison I want. If a policy nearly always selects model A, compare it with always selecting A. Then ask what the remaining decisions contribute. Merely showing that it beats random selection does not isolate the value of adapting to the prompt. 💡

I would also compare routers on the same scored prompt set before interpreting a quality difference. Otherwise a router evaluated on difficult questions and another evaluated on an easier subset can trade places without either improving. Keep the missing rows visible, and report the full workload separately from that matched subset.

What this check does—and doesn't—establish

This is an offline audit of published decisions, not another round of router or model calls. I did not reproduce AutoBench's judges, bootstrap procedure or cost ranking. The source says its router calls predate this release; the ledger is not a guarantee about current vendor behavior. [2]

The useful habit survives those limits: print coverage and concentration before celebrating a quality score. A routing graph gets much more interesting once you know which decisions it actually describes.

References

[1] Peter Kruger, Do LLM Routers Actually Route?.

[2] AutoBench, router benchmark dataset and methodology notes. Counts and original chart derived from its CC BY 4.0 decision table. The script pins the exact revision.

AI disclosure

AI was used to draft the article.

items.title: Bedrock Prompt Shortening: 6 optimizations, 0 changes, a fake +45%
items.summary: In the AgentCore Optimization Loop article, I let AWS rewrite the system prompt of my DevOps agent. The recommendation was good, but it had an effect I didn't measure at the time: the prompt grew. The optimizer kept everything I had written and added two new blocks. The Advanced Prompt Optimization documentation acknowledges this: by default it optimizes for quality only, with no length constraint, and an optimized prompt can end up longer than the original. Longer means more input tokens on every call and, potentially, a longer time to first token. On October 20, 2026, AWS announced an option for that, shortenPrompt , which asks the optimizer for a prompt shorter than the original with an equal or better score. If it can't find one, it gives you yours back. I wanted to answer a concrete question: how much does shortening a prompt that already works actually save me, and at what volume is it worth it? To find out, I used the real classifier prompt of my news agent, the 205 classifications it made in production as the reference, and three target models. The result wasn't what I expected, and neither were the reasons. 📌 TL;DR — What I found In all six optimizations (three models, with and without shortenPrompt ), the prompt the service returned is identical to the original , character for character. compressionRatio = 1.0 on all three models. One job reported a +45% improvement (0.575 → 0.833) for that identical prompt. The cause: 12 failed inferences on the original side, with zero tokens, scored as 0. Another job finished as Completed with SUCCESS even though the optimizer failed on 684 of 689 calls . I only saw it in the CloudWatch error metrics. Even with the 30% cut from the announcement's example, at my volume (~267 calls a month) the job would take between 9 and 55 years to pay for itself. The same prompt with the same news item measures 1,621 tokens on Haiku 5.5, 1,132 on Haiku 4.5, and 917 on Nova 2 Lite . The service counts it as 600 on all three. What Advanced Prompt Optimization Is and What shortenPrompt Adds Advanced Prompt Optimization is Bedrock's full optimizer, different from the simple OptimizePrompt . You give it a JSONL file with your templates (variables in double braces, {% raw %}{{variable}}{% endraw %} ), up to 100 evaluation samples per template, and an evaluation method: the default judge, free-text criteria ( steeringCriteria ), an LLM judge with your rubric, or your own Lambda. The service runs an inference, evaluation, and rewrite loop on each target model and returns one optimized prompt per model. A job accepts up to 10 templates and 5 models, and the documentation talks about 15 to 20 minutes for a prompt with few samples and several hours for many. My jobs took 14 and 29 minutes. shortenPrompt is enabled per template, inside the JSONL , not in the API call: { "version" : "bedrock-2026-05-14" , "templateId" : "news-classifier-shorten" , "promptTemplate" : "..." , "optimizationConfig" : { "shortenPrompt" : true }, "customEvaluationMetricLabel" : "clasificacion_vs_produccion" , "evaluationMetricLambdaArn" : "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1: :function:apo-news-classification-evaluator" , "evaluationSamples" : [ "..." ] } The return logic is simple: the shortened prompt is returned only if it is shorter and scores at least as high as the original. If either condition fails, you get your original prompt back with compressionRatio = 1.0 . The ratio is optimizedTokenCount / originalTokenCount , measured on the template and not on the prompt with the variables filled in. On cost, the documentation says there is no separate service charge : you pay for the tokens it consumes. The pricing page gives the formula: about 16 × N target model inferences per template, where N is the number of samples, plus the optimizer (currently Claude Sonnet 4.6) with 101 × (3700 + 0.35 × P) input tokens, where P is the token count of your template. The optimizer's output tokens have no formula. The Experiment The prompt: my news agent's classifier My agent processes the AWS RSS feed three times a day. Since late September the model no longer computes relevance: it only classifies each news item into a topic ( topic_tier ) and a change type ( change_type ), and a rubric with editable weights computes the 0 to 10 score. If the score reaches 6, a post is generated; if it reaches 7, the item goes into the newsletter. I chose this prompt for three reasons. It has an objective answer, so it can be evaluated without a subjective judge. It runs every day, so it has real volume to compute savings against. And it was already compact, about 1,900 characters: if shortening finds something to cut here, it will find it in almost any prompt. A fragment: topic_tier: el tema al que pertenece el servicio o la capacidad (elige el más específico): • genai_agentes: Bedrock, IA generativa, agentes, MCP, Amazon Quick, AgentCore, SageMaker AI • serverless_core: Lambda, Step Functions, API Gateway, EventBridge, DynamoDB ... change_type: qué tipo de cambio anuncia la noticia (juzga el cambio, no el servicio): • nueva_capacidad: una función o servicio que antes no existía • mejora: una mejora incremental de algo que ya existía (límites, rendimiento, integraciones) ... The reference: what production decided I didn't label anything by hand. The reference for each news item is the classification production made, stored in DynamoDB: 205 news items classified between September 30 and October 22, 2026. I split the set deterministically, by ID hash: 60 items for the optimizer and 145 as a holdout it never sees. With this reference I'm not measuring whether the shortened prompt is more accurate, but whether it behaves the same as the current one. For a shortening, that seems like the right question to me: I'm looking for a cheaper prompt that doesn't break anything, which makes it a regression test. The downside is that if production was wrong, the optimizer learns to repeat the mistake. The evaluator: a deterministic Lambda Advanced Prompt Optimization offers four ways to evaluate, and I ruled out three. The default judge scores accuracy, completeness, and Expression Quality , and that last criterion rewards short answers, so it would have optimized the brevity of the output instead of the classification. steeringCriteria are too vague for a task with an exact answer. An LLM judge adds cost, because the judge reads prompt, response, and reference on every evaluation, and it adds its own noise to something you can settle by comparing two values. I went with a Lambda. The contract the service requires is simple: you receive {"preds": [...], "golds": [...]} and return {"score": float, "scores": [...]} , higher is better. My rule: if the output isn't valid JSON with all the allowed keys and values, the sample scores 0; if it is, it gets 0.5 for the right topic and 0.5 for the right change type. def compute_score ( preds , golds ): """ Mandatory JSON contract; 0.5 for the right topic_tier and 0.5 for the right change_type. """ scores = [ score_one ( p , g ) for p , g in zip ( preds , golds )] return { " score " : sum ( scores ) / len ( scores ) if scores else 0.0 , " scores " : scores } The service reads the docstring as the metric description and reviews the full code before using it. That review cost me my first job; I cover it in the gotchas. The template: what the optimizer can touch and what it can't In production the prompt goes in as the system prompt, the news item as the user message, and the output uses Structured Outputs . Advanced Prompt Optimization takes a single text template and doesn't accept structured outputs, so the JSON contract has to live inside the prompt. I protected it with : the optimizer can rewrite the classification instructions, but not the news item or the output format. {% raw %} Noticia a clasificar: Título: {{title}} Descripción: {{description}} Responde ÚNICAMENTE con un objeto JSON, sin texto antes ni después, con exactamente estas claves: change_type, topic_tier, topic, reason, keyPoints (lista de textos) y emojis (lista de textos). En topic_tier y change_type usa solo las claves listadas arriba. {% endraw %} In the same job I put two identical copies of the template, one optimized for quality only (the default behavior) and one with shortenPrompt: true , to compare them under the same conditions. Advanced Prompt Optimization only optimizes Bedrock models, and my working account can't invoke Haiku 5.5 on Bedrock. The account that can hadn't submitted the Anthropic use case form, so Haiku 4.5 didn't run there. I ended up running one job per account, with the same data and the same evaluator: Claude Haiku 5.5 (the production model) in one, and Claude Haiku 4.5 (the production model until October 8) plus Amazon Nova 2 Lite in the other. Nova is the model I dropped in March because it didn't support structured outputs; since Advanced Prompt Optimization works with plain text, that limitation doesn't matter here. That same missing form ended up affecting the Haiku 5.5 job too, as I explain in Finding 3. Hypotheses, written before seeing results I followed the same method as in previous articles: before reading the job results, I wrote down each hypothesis with the criterion that would refute it. H1 — Shortening finds something to cut. At least one model returns compressionRatio < 0.9 . Refuted if all three return 1.0 or a ratio above 0.9. H2 — The shortened prompt behaves the same on the holdout. The score difference against the original, on the same model, stays within the noise floor. Refuted if it falls below that floor. H3 — At my volume, the savings don't pay for the job. At ~267 calls a month, the monthly savings don't cover the job cost in under 12 months on any model. Refuted if any model recovers the cost in a year or less. H4 — Optimized prompts aren't portable. The prompt optimized for one model loses more than the noise floor when run on another. Refuted if they perform the same on all three models. 📋 Recorded deviations : (1) the original design used only Nova 2 Lite, because Haiku 5.5 wasn't available on Bedrock in my working account; (2) I moved to three models split across two accounts; (3) the job runs Haiku 5.5 with its default configuration, which uses thinking, unlike production (see gotchas); (4) the first two jobs failed because of the Lambda code validator; (5) I stopped a job running the old evaluator, and its window overlaps by a few minutes with the good job in that account, which slightly inflates the costs measured there; (6) my holdout baseline ran in parallel with the Haiku 4.5 job. All the code is at github.com/codecr/bedrock-prompt-shortening : scripts numbered 01 to 07, the evaluator, and the cleanup. Baseline: How Much the Prompt Differs from Itself Before looking at any optimized prompt, I ran the original on the 145 holdout news items, twice on each model. The second run matters because the model isn't deterministic: if two variants differ by less than the original prompt differs from itself, that difference means nothing. Haiku 5.5 ran as it does in production, without thinking and with low effort. Haiku 5.5 doesn't reach 1.0 even against references it mostly generated itself, because in production it runs with a separate system prompt and structured outputs, and changing how you call the model already moves the result. And the noise floor is high: the same prompt changes the classification of between 5 and 17 of 145 news items from one run to the next. An improvement smaller than that can't be told apart from chance. A business data point: with the active rubric, Haiku 5.5's classification changes the decision to generate a post on 10 of the 145 news items compared with what production decided. That margin of error already exists in my pipeline today, and I hadn't measured it. 🔢 ProTip #1 : The same text doesn't measure the same on every model. My prompt with the same news item is 1,621 tokens on Haiku 5.5 versus 1,132 on Haiku 4.5: 43% more. Before calculating how much trimming a prompt saves you, measure its tokens on the model where it will run . And don't use the job's originalTokenCount for that: the service counted my template as 600 tokens on all three models, with its own count that isn't the tokenizer you're billed for. Finding 1: Six Optimizations, Zero Changes This is the complete result of the two jobs. "Identical" means identical character for character to the original, once the tags are removed, which the service always strips. Model Template Original score → "optimized" compressionRatio Failed inferences (orig / opt) Did the prompt change? Haiku 5.5 quality 0.808 → 0.850 — 0 / 0 No Haiku 5.5 shorten 0.825 → 0.825 1.0 0 / 0 No Haiku 4.5 quality 0.575 → 0.833 — 12 / 0 No Haiku 4.5 shorten 0.625 → 0.625 1.0 13 / 13 No Nova 2 Lite quality 0.708 → 0.708 — 1 / 1 No Nova 2 Lite shorten 0.708 → 0.708 1.0 0 / 0 No H1 is refuted: no model returned a ratio below 1.0. But of the six rows, only the two Nova rows are a clean result. On Nova 2 Lite the optimizer worked, the model answered almost every inference, and the service found neither a better prompt nor a shorter one that scored as high. For a prompt that was already compact, evaluated with a strict criterion, that's a reasonable answer: there was nothing to cut without losing quality. When it returns the original, the service copies the original's measurement into the "optimized" metrics, which is why both columns match down to the last decimal. Haiku 4.5 and Haiku 5.5 aren't clean cases, for two different reasons the job result doesn't mention. Finding 2: The +45% That Never Existed Back to the third row. For Haiku 4.5, optimizing for quality only, the job summary reports that the score rose from 0.575 to 0.833 , a 45% gain, and that average time to first token dropped from 1.12 s to 0.60 s. The "optimized" prompt is identical to the original. I went through the results file sample by sample. On the original side, 12 of the 60 inferences came back empty : a blank response, inputTokens: 0 , outputTokens: 0 , zero latency. The evaluator received an empty string, which isn't valid JSON, and scored it 0. On the "optimized" side none failed. The entire improvement comes from those 12 failed calls. Bedrock's CloudWatch metrics show what happened: during the job window, Haiku 4.5 logged 607 server errors ( InvocationServerErrors ). Some may be mine: my holdout baseline ran 230 calls against the same model in parallel, and my client retried 5xx errors. But the job's 25 empty inferences belong to the job. The quota wasn't the problem: Haiku 4.5 has 10,000 requests per minute in that account. There's another detail in that same row. Even excluding the 12 failures, the original scores 0.719 versus 0.833 for the same text in the same job. It's the same noise floor as the baseline, now inside the job: with 60 samples and a model that agrees with itself 88% of the time, two measurements of the same prompt differ by more than 10 points. 🚨 ProTip #2 : Don't trust the summary's averageScore . Before accepting an optimized prompt, do two things the service doesn't do for you: compare the prompt text against the original (in my six cases it was identical), and count how many samples in dataset[] have outputTokens: 0 . A failed inference enters the average as one more 0.0, and in my case it produced a 45% improvement on a prompt that didn't change. The repo's 05_fetch_results.py script runs both checks. Finding 3: SUCCESS Without an Optimizer The Haiku 5.5 job finished as Completed , with both entries at SUCCESS , no errors in the results file, and a +5% improvement on the quality template (0.808 → 0.850) for, once again, a prompt identical to the original. That +5% is the size of how much the same prompt varies against itself: in my baseline, Haiku 5.5 changed the classification of 12 of 145 news items between two runs. On its own it says nothing. The problem was in the optimizer's metrics. Haiku 5.5 ran 1,925 inferences during the job window. The pricing formula predicts 16 × 60 × 2 = 1,920 : the target model did exactly the expected work. But the optimizer, Claude Sonnet 4.6, logged 689 invocations and 684 client errors ( InvocationClientErrors ), with only 7,756 input tokens in total. In the other account, the same optimizer consumed 2.49 million tokens. I found the cause by invoking Sonnet 4.6 by hand in that account: "Model use case details have not been submitted for this account" . It's the same Anthropic form that kept me from using Haiku 4.5 there. The optimizer runs with my credentials, not a service role, and my account couldn't invoke it. The job didn't catch it at creation, and didn't report it in failureMessage or in the result entries. It evaluated the original prompt, couldn't generate candidates, and handed it back to me with SUCCESS . This kind of failure is hard to spot because the result looks normal. If I hadn't checked CloudWatch to calculate costs, I would have written that Haiku 5.5 found nothing to cut. 🔍 ProTip #3 : Advanced Prompt Optimization doesn't use a service role: it invokes the target models, the optimizer , and your Lambda with the credentials of whoever creates the job (Forward Access Session). Before launching a job, verify that your account can invoke Claude Sonnet 4.6 with a test call. At job creation the service validates that you can invoke the target models ( "No inference API is accessible for model" ), but it doesn't validate the optimizer. And after each job, check InvocationClientErrors for us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 in Bedrock's CloudWatch metrics. Finding 4: Would It Have Been Worth It? No prompt changed, so there are no measured savings. Even so, the original question can be answered with the jobs' real costs, assuming shortening had achieved the announcement's example: compressionRatio = 0.7 , 30% fewer tokens in the template. The Haiku 4.5 and Nova figures include a few minutes of the job I stopped, so a clean job comes out somewhat cheaper. The optimizer is the most expensive part: about $3.14 per template-model pair. With that data I calculated the cost of optimizing one template for one model and what it would save per month at my real volume (205 news items in 23 days, about 267 calls a month), with the 30% cut applied to the template's 600 tokens: Model Job cost (1 template) Savings per month Pays for itself in Calls per month to pay for it in one month Claude Haiku 5.5 $3.48 $0.0053 55 years 175,955 Claude Haiku 4.5 $5.83 $0.0529 9 years 29,453 Amazon Nova 2 Lite $3.93 $0.0159 21 years 66,168 H3 is confirmed by a wide margin. The table also shows that shortening pays off more on the more expensive model: Haiku 4.5 costs 10 times more per input token than Haiku 5.5 on Bedrock. On the production model, which is the cheapest, shortening matters less. My table slightly underestimates the Haiku 5.5 savings, because it calculates on the 600 tokens the service counts and not on the ones its tokenizer bills; even correcting for that, the order of magnitude doesn't change. This doesn't mean shortening is useless; it means the math depends more on volume than on the cut percentage. At about 30,000 calls a month on Haiku 4.5, or about 176,000 on Haiku 5.5, the job pays for itself in a month. At 267, it doesn't. As for latency, the other benefit the announcement mentions, I have nothing to measure: without a shorter prompt there's no TTFT difference. The improvement the job summary shows (1.12 s → 0.60 s on Haiku 4.5) is two measurements of the same text, taken while the model was returning server errors; I don't attribute it to the prompt. What the Documentation Doesn't Tell You Beyond the findings above, these are the gotchas that cost me a job or a good while. 🧪 ProTip #4 : In modelConfigurations , the additionalModelRequestFields field only accepts topK . I tried passing thinking: disabled and output_config.effort: low for Haiku 5.5, the way I run it in production, and the job was rejected at creation: "contains unsupported keys: [output_config, thinking]. Supported keys: [topK]" . The optimizer tunes the prompt for Haiku 5.5 with its default configuration, which uses thinking: on a sample of 12 news items that meant 57% more output tokens and 0.75 s more latency than the production configuration, with the same score. In practice, you're optimizing for a different configuration than the one you'll run. 🛑 ProTip #5 : The service reviews your Lambda evaluator's code before using it, and rejects it if it finds anything it considers dangerous. My first job failed with "Metric code validation failed: Uses potentially dangerous builtin: compile()" because of a re.compile() : the analysis doesn't distinguish the re method from the compile builtin. Use re.match(pattern, text) directly. The job doesn't fail at creation either: it fails about three minutes later, with a generic failureMessage that points you to the results file in S3, where the real per-entry reason is. ⏱️ ProTip #6 : A job's terminal states are Completed , Failed , Stopped , and PartiallyCompleted . The official sample's wait loop only considers the first three, so with a partial result it waits forever. I also found some differences between the user guide and the real API: The delete operation is BatchDeleteAdvancedPromptOptimizationJob , singular (the guide uses the plural), and it returns advancedPromptOptimizationJobs[] and errors[] . The ListAdvancedPromptOptimizationJobs response uses the jobSummaries key, not the one shown in the guide's example. The encryption parameter is called encryptionKeyArn , not encryptionConfig . The evaluation page asks for a resource-based policy so bedrock.amazonaws.com can invoke your Lambda; the prerequisites page says the service invokes it with your credentials. I configured both. Hypothesis Verdicts Hypothesis Result H1 — Shortening finds something to cut Refuted. compressionRatio = 1.0 on all three models. The only clean result, Nova 2 Lite, returned the original. H2 — The shortened prompt behaves the same on the holdout Couldn't be tested. There was no shortened prompt. H3 — At my volume, the savings don't pay for the job Confirmed. Not even with a hypothetical 30% cut: between 9 and 55 years. H4 — Optimized prompts aren't portable Couldn't be tested. The six "optimized" prompts are the original. Two of the four hypotheses went untested. The portability matrix I had ready made no sense with six identical prompts, so I didn't run it. Limits of the Experiment One template, one domain. My prompt was already compact and the task has an exact answer. With a long, redundant prompt, shortening would probably cut something. I didn't run that positive control, so I can't separate "the service doesn't cut" from "my prompt had nothing to cut." The Nova case suggests the latter. The reference is production, not the truth. I'm measuring regression, not accuracy. 60 samples and a single job per model. I don't know how much the optimizer varies between runs of the same job. Haiku 5.5 was optimized with a different configuration than production , and its job had no working optimizer. That result doesn't count. Haiku 4.5 had server errors during the job, and my own baseline was running in parallel against the same model. Production doesn't run on Bedrock but on the Anthropic API, so even if the prompt had changed, taking it to production would have been another experiment. The human decision doesn't work as a second reference : of the dataset's news items with a post, 133 were approved and only 3 rejected. Conclusion Back to the opening question: how much does shortening a prompt that already works save me? In my case, nothing, for two reasons. My prompt was already compact, and the experiment's only clean result returned the original. And even if it had been cut by 30%, at 267 calls a month the savings would be cents per year against a job costing several dollars. Shortening prompts is a volume optimization, and it's worth doing the math before launching the job: tokens saved per call, times calls per month, times price per token, against roughly $3 to $6 per template and model. What helped me most from the exercise was seeing how the service reports. In one day I got a +45% improvement that came from failed inferences counted as zero, and a SUCCESS from a job whose optimizer never managed to run. Neither case shows up in the job result. I found them by comparing the text of the returned prompt and checking CloudWatch's error metrics. Something similar happened to me with the Optimization Loop A/B test : the number an optimizer reports has to be verified independently before you make a decision with it. 🚀 Final ProTip : Before optimizing a prompt for cost, calculate the break-even point with your real volume and the price of the model where it runs. If it doesn't pay for itself within a year, there's no point running it for cost; run it only if you have a quality problem to solve. And if you run it, check three things before accepting the result: whether the text changed, how many inferences came back empty, and whether the optimizer logged errors in CloudWatch. Have you measured how many calls a month your production prompts make? Is your volume at the scale where this math actually matters? If anyone is seeing real savings with shortening, I'd really like to know at what volume — the comments are open.
