items.summary_html:
In the AgentCore Optimization Loop article, I let AWS rewrite the system prompt of my DevOps agent. The recommendation was good, but it had an effect I didn't measure at the time: the prompt grew. The optimizer kept everything I had written and added two new blocks.

The Advanced Prompt Optimization documentation acknowledges this: by default it optimizes for quality only, with no length constraint, and an optimized prompt can end up longer than the original. Longer means more input tokens on every call and, potentially, a longer time to first token.

On October 20, 2026, AWS announced an option for that, shortenPrompt, which asks the optimizer for a prompt shorter than the original with an equal or better score. If it can't find one, it gives you yours back.

I wanted to answer a concrete question: how much does shortening a prompt that already works actually save me, and at what volume is it worth it? To find out, I used the real classifier prompt of my news agent, the 205 classifications it made in production as the reference, and three target models. The result wasn't what I expected, and neither were the reasons.

📌 TL;DR — What I found

  • In all six optimizations (three models, with and without shortenPrompt), the prompt the service returned is identical to the original, character for character. compressionRatio = 1.0 on all three models.
  • One job reported a +45% improvement (0.575 → 0.833) for that identical prompt. The cause: 12 failed inferences on the original side, with zero tokens, scored as 0.
  • Another job finished as Completed with SUCCESS even though the optimizer failed on 684 of 689 calls. I only saw it in the CloudWatch error metrics.
  • Even with the 30% cut from the announcement's example, at my volume (~267 calls a month) the job would take between 9 and 55 years to pay for itself.
  • The same prompt with the same news item measures 1,621 tokens on Haiku 5.5, 1,132 on Haiku 4.5, and 917 on Nova 2 Lite. The service counts it as 600 on all three.
What Advanced Prompt Optimization Is and What shortenPrompt Adds

Advanced Prompt Optimization is Bedrock's full optimizer, different from the simple OptimizePrompt. You give it a JSONL file with your templates (variables in double braces, {% raw %}{{variable}}{% endraw %}), up to 100 evaluation samples per template, and an evaluation method: the default judge, free-text criteria (steeringCriteria), an LLM judge with your rubric, or your own Lambda. The service runs an inference, evaluation, and rewrite loop on each target model and returns one optimized prompt per model. A job accepts up to 10 templates and 5 models, and the documentation talks about 15 to 20 minutes for a prompt with few samples and several hours for many. My jobs took 14 and 29 minutes.

shortenPrompt is enabled per template, inside the JSONL, not in the API call:

{
  "version": "bedrock-2026-05-14",
  "templateId": "news-classifier-shorten",
  "promptTemplate": "...",
  "optimizationConfig": { "shortenPrompt": true },
  "customEvaluationMetricLabel": "clasificacion_vs_produccion",
  "evaluationMetricLambdaArn": "arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1::function:apo-news-classification-evaluator",
  "evaluationSamples": [ "..." ]
}

The return logic is simple: the shortened prompt is returned only if it is shorter and scores at least as high as the original. If either condition fails, you get your original prompt back with compressionRatio = 1.0. The ratio is optimizedTokenCount / originalTokenCount, measured on the template and not on the prompt with the variables filled in.

On cost, the documentation says there is no separate service charge: you pay for the tokens it consumes. The pricing page gives the formula: about 16 × N target model inferences per template, where N is the number of samples, plus the optimizer (currently Claude Sonnet 4.6) with 101 × (3700 + 0.35 × P) input tokens, where P is the token count of your template. The optimizer's output tokens have no formula.

The Experiment The prompt: my news agent's classifier

My agent processes the AWS RSS feed three times a day. Since late September the model no longer computes relevance: it only classifies each news item into a topic (topic_tier) and a change type (change_type), and a rubric with editable weights computes the 0 to 10 score. If the score reaches 6, a post is generated; if it reaches 7, the item goes into the newsletter.

I chose this prompt for three reasons. It has an objective answer, so it can be evaluated without a subjective judge. It runs every day, so it has real volume to compute savings against. And it was already compact, about 1,900 characters: if shortening finds something to cut here, it will find it in almost any prompt. A fragment:

topic_tier: el tema al que pertenece el servicio o la capacidad (elige el más específico):
• genai_agentes: Bedrock, IA generativa, agentes, MCP, Amazon Quick, AgentCore, SageMaker AI
• serverless_core: Lambda, Step Functions, API Gateway, EventBridge, DynamoDB
...
change_type: qué tipo de cambio anuncia la noticia (juzga el cambio, no el servicio):
• nueva_capacidad: una función o servicio que antes no existía
• mejora: una mejora incremental de algo que ya existía (límites, rendimiento, integraciones)
...
The reference: what production decided

I didn't label anything by hand. The reference for each news item is the classification production made, stored in DynamoDB: 205 news items classified between September 30 and October 22, 2026. I split the set deterministically, by ID hash: 60 items for the optimizer and 145 as a holdout it never sees.

With this reference I'm not measuring whether the shortened prompt is more accurate, but whether it behaves the same as the current one. For a shortening, that seems like the right question to me: I'm looking for a cheaper prompt that doesn't break anything, which makes it a regression test. The downside is that if production was wrong, the optimizer learns to repeat the mistake.

The evaluator: a deterministic Lambda

Advanced Prompt Optimization offers four ways to evaluate, and I ruled out three. The default judge scores accuracy, completeness, and Expression Quality, and that last criterion rewards short answers, so it would have optimized the brevity of the output instead of the classification. steeringCriteria are too vague for a task with an exact answer. An LLM judge adds cost, because the judge reads prompt, response, and reference on every evaluation, and it adds its own noise to something you can settle by comparing two values.

I went with a Lambda. The contract the service requires is simple: you receive {"preds": [...], "golds": [...]} and return {"score": float, "scores": [...]}, higher is better. My rule: if the output isn't valid JSON with all the allowed keys and values, the sample scores 0; if it is, it gets 0.5 for the right topic and 0.5 for the right change type.

def compute_score(preds, golds):
    """Mandatory JSON contract; 0.5 for the right topic_tier and 0.5 for the right change_type."""
    scores = [score_one(p, g) for p, g in zip(preds, golds)]
    return {"score": sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else 0.0, "scores": scores}

The service reads the docstring as the metric description and reviews the full code before using it. That review cost me my first job; I cover it in the gotchas.

The template: what the optimizer can touch and what it can't

In production the prompt goes in as the system prompt, the news item as the user message, and the output uses Structured Outputs. Advanced Prompt Optimization takes a single text template and doesn't accept structured outputs, so the JSON contract has to live inside the prompt. I protected it with : the optimizer can rewrite the classification instructions, but not the news item or the output format.

{% raw %}Noticia a clasificar:
Título: {{title}}
Descripción: {{description}}

Responde ÚNICAMENTE con un objeto JSON, sin texto antes ni después, con exactamente estas claves:
change_type, topic_tier, topic, reason, keyPoints (lista de textos) y emojis (lista de textos).
En topic_tier y change_type usa solo las claves listadas arriba.{% endraw %}

In the same job I put two identical copies of the template, one optimized for quality only (the default behavior) and one with shortenPrompt: true, to compare them under the same conditions.

Three models and two accounts

This part of the design changed along the way. Since October 8, my agent consumes Claude Haiku 5.5 through the Anthropic API, not through Bedrock. Advanced Prompt Optimization only optimizes Bedrock models, and my working account can't invoke Haiku 5.5 on Bedrock. The account that can hadn't submitted the Anthropic use case form, so Haiku 4.5 didn't run there.

I ended up running one job per account, with the same data and the same evaluator: Claude Haiku 5.5 (the production model) in one, and Claude Haiku 4.5 (the production model until October 8) plus Amazon Nova 2 Lite in the other. Nova is the model I dropped in March because it didn't support structured outputs; since Advanced Prompt Optimization works with plain text, that limitation doesn't matter here. That same missing form ended up affecting the Haiku 5.5 job too, as I explain in Finding 3.

Hypotheses, written before seeing results

I followed the same method as in previous articles: before reading the job results, I wrote down each hypothesis with the criterion that would refute it.

  1. H1 — Shortening finds something to cut. At least one model returns compressionRatio < 0.9. Refuted if all three return 1.0 or a ratio above 0.9.
  2. H2 — The shortened prompt behaves the same on the holdout. The score difference against the original, on the same model, stays within the noise floor. Refuted if it falls below that floor.
  3. H3 — At my volume, the savings don't pay for the job. At ~267 calls a month, the monthly savings don't cover the job cost in under 12 months on any model. Refuted if any model recovers the cost in a year or less.
  4. H4 — Optimized prompts aren't portable. The prompt optimized for one model loses more than the noise floor when run on another. Refuted if they perform the same on all three models.

📋 Recorded deviations: (1) the original design used only Nova 2 Lite, because Haiku 5.5 wasn't available on Bedrock in my working account; (2) I moved to three models split across two accounts; (3) the job runs Haiku 5.5 with its default configuration, which uses thinking, unlike production (see gotchas); (4) the first two jobs failed because of the Lambda code validator; (5) I stopped a job running the old evaluator, and its window overlaps by a few minutes with the good job in that account, which slightly inflates the costs measured there; (6) my holdout baseline ran in parallel with the Haiku 4.5 job.

All the code is at github.com/codecr/bedrock-prompt-shortening: scripts numbered 01 to 07, the evaluator, and the cleanup.

Baseline: How Much the Prompt Differs from Itself

Before looking at any optimized prompt, I ran the original on the 145 holdout news items, twice on each model. The second run matters because the model isn't deterministic: if two variants differ by less than the original prompt differs from itself, that difference means nothing. Haiku 5.5 ran as it does in production, without thinking and with low effort.

Model Score vs production JSON contract Agrees with itself Tokens in / out Median TTFT Cost per 1,000 calls Claude Haiku 5.5 0.848 100% 133/145 (91.7%) 1,621 / 334 1.11 s $0.36 Claude Haiku 4.5 0.840 100% 128/145 (88.3%) 1,132 / 284 0.66 s $2.81 Amazon Nova 2 Lite 0.760 100% 140/145 (96.6%) 917 / 191 0.47 s $0.83

Nova is the most stable and the one that agrees least with production: it repeats its answer 96.6% of the time, but being consistent doesn't make it more accurate. Haiku 5.5 doesn't reach 1.0 even against references it mostly generated itself, because in production it runs with a separate system prompt and structured outputs, and changing how you call the model already moves the result. And the noise floor is high: the same prompt changes the classification of between 5 and 17 of 145 news items from one run to the next. An improvement smaller than that can't be told apart from chance.

A business data point: with the active rubric, Haiku 5.5's classification changes the decision to generate a post on 10 of the 145 news items compared with what production decided. That margin of error already exists in my pipeline today, and I hadn't measured it.

🔢 ProTip #1: The same text doesn't measure the same on every model. My prompt with the same news item is 1,621 tokens on Haiku 5.5 versus 1,132 on Haiku 4.5: 43% more. Before calculating how much trimming a prompt saves you, measure its tokens on the model where it will run. And don't use the job's originalTokenCount for that: the service counted my template as 600 tokens on all three models, with its own count that isn't the tokenizer you're billed for.

Finding 1: Six Optimizations, Zero Changes

This is the complete result of the two jobs. "Identical" means identical character for character to the original, once the tags are removed, which the service always strips.

Model Template Original score → "optimized" compressionRatio Failed inferences (orig / opt) Did the prompt change? Haiku 5.5 quality 0.808 → 0.850 — 0 / 0 No Haiku 5.5 shorten 0.825 → 0.825 1.0 0 / 0 No Haiku 4.5 quality 0.575 → 0.833 — 12 / 0 No Haiku 4.5 shorten 0.625 → 0.625 1.0 13 / 13 No Nova 2 Lite quality 0.708 → 0.708 — 1 / 1 No Nova 2 Lite shorten 0.708 → 0.708 1.0 0 / 0 No

H1 is refuted: no model returned a ratio below 1.0. But of the six rows, only the two Nova rows are a clean result.

On Nova 2 Lite the optimizer worked, the model answered almost every inference, and the service found neither a better prompt nor a shorter one that scored as high. For a prompt that was already compact, evaluated with a strict criterion, that's a reasonable answer: there was nothing to cut without losing quality. When it returns the original, the service copies the original's measurement into the "optimized" metrics, which is why both columns match down to the last decimal.

Haiku 4.5 and Haiku 5.5 aren't clean cases, for two different reasons the job result doesn't mention.

Finding 2: The +45% That Never Existed

Back to the third row. For Haiku 4.5, optimizing for quality only, the job summary reports that the score rose from 0.575 to 0.833, a 45% gain, and that average time to first token dropped from 1.12 s to 0.60 s. The "optimized" prompt is identical to the original.

I went through the results file sample by sample. On the original side, 12 of the 60 inferences came back empty: a blank response, inputTokens: 0, outputTokens: 0, zero latency. The evaluator received an empty string, which isn't valid JSON, and scored it 0. On the "optimized" side none failed. The entire improvement comes from those 12 failed calls.

Bedrock's CloudWatch metrics show what happened: during the job window, Haiku 4.5 logged 607 server errors (InvocationServerErrors). Some may be mine: my holdout baseline ran 230 calls against the same model in parallel, and my client retried 5xx errors. But the job's 25 empty inferences belong to the job. The quota wasn't the problem: Haiku 4.5 has 10,000 requests per minute in that account.

There's another detail in that same row. Even excluding the 12 failures, the original scores 0.719 versus 0.833 for the same text in the same job. It's the same noise floor as the baseline, now inside the job: with 60 samples and a model that agrees with itself 88% of the time, two measurements of the same prompt differ by more than 10 points.

🚨 ProTip #2: Don't trust the summary's averageScore. Before accepting an optimized prompt, do two things the service doesn't do for you: compare the prompt text against the original (in my six cases it was identical), and count how many samples in dataset[] have outputTokens: 0. A failed inference enters the average as one more 0.0, and in my case it produced a 45% improvement on a prompt that didn't change. The repo's 05_fetch_results.py script runs both checks.

Finding 3: SUCCESS Without an Optimizer

The Haiku 5.5 job finished as Completed, with both entries at SUCCESS, no errors in the results file, and a +5% improvement on the quality template (0.808 → 0.850) for, once again, a prompt identical to the original. That +5% is the size of how much the same prompt varies against itself: in my baseline, Haiku 5.5 changed the classification of 12 of 145 news items between two runs. On its own it says nothing. The problem was in the optimizer's metrics.

Haiku 5.5 ran 1,925 inferences during the job window. The pricing formula predicts 16 × 60 × 2 = 1,920: the target model did exactly the expected work. But the optimizer, Claude Sonnet 4.6, logged 689 invocations and 684 client errors (InvocationClientErrors), with only 7,756 input tokens in total. In the other account, the same optimizer consumed 2.49 million tokens.

I found the cause by invoking Sonnet 4.6 by hand in that account: "Model use case details have not been submitted for this account". It's the same Anthropic form that kept me from using Haiku 4.5 there. The optimizer runs with my credentials, not a service role, and my account couldn't invoke it. The job didn't catch it at creation, and didn't report it in failureMessage or in the result entries. It evaluated the original prompt, couldn't generate candidates, and handed it back to me with SUCCESS.

This kind of failure is hard to spot because the result looks normal. If I hadn't checked CloudWatch to calculate costs, I would have written that Haiku 5.5 found nothing to cut.

🔍 ProTip #3: Advanced Prompt Optimization doesn't use a service role: it invokes the target models, the optimizer, and your Lambda with the credentials of whoever creates the job (Forward Access Session). Before launching a job, verify that your account can invoke Claude Sonnet 4.6 with a test call. At job creation the service validates that you can invoke the target models ("No inference API is accessible for model"), but it doesn't validate the optimizer. And after each job, check InvocationClientErrors for us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6 in Bedrock's CloudWatch metrics.

Finding 4: Would It Have Been Worth It?

No prompt changed, so there are no measured savings. Even so, the original question can be answered with the jobs' real costs, assuming shortening had achieved the announcement's example: compressionRatio = 0.7, 30% fewer tokens in the template.

According to CloudWatch, the jobs consumed:

Model Role in the job Invocations Tokens in / out Cost Claude Sonnet 4.6 Optimizer (4 pairs) 384 2,488,824 / 262,585 $12.55 Claude Haiku 4.5 Target 3,396 3,152,146 / 766,911 $7.69 Amazon Nova 2 Lite Target 2,811 2,673,178 / 553,897 $2.41 Claude Haiku 5.5 Target 1,925 3,107,401 / 1,021,435 $0.90 Claude Sonnet 4.6 Failed optimizer (2 pairs) 689 7,756 / 2,733 $0.07

Total: $23.61, plus about $1.40 for the holdout validation. The Haiku 4.5 and Nova figures include a few minutes of the job I stopped, so a clean job comes out somewhat cheaper. The optimizer is the most expensive part: about $3.14 per template-model pair.

With that data I calculated the cost of optimizing one template for one model and what it would save per month at my real volume (205 news items in 23 days, about 267 calls a month), with the 30% cut applied to the template's 600 tokens:

Model Job cost (1 template) Savings per month Pays for itself in Calls per month to pay for it in one month Claude Haiku 5.5 $3.48 $0.0053 55 years 175,955 Claude Haiku 4.5 $5.83 $0.0529 9 years 29,453 Amazon Nova 2 Lite $3.93 $0.0159 21 years 66,168

H3 is confirmed by a wide margin. The table also shows that shortening pays off more on the more expensive model: Haiku 4.5 costs 10 times more per input token than Haiku 5.5 on Bedrock. On the production model, which is the cheapest, shortening matters less. My table slightly underestimates the Haiku 5.5 savings, because it calculates on the 600 tokens the service counts and not on the ones its tokenizer bills; even correcting for that, the order of magnitude doesn't change.

This doesn't mean shortening is useless; it means the math depends more on volume than on the cut percentage. At about 30,000 calls a month on Haiku 4.5, or about 176,000 on Haiku 5.5, the job pays for itself in a month. At 267, it doesn't.

As for latency, the other benefit the announcement mentions, I have nothing to measure: without a shorter prompt there's no TTFT difference. The improvement the job summary shows (1.12 s → 0.60 s on Haiku 4.5) is two measurements of the same text, taken while the model was returning server errors; I don't attribute it to the prompt.

What the Documentation Doesn't Tell You

Beyond the findings above, these are the gotchas that cost me a job or a good while.

🧪 ProTip #4: In modelConfigurations, the additionalModelRequestFields field only accepts topK. I tried passing thinking: disabled and output_config.effort: low for Haiku 5.5, the way I run it in production, and the job was rejected at creation: "contains unsupported keys: [output_config, thinking]. Supported keys: [topK]". The optimizer tunes the prompt for Haiku 5.5 with its default configuration, which uses thinking: on a sample of 12 news items that meant 57% more output tokens and 0.75 s more latency than the production configuration, with the same score. In practice, you're optimizing for a different configuration than the one you'll run.

🛑 ProTip #5: The service reviews your Lambda evaluator's code before using it, and rejects it if it finds anything it considers dangerous. My first job failed with "Metric code validation failed: Uses potentially dangerous builtin: compile()" because of a re.compile(): the analysis doesn't distinguish the re method from the compile builtin. Use re.match(pattern, text) directly. The job doesn't fail at creation either: it fails about three minutes later, with a generic failureMessage that points you to the results file in S3, where the real per-entry reason is.

⏱️ ProTip #6: A job's terminal states are Completed, Failed, Stopped, and PartiallyCompleted. The official sample's wait loop only considers the first three, so with a partial result it waits forever.

I also found some differences between the user guide and the real API:

  • The delete operation is BatchDeleteAdvancedPromptOptimizationJob, singular (the guide uses the plural), and it returns advancedPromptOptimizationJobs[] and errors[].
  • The ListAdvancedPromptOptimizationJobs response uses the jobSummaries key, not the one shown in the guide's example.
  • The encryption parameter is called encryptionKeyArn, not encryptionConfig.
  • The evaluation page asks for a resource-based policy so bedrock.amazonaws.com can invoke your Lambda; the prerequisites page says the service invokes it with your credentials. I configured both.
Hypothesis Verdicts
Hypothesis Result H1 — Shortening finds something to cut Refuted. compressionRatio = 1.0 on all three models. The only clean result, Nova 2 Lite, returned the original. H2 — The shortened prompt behaves the same on the holdout Couldn't be tested. There was no shortened prompt. H3 — At my volume, the savings don't pay for the job Confirmed. Not even with a hypothetical 30% cut: between 9 and 55 years. H4 — Optimized prompts aren't portable Couldn't be tested. The six "optimized" prompts are the original.

Two of the four hypotheses went untested. The portability matrix I had ready made no sense with six identical prompts, so I didn't run it.

Limits of the Experiment
  • One template, one domain. My prompt was already compact and the task has an exact answer. With a long, redundant prompt, shortening would probably cut something. I didn't run that positive control, so I can't separate "the service doesn't cut" from "my prompt had nothing to cut." The Nova case suggests the latter.
  • The reference is production, not the truth. I'm measuring regression, not accuracy.
  • 60 samples and a single job per model. I don't know how much the optimizer varies between runs of the same job.
  • Haiku 5.5 was optimized with a different configuration than production, and its job had no working optimizer. That result doesn't count.
  • Haiku 4.5 had server errors during the job, and my own baseline was running in parallel against the same model.
  • Production doesn't run on Bedrock but on the Anthropic API, so even if the prompt had changed, taking it to production would have been another experiment.
  • The human decision doesn't work as a second reference: of the dataset's news items with a post, 133 were approved and only 3 rejected.
Conclusion

Back to the opening question: how much does shortening a prompt that already works save me?

In my case, nothing, for two reasons. My prompt was already compact, and the experiment's only clean result returned the original. And even if it had been cut by 30%, at 267 calls a month the savings would be cents per year against a job costing several dollars. Shortening prompts is a volume optimization, and it's worth doing the math before launching the job: tokens saved per call, times calls per month, times price per token, against roughly $3 to $6 per template and model.

What helped me most from the exercise was seeing how the service reports. In one day I got a +45% improvement that came from failed inferences counted as zero, and a SUCCESS from a job whose optimizer never managed to run. Neither case shows up in the job result. I found them by comparing the text of the returned prompt and checking CloudWatch's error metrics.

Something similar happened to me with the Optimization Loop A/B test: the number an optimizer reports has to be verified independently before you make a decision with it.

🚀 Final ProTip: Before optimizing a prompt for cost, calculate the break-even point with your real volume and the price of the model where it runs. If it doesn't pay for itself within a year, there's no point running it for cost; run it only if you have a quality problem to solve. And if you run it, check three things before accepting the result: whether the text changed, how many inferences came back empty, and whether the optimizer logged errors in CloudWatch.

Have you measured how many calls a month your production prompts make? Is your volume at the scale where this math actually matters? If anyone is seeing real savings with shortening, I'd really like to know at what volume — the comments are open.

See you in the next article! 🚀

items.title: Continue, compact, fork or start fresh? A 120-run coding-agent experiment
items.summary: When a coding agent finishes a task, should the next task continue the conversation, compact it, fork it, or start fresh? We compared five session strategies across two models and two rounds: 120 runs . There was no universal winner. Keeping history could be expensive without improving delivery in one model, yet faster in another. Experiment design Every strategy received the same target instructions, repository, documentation and evidence. Fresh meant no inherited chat, not an empty project. Fresh: start from the task and repository. Continue: retain the full conversation. Compact: continue after native compaction. Fork: copy history into a new session identity. Fresh + summary: start fresh with a shared, frozen handoff summary generated by Sol. Two rounds × two models × two target tasks × five strategies × three repetitions = 120 runs. Models were gpt-6.1-sol (medium) and deepseek-flash (medium requested, high resolved by the runtime; displayed as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash). History came from real development. The second round used more complex prior work—durable queues, idempotency, leases, cancellation and recovery—but was not longer . Sol history went from roughly 442k to 425k tokens; DeepSeek from 331k to 295k. This is not a controlled context-length staircase. The target tasks were E2E verification of an existing export feature, including honest reporting of expected failures, and a redaction bugfix. The fix had to preserve structural identities and raw diff comparisons while using redacted text for both display and layout width. One group, all five strategies Sol · complex prior-work round · E2E verification : Strategy Mean recorded cost/run (USD) Median minutes Complete deliveries Fresh $0.194 2.7 3/3 Continue $2.293 14.0 3/3 Compact ≥$0.548 6.8 2/3 Fork $3.813 14.2 3/3 Fresh + summary $0.207 2.6 3/3 The ≥ value is a recorded lower bound after interruption. Failed attempts remain in the means. Summary preparation and prior development are excluded. In this group, full history increased cost and time without adding completed deliveries. That ordering did not generalize: in DeepSeek's complex-round E2E, Fresh took 6.8 minutes, Continue 3.0, and Fork 2.2, all with 3/3 complete deliveries. Cache hits do not make an entire task cheap For Sol's complex-round E2E, Continue averaged $1.266 in cache-read cost alone , versus $0.194 for the entire Fresh run —about 6.5×. This compares task-level costs, not token unit prices. Continue cumulatively read about 6.33 million cached tokens per run across repeated calls. Full-history groups produced roughly 2.8–3.8× the output tokens of Fresh. Traces contained longer verification, scripts and repeated checks; we cannot label every additional step unnecessary. A long-input pricing tier also contributed. Repricing the same recorded usage without its surcharge attributed about 47% of Continue's and 49% of Fork's recorded cost to the tier in this group. Pricing effects are not evidence of “context gravity.” A summary remains a hypothesis Fresh + summary was close to Fresh for Sol. In DeepSeek's complex E2E it cost about $0.082 and took 4.1 minutes, versus $0.103 and 6.8 minutes for Fresh. Yet across both bugfix rounds, summary runs passed functional checks 4/6, versus 6/6 for Fresh. We would try a fresh session with a short summary first. The experiments have not shown it is the best choice. We used a shared frozen summary rather than a newly tailored summary for each target task; the main comparison excludes preparation cost. Correctness and measurement boundaries Of 120 runs, 102 completed successfully . The other 18 comprised 14 runtime failures/timeouts and four completed runs with functional boundary defects. Some interrupted runs already passed code acceptance but had not finished the delivery protocol. Defects included visible paths mistakenly treated as immutable identities, and layout width calculated from original text after display redaction. The latter violates the task boundary; it does not by itself demonstrate a plaintext leak. Three repetitions per group used one fixed development history per round. Four E2E judgments were corrected after manual review of permitted verification-script locations; original judgments were retained and models were not rerun. Cache warmth, routing and host load were not fully controlled. Costs are fixed-rate API-equivalent estimates , not current prices or subscription bills. They include recorded uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output, plus native compaction. Recorded cache writes were zero; incomplete usage can understate interrupted-run costs. We have neither established a stable best strategy nor identified a context-gravity threshold. Next we want to test task-specific summaries, count preparation costs, and examine decisions that exist only in old chat rather than repository files. Originally published on the Sunny Code engineering blog , with interactive comparisons, methodology and downloadable aggregate data.
items.summary_html:
When a coding agent finishes a task, should the next task continue the conversation, compact it, fork it, or start fresh?

We compared five session strategies across two models and two rounds: 120 runs. There was no universal winner. Keeping history could be expensive without improving delivery in one model, yet faster in another.

Experiment design

Every strategy received the same target instructions, repository, documentation and evidence. Fresh meant no inherited chat, not an empty project.

  • Fresh: start from the task and repository.
  • Continue: retain the full conversation.
  • Compact: continue after native compaction.
  • Fork: copy history into a new session identity.
  • Fresh + summary: start fresh with a shared, frozen handoff summary generated by Sol.

Two rounds × two models × two target tasks × five strategies × three repetitions = 120 runs. Models were gpt-6.1-sol (medium) and deepseek-flash (medium requested, high resolved by the runtime; displayed as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash).

History came from real development. The second round used more complex prior work—durable queues, idempotency, leases, cancellation and recovery—but was not longer. Sol history went from roughly 442k to 425k tokens; DeepSeek from 331k to 295k. This is not a controlled context-length staircase.

The target tasks were E2E verification of an existing export feature, including honest reporting of expected failures, and a redaction bugfix. The fix had to preserve structural identities and raw diff comparisons while using redacted text for both display and layout width.

One group, all five strategies

Sol · complex prior-work round · E2E verification:

Strategy Mean recorded cost/run (USD) Median minutes Complete deliveries Fresh $0.194 2.7 3/3 Continue $2.293 14.0 3/3 Compact ≥$0.548 6.8 2/3 Fork $3.813 14.2 3/3 Fresh + summary $0.207 2.6 3/3

The ≥ value is a recorded lower bound after interruption. Failed attempts remain in the means. Summary preparation and prior development are excluded.

In this group, full history increased cost and time without adding completed deliveries. That ordering did not generalize: in DeepSeek's complex-round E2E, Fresh took 6.8 minutes, Continue 3.0, and Fork 2.2, all with 3/3 complete deliveries.

Cache hits do not make an entire task cheap

For Sol's complex-round E2E, Continue averaged $1.266 in cache-read cost alone, versus $0.194 for the entire Fresh run—about 6.5×. This compares task-level costs, not token unit prices.

Continue cumulatively read about 6.33 million cached tokens per run across repeated calls. Full-history groups produced roughly 2.8–3.8× the output tokens of Fresh. Traces contained longer verification, scripts and repeated checks; we cannot label every additional step unnecessary.

A long-input pricing tier also contributed. Repricing the same recorded usage without its surcharge attributed about 47% of Continue's and 49% of Fork's recorded cost to the tier in this group. Pricing effects are not evidence of “context gravity.”

A summary remains a hypothesis

Fresh + summary was close to Fresh for Sol. In DeepSeek's complex E2E it cost about $0.082 and took 4.1 minutes, versus $0.103 and 6.8 minutes for Fresh. Yet across both bugfix rounds, summary runs passed functional checks 4/6, versus 6/6 for Fresh.

We would try a fresh session with a short summary first. The experiments have not shown it is the best choice. We used a shared frozen summary rather than a newly tailored summary for each target task; the main comparison excludes preparation cost.

Correctness and measurement boundaries

Of 120 runs, 102 completed successfully. The other 18 comprised 14 runtime failures/timeouts and four completed runs with functional boundary defects. Some interrupted runs already passed code acceptance but had not finished the delivery protocol.

Defects included visible paths mistakenly treated as immutable identities, and layout width calculated from original text after display redaction. The latter violates the task boundary; it does not by itself demonstrate a plaintext leak.

Three repetitions per group used one fixed development history per round. Four E2E judgments were corrected after manual review of permitted verification-script locations; original judgments were retained and models were not rerun. Cache warmth, routing and host load were not fully controlled.

Costs are fixed-rate API-equivalent estimates, not current prices or subscription bills. They include recorded uncached input, cache reads, cache writes and output, plus native compaction. Recorded cache writes were zero; incomplete usage can understate interrupted-run costs.

We have neither established a stable best strategy nor identified a context-gravity threshold. Next we want to test task-specific summaries, count preparation costs, and examine decisions that exist only in old chat rather than repository files.

Originally published on the Sunny Code engineering blog, with interactive comparisons, methodology and downloadable aggregate data.

items.title: What smart people are saying about Anthropic's IPO paperwork
items.summary: Anthropic, led by Dario Amodei, filed its S-1 paperwork in Monday. Bloomberg/Getty Images Anthropic filed its S-1 on Monday, revealing the company's internal financials. Investors, researchers, and tech onlookers shared their thoughts. Some applied S-1 learnings to their own industries, like startups and venture capital. Anthropic is ready to IPO. Analysts and onlookers are weighing in. On Monday, the AI lab filed its hotly anticipated S-1 paperwork . The prospectus offered an inside look at Anthropic's financials: a net loss of about $42 billion in 2025 and revenue of $4.6 billion. It plans to trade under the ticker symbol ANT. The S-1 sets the stage for a blockbuster IPO . Here's what smart people are saying about Anthropic's filing: Sarah Guo, founder of Conviction Conviction founder Sarah Guo said she was interested to see how Anthropic's mission changes (or doesn't) after going public. Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference Venture capitalist Sarah Guo opened her X post with a big "CONGRATS" to Anthropic on the S-1 filing. Guo shared her first takeaways: the inflection in operating profit, the focus on novel discovery, the mismatch between consumption-based revenue and long-term compute obligations, and more. "I am curious to see how 1) a company with strong mission changes - or doesn't - how it operates under quarterly public inspection and 2) how public opinion may change when retail owns a piece of the upside," Guo wrote. Ann Bordetsky, founder of Elora Capital Ann Bordetsky said that the S-1 set a "(high) bar." Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch Ann Bordetsky was a partner at New Enterprise Associates' technology practice before founding her own firm, Elora Capital. She wrote on X that the S-1 was a "juicy read." The filing will set "a (high) bar for how capital markets evaluate AI startups," Bordetsky wrote. SemiAnalysis SemiAnalysis, the research firm founded by Dylan Patel , posted the "most mind blowing stat" it had seen in the S-1. It cited Anthropic's raised capital, compared to its cash and investments. Anthropic is "growing at a rapid pace" and "profitable on an operating income basis as of the June quarter," SemiAnalysis wrote. "This is likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism," the firm wrote. Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital Altimeter is invested in Anthropic. Gerstner quickly congratulated the team. Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images Brad Gerstner heaped his praise on Anthropic. He congratulated the team on "another important milestone!" Altimeter will partner with Anthropic through "major participation in the IPO on top of our existing ownership," Gerstner wrote. He used an American flag and a rocket emoji. Gerstner's venture capital firm is a longtime investor in Anthropic, co-leading the AI lab's Series H in May. Vivek Gopalan, partner at 8VC Vivek Gopalan is an investor at 8VC, the venture capital firm cofounded by Joe Lonsdale . items.summary_html:
Anthropic, led by Dario Amodei, filed its S-1 paperwork in Monday.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • Anthropic filed its S-1 on Monday, revealing the company's internal financials.
  • Investors, researchers, and tech onlookers shared their thoughts.
  • Some applied S-1 learnings to their own industries, like startups and venture capital.

Anthropic is ready to IPO. Analysts and onlookers are weighing in.

On Monday, the AI lab filed its hotly anticipated S-1 paperwork. The prospectus offered an inside look at Anthropic's financials: a net loss of about $42 billion in 2025 and revenue of $4.6 billion. It plans to trade under the ticker symbol ANT.

The S-1 sets the stage for a blockbuster IPO. Here's what smart people are saying about Anthropic's filing:

Sarah Guo, founder of ConvictionConviction founder Sarah Guo said she was interested to see how Anthropic's mission changes (or doesn't) after going public.

Big Event Media/Getty Images for HumanX Conference

Venture capitalist Sarah Guo opened her X post with a big "CONGRATS" to Anthropic on the S-1 filing.

Guo shared her first takeaways: the inflection in operating profit, the focus on novel discovery, the mismatch between consumption-based revenue and long-term compute obligations, and more.

"I am curious to see how 1) a company with strong mission changes - or doesn't - how it operates under quarterly public inspection and 2) how public opinion may change when retail owns a piece of the upside," Guo wrote.

Ann Bordetsky, founder of Elora CapitalAnn Bordetsky said that the S-1 set a "(high) bar."

Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch

Ann Bordetsky was a partner at New Enterprise Associates' technology practice before founding her own firm, Elora Capital. She wrote on X that the S-1 was a "juicy read."

The filing will set "a (high) bar for how capital markets evaluate AI startups," Bordetsky wrote.

SemiAnalysis

SemiAnalysis, the research firm founded by Dylan Patel, posted the "most mind blowing stat" it had seen in the S-1. It cited Anthropic's raised capital, compared to its cash and investments.

Anthropic is "growing at a rapid pace" and "profitable on an operating income basis as of the June quarter," SemiAnalysis wrote.

"This is likely the most efficient scaling of a business in the history of capitalism," the firm wrote.

Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter CapitalAltimeter is invested in Anthropic. Gerstner quickly congratulated the team.

Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images

Brad Gerstner heaped his praise on Anthropic. He congratulated the team on "another important milestone!"

Altimeter will partner with Anthropic through "major participation in the IPO on top of our existing ownership," Gerstner wrote. He used an American flag and a rocket emoji.

items.title: Claude Code’s top enterprise users outspend other Claude users 20 to 1, Anthropic’s IPO filing says
items.summary: Anthropic’s IPO filing makes Claude Code the center of its enterprise growth story. The company on Monday filed to go public on Nasdaq. Its S-1 says the average Claude Enterprise user without Claude Code spent less than $75 a month in the third quarter. The top 5% of Claude Code users on Enterprise spent about 20 times that. Anthropic’s S-1 prospectus spells out a classic land-and-expand play, with Claude Code doing the landing. An engineer picks up Claude Code, likes it, and starts pushing it internally. Anthropic’s sales team show up later, and by then, the filing says, “Claude is often already in use.” Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like” Anthropic calls Claude Code “the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like” and says non-technical teams are adopting it too. That’s wild for a tool that started in the terminal. The revenue lines up with that story: Anthropic says it had more than 11,900 customers paying $100,000 or more over the trailing 12 months as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 a year earlier. Revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same stretch of 2025. Token usage accounted for 50% of that. Anthropic’s own engineers? Claude wrote more than 90% of the contributions to the company’s codebase in September, according to the filing. Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic Anthropic also says the average engineer produced more than 45 times as much code per day in the third quarter as in 2024. Anthropic says its engineers increasingly direct and review Claude’s work, though it doesn’t define “contributions” or say how much human review that code gets. I’ve been building one project a week with Claude Code, and I hardly know what I’m doing. The potential velocity is very real. The S-1 also explains why Anthropic cares about Claude Code beyond coding. The company sells the software that runs Claude Code to other developers. “A model alone is not an agent,” the S-1 says. Developers can run Anthropic’s harness on their own servers through the Agent SDK, or pay Anthropic to run it as Claude Managed Agents. That puts Anthropic closer to the companies building coding agents on top of its models. TNS covered how GitHub and Anthropic used their own agents for major Rust rewrites with very different playbooks, and how AWS open-sourced an agent it says is 45% cheaper than Claude Code and Codex . The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models. The S-1 names Google and OpenAI as Anthropic’s primary competitors in frontier models. Cursor, Replit, and Cognition don’t appear in it. In its risk factors, Anthropic lists Claude Code among the critical tools in its own development work, so problems with the product “could directly impair our ability to develop and deploy future models.” It also warns that as Claude takes on more engineering and research, the company “may lose visibility across certain processes in a way that may become difficult for any individual or group of humans to understand and control.” That sits alongside Anthropic’s public call to pace the frontier, a stance Dario Amodei says may have cost the company an AI lead . Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The filing doesn’t include a price range.

items.title: DDR5 Costs Five Times More. My 2013 Workstation Runs a 125B Model Anyway.
items.summary: 38 to 48 tokens per second from a Xeon without AVX2 and two 2017 GPUs, and what three home PCs taught me about where local LLM speed really comes from. The X79 up close: two used Titan Xp cards from 2017, the Xeon’s cooler at the top right and, on the left, a four-slot M.2 adapter of which this 2011 board can use only the first slot. “Many people show off by spending thousands of euros on technology built by someone else, just to keep up with fashion. I dig into technology to squeeze everything out of it, recycling included.” That is how I described my approach this week, and I think it is a fairly cyberpunk way to do AI at home. William Gibson put it better in 1982: the street finds its own uses for things. This year, recycling is also a matter of money. Memory used to be the part nobody worried about when building a PC; in a year it has become one of the most expensive. In Germany, DDR5 kits cost 5.4 times their July 2025 price in September, and DDR4, the usual way out, keeps climbing too ( 3DCenter’s index ). The memory makers are moving their capacity to AI data centers, and home PCs get what is left. The optimistic forecasts see relief at the end of 2027, when new fabs start producing ( Counterpoint ). I don’t believe it. Samsung has told its investors that supply will be even tighter in 2027 ( TweakTown ), and TrendForce warns that PCs could get less DRAM next year, not more, as capacity moves to servers. I expect it to get worse before it gets better. If at the end of 2027 a 32 GB DDR5 kit costs less in Germany than the roughly €500 it costs today, I was wrong. Until then, the cheapest way into local AI is likely to be hardware that already exists. Mine is an ASUS P9X79 board (2011) with a 12-core Xeon E5–2697 v2 (2013), a workstation platform I have owned for years. Every now and then I box it up, every now and then I take it out again. In August it got two used NVIDIA Titan Xp cards (2017) for Dumpster Inference , the first part of this series. This week it got 64 GB of DDR3 and an NVMe drive on a PCIe adapter, and I asked it to run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model . It answered at 38 tokens per second with IQ3_S, the most accurate of the three quantized files I tried, and at 48.6 with the 2-bit one. Then I did what I always do before believing a number: I ran the same engine, the same model files and the same scripts on two more machines in my house. The comparison taught me more than the headline did. The machine and what it cost What the X79 cost me in October 2026, next to asking prices for the same parts on 23 October 2026 (eBay Italy and Germany, Subito, Idealo; listings, not completed sales). The core of the machine, with twelve cores, 64 GB of RAM on four channels and 24 GB of VRAM, cost me €750. At today’s asking prices it is €710–910, about the price of a single new RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (€720–780), and the two GPUs are two-thirds of it. The CPU is old in a way that matters. It is an Ivy Bridge part with AVX but no AVX2 and no FMA , the instructions most local-inference software expects. The Titan Xp is Pascal: no tensor cores, no BF16. Together they are close to the oldest hardware the engine I used can still run on. The engine: why a 125B model fits at all Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is far too big for 24 GB of VRAM. In early September, on my fastest PC (then an RTX 4070 and an RTX 5060 Ti, 28 GB of VRAM), llama.cpp ran its 1-bit version at 5.5 tokens per second , with most experts on the CPU and no speculative decoding. Strata is an open-source (MIT) engine built for exactly this model. The model has 48 layers with 512 small “experts” each, 24,576 in all, and every token goes through 10 of them in each layer, plus one shared expert. Strata keeps the most-used experts on the GPUs and adapts that cache to the conversation. It keeps every expert in RAM, and the CPU computes the few the GPUs don’t have, at the same time. It also drafts a few tokens ahead with the model’s own small prediction layer (MTP) and checks them in one pass. A 28.8 GB n-gram lookup table stays on the SSD, and a few rows of it are read for every token. The quantized weights come from ISTA-DASLab at three sizes: IQ2_XS (2-bit), IQ3_XXS (3-bit) and IQ3_S, whose experts are stored at 3.33 bits per weight and which Strata describes as matching the full model on the published tests. Strata’s documentation is candid about old hardware. The AVX-only CPU path is experimental, and the authors write that it is “untested on a real old CPU by us” ( INSTALL.md ). They forced that path on a modern Ryzen, with a deliberately small expert cache, and got 11–17 tokens per second; “an old Xeon with DDR3 will be slower than these” , they add. Contributors had run earlier versions on a Xeon E5–2680 (2.87 tokens per second with a GTX 1080 Ti) and on E5–2687W and X5690 machines, and the Xeons in the project’s community benchmarks are 2014–2016 parts with AVX2. So this X79 is, as far as I can tell, the first published measurement of the current engine on the kind of machine that path was written for. Results on the X79 Strata 0.1.45 on the X79: 32K context, no vision, every expert in RAM, model on NVMe over PCIe. Medians of six runs. For large models I use a simple bar: above 10 tokens per second, a model is usable for real work. The 2013 machine clears it almost four times over, even with the largest file. In every run it also found a password hidden at line 211 of a 320-line, 11,864-token log. That is a recall check, not a quality test, but it shows that the long prompt really is read. Three machines, one engine This is the part that changed my mind. I ran the same IQ2_XS files, the same Strata version and the same scripts on two more PCs in my house, all three from NVMe drives: soft-14 (2019): Ryzen 7 3700X, 64 GB DDR4 (four modules of a 3600 kit, running at 3000 MT/s), 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (Blackwell), 32 GB of VRAM. soft-2 (2020): Ryzen 5 5600X, 32 GB DDR4–3600, RTX 3060 + RTX 4070 (Ampere and Ada), 24 GB of VRAM, the same as the X79. The same engine, model files and scripts on three machines (IQ2_XS, 32K context). The ranges of the six runs and the soft-2 caveat are in the notes under the table. For months I had argued that, for local inference, memory bandwidth matters more than the GPU. I measured it on this same X79 platform in August: with llama.cpp and the experts on the CPU, bandwidth and AVX2 decided everything. Here the X79 has 50% more RAM bandwidth than soft-14 and 22% more VRAM bandwidth per card, and it still runs at 57–68% of soft-14’s speed, depending on the file: The X79 against soft-14 with each file: 57–68% of the speed, with 50% more RAM bandwidth. My next suspect was the age of the GPUs, and soft-2 complicates that. Its GPUs are two and three generations newer than the Titans, with tensor cores, and its CPU is modern, with AVX2. In the same low-RAM mode, with the same 24 GB of VRAM and similar RAM bandwidth, it runs at 43.9 tokens per second against the X79’s 43.7 , and the ranges overlap. The two machines differ in five things at once, so some effects may cancel out, but a newer architecture on its own clearly did not buy much here. What soft-14 has more of is expert cache . Its two 16 GB cards hold about 16,000 experts; the Titans hold 10,500 and soft-2’s cards 9,800. In a split, each card keeps its own copy of the dense weights and its own prompt buffers, so 24 GB on two cards is far from 24 GB of cache. On soft-14, 1–3% of the experts a token needs are missing from the cache; on the other two, about 5%. That is several times as many experts left to the CPU, on machines whose RAM is slow. What the gap is made of That was a hypothesis, so on Sunday morning I tested it on the X79 and soft-14, on the same day, with the same files and scripts. I asked three questions. Is it the cache? I cut soft-14’s expert cache down to about the X79’s size and left everything else as it was: First test, 25 October: soft-14 with its expert cache cut to about the X79’s size, everything else unchanged. The smaller cache cost soft-14 15%, about half of its lead over the X79. The other half is the rest of the machine: Blackwell against Pascal, an AVX2 Zen 2 against an AVX-only Ivy Bridge for the experts the cache misses, CUDA 13 against the experimental CUDA 12 path. Strata’s documentation says that “More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU” . On my machines, that explains half of the gap. Is it the speculative decoding? Drafting tokens ahead could flatter one machine more than the other, even with the same share of drafts accepted, because the fixed cost of each check weighs differently on a fast step and on a slow one. So I switched the draft layer off on both, each at its normal cache size: Second test: MTP drafts on and off, each machine at its normal cache size. On my mixed prompts, drafting is worth about a third more speed on both machines, and it does not change the comparison. What about the number on Strata’s README? It is the first thing a reader sees: a single RTX 5070 12 GB, with a Ryzen 5 7600 and DDR5, writes 79 tokens per second with IQ2_XS, more than soft-14 does with two cards. But that figure comes from a coding-agent prompt, greedy decoding and 256 generated tokens ( the 0.1.26 speed report ), and on code the draft layer guesses far better: 77–85% of drafts accepted in those runs, 62–64% in mine. Their prompts are not published, so I built the same kind of test from an excerpt of Strata’s own source code: Third test: a coding-agent style prompt on my two machines, next to the RTX 5070 figure in Strata’s README (different engine version, operating system and prompt text). On the same kind of work, soft-14 is ahead of the 5070 and the X79 reaches 62% of soft-14. Strata’s own benchmark tool tells the same story in its chat test: 52.7 tokens per second on the X79, 90.4 on soft-14. The 5070 also tells me something about my own conclusion. It holds fewer experts than either of my machines and still writes 78.6, with one card and no hand-off between GPUs, a CPU with AVX-512 and fast DDR5. Its misses are presumably cheap. All three of my machines have slow RAM, 21–32 GB/s on a triad, and on them the cache matters more. The engine changes the rules, but there is no single new rule. With llama.cpp and the experts on the CPU, buy bandwidth and a CPU with AVX2. With an engine that caches experts on the GPU, cache size explains about half of the difference between my machines, and the GPU and the CPU that computes the misses explain the rest. On an old machine with slow RAM, more VRAM per card is the biggest single lever. It is not the only one. Under my real chat settings Benchmarks at 32K without images are not how I use the model. My daily chat runs on soft-14 with a 256K context window and images on, so I gave the X79 exactly those settings, with the 3-bit model: The X79 under my daily chat settings: IQ3_XXS, 256K context, vision encoder on the GPU. The 256K KV cache and the vision encoder take VRAM away from the expert cache (5,200 experts on the two cards instead of 8,200, 8.3 GiB instead of 13.2), and that costs about a sixth of the speed. It is still a usable machine for a long conversation with pictures. Tuning the old box Three things changed the X79’s numbers while I measured it. The disk matters, even while generating. My first measurements had the model on an NVMe drive in a USB enclosure, and Strata’s setup warned that the drive looked rotational and that “its n-gram table is read from it at random, which can stall prompts for minutes”. On Saturday the drive moved onto a PCIe adapter (Gen3 x4). I expected faster starts. I did not expect faster generation: The same Crucial P3 drive in a USB enclosure and on a PCIe Gen3 x4 adapter, every expert in RAM. The reason is the 28.8 GB n-gram table. It does not fit in the OS file cache next to 35.5–50 GB of experts (with IQ3_S, only about 12 GB of RAM is left), so the engine reads a few rows of it from the disk for every token , at 186 µs per random read on this drive. I did not measure the USB enclosure’s random reads before moving the drive, but the generation speeds show the difference. With the cache emptied before each start, a cold long prompt now runs as fast as a warm one (481 against 471 tokens per second). A much faster drive, a Samsung 980 PRO I had in a drawer (3.0 GB/s sequential and 80 µs per random read, against the Crucial P3’s 917 MB/s and 186 µs), halved the cold start (IQ2_XS from 60 to 30 s, IQ3_S from 87 to 38 s) and left generation where it was (47.7 and 36.7 tokens per second, within run-to-run variation). Reading a prompt is pure compute, and Pascal has no tensor cores: an 11,864-token prompt takes about 25 seconds to read instead of under 8. Power. At that price it is about 4.5 cents per hour of nonstop generation (kW × price per kWh), or, at 34.6 tokens per second, about €0.37 per million tokens. To me, hardware can always be pushed further, but from 2000 on it became a race to hardware obsolescence, papered over with bad software. Before buying anything, squeeze the software. The X79 goes back on the shelf as a working machine. Recovering an object like this, one that not long ago would have been junk, and running inference on it is something I find remarkable: this time it ran a model that a few months ago I would not have tried to run at home. Method Same engine on every machine: Strata 0.1.45, MTP speculative decoding (4 draft tokens; 59–65% of them accepted on the seven mixed prompts, on every machine and size, and 70–76% on the code test), int8 KV cache, 32K context and no vision unless stated. The prebuilt 0.1.45 engine is no longer downloadable, and CUDA 12.0 needed a one-line fix to a debug print, which does not touch the computation. Documentation links point to the v0.1.45 tag. Same model files: the ISTA-DASLab GGUFs, copied over the LAN and checked (the shared n-gram table by SHA-256). Storage: the X79’s main numbers come from a Crucial P3 500 GB on a PCIe Gen3 x4 adapter (917 MB/s sequential, 186 µs per random 4 KiB read). Rows marked “USB enclosure” are earlier runs with the same drive over USB. The Samsung 980 PRO runs, including all of 25 October’s, used the same adapter, with the model files copied from soft-14 and checked. soft-14 and soft-2 run from internal NVMe drives. Speed: seven different prompts, 400 tokens each (thinking on, the model’s default, counted in the 400), temperature 0.7. Both passwords sit about two-thirds of the way in; I did not test other depths. 38 to 48 tokens per second from a Xeon without AVX2 and two 2017 GPUs, and what three home PCs taught me about where local LLM speed really comes from.The X79 up close: two used Titan Xp cards from 2017, the Xeon’s cooler at the top right and, on the left, a four-slot M.2 adapter of which this 2011 board can use only the first slot.

“Many people show off by spending thousands of euros on technology built by someone else, just to keep up with fashion. I dig into technology to squeeze everything out of it, recycling included.” That is how I described my approach this week, and I think it is a fairly cyberpunk way to do AI at home. William Gibson put it better in 1982: the street finds its own uses for things.

This year, recycling is also a matter of money. Memory used to be the part nobody worried about when building a PC; in a year it has become one of the most expensive. In Germany, DDR5 kits cost 5.4 times their July 2025 price in September, and DDR4, the usual way out, keeps climbing too (3DCenter’s index). The memory makers are moving their capacity to AI data centers, and home PCs get what is left. The optimistic forecasts see relief at the end of 2027, when new fabs start producing (Counterpoint). I don’t believe it. Samsung has told its investors that supply will be even tighter in 2027 (TweakTown), and TrendForce warns that PCs could get less DRAM next year, not more, as capacity moves to servers. I expect it to get worse before it gets better. If at the end of 2027 a 32 GB DDR5 kit costs less in Germany than the roughly €500 it costs today, I was wrong. Until then, the cheapest way into local AI is likely to be hardware that already exists.

Mine is an ASUS P9X79 board (2011) with a 12-core Xeon E5–2697 v2 (2013), a workstation platform I have owned for years. Every now and then I box it up, every now and then I take it out again. In August it got two used NVIDIA Titan Xp cards (2017) for Dumpster Inference, the first part of this series. This week it got 64 GB of DDR3 and an NVMe drive on a PCIe adapter, and I asked it to run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. It answered at 38 tokens per second with IQ3_S, the most accurate of the three quantized files I tried, and at 48.6 with the 2-bit one.

Then I did what I always do before believing a number: I ran the same engine, the same model files and the same scripts on two more machines in my house. The comparison taught me more than the headline did.

The machine and what it costWhat the X79 cost me in October 2026, next to asking prices for the same parts on 23 October 2026 (eBay Italy and Germany, Subito, Idealo; listings, not completed sales).

The core of the machine, with twelve cores, 64 GB of RAM on four channels and 24 GB of VRAM, cost me €750. At today’s asking prices it is €710–910, about the price of a single new RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (€720–780), and the two GPUs are two-thirds of it.

The CPU is old in a way that matters. It is an Ivy Bridge part with AVX but no AVX2 and no FMA, the instructions most local-inference software expects. The Titan Xp is Pascal: no tensor cores, no BF16. Together they are close to the oldest hardware the engine I used can still run on.

The engine: why a 125B model fits at all

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next is far too big for 24 GB of VRAM. In early September, on my fastest PC (then an RTX 4070 and an RTX 5060 Ti, 28 GB of VRAM), llama.cpp ran its 1-bit version at 5.5 tokens per second, with most experts on the CPU and no speculative decoding.

Strata is an open-source (MIT) engine built for exactly this model. The model has 48 layers with 512 small “experts” each, 24,576 in all, and every token goes through 10 of them in each layer, plus one shared expert. Strata keeps the most-used experts on the GPUs and adapts that cache to the conversation. It keeps every expert in RAM, and the CPU computes the few the GPUs don’t have, at the same time. It also drafts a few tokens ahead with the model’s own small prediction layer (MTP) and checks them in one pass. A 28.8 GB n-gram lookup table stays on the SSD, and a few rows of it are read for every token.

The quantized weights come from ISTA-DASLab at three sizes: IQ2_XS (2-bit), IQ3_XXS (3-bit) and IQ3_S, whose experts are stored at 3.33 bits per weight and which Strata describes as matching the full model on the published tests.

Strata’s documentation is candid about old hardware. The AVX-only CPU path is experimental, and the authors write that it is “untested on a real old CPU by us” (INSTALL.md). They forced that path on a modern Ryzen, with a deliberately small expert cache, and got 11–17 tokens per second; “an old Xeon with DDR3 will be slower than these”, they add. Contributors had run earlier versions on a Xeon E5–2680 (2.87 tokens per second with a GTX 1080 Ti) and on E5–2687W and X5690 machines, and the Xeons in the project’s community benchmarks are 2014–2016 parts with AVX2. So this X79 is, as far as I can tell, the first published measurement of the current engine on the kind of machine that path was written for.

Results on the X79Strata 0.1.45 on the X79: 32K context, no vision, every expert in RAM, model on NVMe over PCIe. Medians of six runs.

For large models I use a simple bar: above 10 tokens per second, a model is usable for real work. The 2013 machine clears it almost four times over, even with the largest file. In every run it also found a password hidden at line 211 of a 320-line, 11,864-token log. That is a recall check, not a quality test, but it shows that the long prompt really is read.

Three machines, one engine

This is the part that changed my mind. I ran the same IQ2_XS files, the same Strata version and the same scripts on two more PCs in my house, all three from NVMe drives:

  • soft-14 (2019): Ryzen 7 3700X, 64 GB DDR4 (four modules of a 3600 kit, running at 3000 MT/s), 2× RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB (Blackwell), 32 GB of VRAM.
  • soft-2 (2020): Ryzen 5 5600X, 32 GB DDR4–3600, RTX 3060 + RTX 4070 (Ampere and Ada), 24 GB of VRAM, the same as the X79.
The same engine, model files and scripts on three machines (IQ2_XS, 32K context). The ranges of the six runs and the soft-2 caveat are in the notes under the table.

For months I had argued that, for local inference, memory bandwidth matters more than the GPU. I measured it on this same X79 platform in August: with llama.cpp and the experts on the CPU, bandwidth and AVX2 decided everything. Here the X79 has 50% more RAM bandwidth than soft-14 and 22% more VRAM bandwidth per card, and it still runs at 57–68% of soft-14’s speed, depending on the file:

The X79 against soft-14 with each file: 57–68% of the speed, with 50% more RAM bandwidth.

My next suspect was the age of the GPUs, and soft-2 complicates that. Its GPUs are two and three generations newer than the Titans, with tensor cores, and its CPU is modern, with AVX2. In the same low-RAM mode, with the same 24 GB of VRAM and similar RAM bandwidth, it runs at 43.9 tokens per second against the X79’s 43.7, and the ranges overlap. The two machines differ in five things at once, so some effects may cancel out, but a newer architecture on its own clearly did not buy much here.

What soft-14 has more of is expert cache. Its two 16 GB cards hold about 16,000 experts; the Titans hold 10,500 and soft-2’s cards 9,800. In a split, each card keeps its own copy of the dense weights and its own prompt buffers, so 24 GB on two cards is far from 24 GB of cache. On soft-14, 1–3% of the experts a token needs are missing from the cache; on the other two, about 5%. That is several times as many experts left to the CPU, on machines whose RAM is slow.

That was a hypothesis, so on Sunday morning I tested it on the X79 and soft-14, on the same day, with the same files and scripts. I asked three questions.

Is it the cache? I cut soft-14’s expert cache down to about the X79’s size and left everything else as it was:

First test, 25 October: soft-14 with its expert cache cut to about the X79’s size, everything else unchanged.

The smaller cache cost soft-14 15%, about half of its lead over the X79. The other half is the rest of the machine: Blackwell against Pascal, an AVX2 Zen 2 against an AVX-only Ivy Bridge for the experts the cache misses, CUDA 13 against the experimental CUDA 12 path. Strata’s documentation says that “More VRAM matters more than a faster GPU”. On my machines, that explains half of the gap.

Is it the speculative decoding? Drafting tokens ahead could flatter one machine more than the other, even with the same share of drafts accepted, because the fixed cost of each check weighs differently on a fast step and on a slow one. So I switched the draft layer off on both, each at its normal cache size:

Second test: MTP drafts on and off, each machine at its normal cache size.

On my mixed prompts, drafting is worth about a third more speed on both machines, and it does not change the comparison.

What about the number on Strata’s README? It is the first thing a reader sees: a single RTX 5070 12 GB, with a Ryzen 5 7600 and DDR5, writes 79 tokens per second with IQ2_XS, more than soft-14 does with two cards. Their prompts are not published, so I built the same kind of test from an excerpt of Strata’s own source code:

Third test: a coding-agent style prompt on my two machines, next to the RTX 5070 figure in Strata’s README (different engine version, operating system and prompt text).

On the same kind of work, soft-14 is ahead of the 5070 and the X79 reaches 62% of soft-14. Strata’s own benchmark tool tells the same story in its chat test: 52.7 tokens per second on the X79, 90.4 on soft-14.

All three of my machines have slow RAM, 21–32 GB/s on a triad, and on them the cache matters more.

The engine changes the rules, but there is no single new rule. With llama.cpp and the experts on the CPU, buy bandwidth and a CPU with AVX2. On an old machine with slow RAM, more VRAM per card is the biggest single lever. It is not the only one.

Under my real chat settings

Benchmarks at 32K without images are not how I use the model. My daily chat runs on soft-14 with a 256K context window and images on, so I gave the X79 exactly those settings, with the 3-bit model:

The X79 under my daily chat settings: IQ3_XXS, 256K context, vision encoder on the GPU.

The 256K KV cache and the vision encoder take VRAM away from the expert cache (5,200 experts on the two cards instead of 8,200, 8.3 GiB instead of 13.2), and that costs about a sixth of the speed. It is still a usable machine for a long conversation with pictures.

For the cut-down test, soft-14’s first card was set with --expert-cache and the second with --vram-reserve-later-mib, with the layer split held where each machine put it by itself (layer 24 on soft-14, 25 on the X79).
  • Without MTP: no draft layer, prompt-lookup drafts off and the shortest verify window the engine accepts with these files (--spec 2), at the same cache size as the run with drafts.
  • Coding-agent test: a 3,100–3,600-token excerpt of Strata’s serve/server.py with an agent-style task, a different excerpt each run, temperature 0, 256 tokens, thinking off; first run discarded, median of three. Strata's benchmark is tools/strata_bench.py with its defaults (three runs per test, thinking off).
  • PCIe links, as Strata’s own probe measured them: 11.8 GB/s per card on the X79 (PCIe 3.0 x16 on separate CPU ports); 6.3 and 14.1 GB/s on soft-14 (PCIe 4.0, an x4 chipset slot and an x8 slot).
  • Cold start: on the X79 the OS file cache was emptied before each start. soft-14’s start times were not taken cold, so I don’t compare them.
  • Long context: an 11,864-token prompt with a password hidden at line 211 of 320, and a 59,910-token one with the password at line 1,060 of 1,600, both with low reasoning effort. Found every time. Both passwords sit about two-thirds of the way in; I did not test other depths.
  • Chat settings: 256K context, vision encoder on the GPU (my choice: with 12 GB cards setup does not turn images on by default), prompt-cache checkpoints every 1,024 tokens, as in my daily chat. Strata 0.1.45 supports images and mid-prompt checkpoints on a layer split, and admits Pascal cards through its experimental CUDA 12 engine (OLDER_GPUS.md); nothing was patched on the X79.
  • Power: GPU power from the NVIDIA driver and CPU package power from Intel RAPL, sampled every 0.5 s during each phase. RAM, board, disks and fans are estimated (about 45 W), and so is power-supply efficiency (88–92%). Electricity at the energy price of my contract, €0.10 per kWh, before network charges and taxes; the text also gives the cost at an all-in €0.25. These are estimates, not wall-meter readings.
  • RAM bandwidth: a STREAM-style OpenMP triad, best of ten iterations, three repeats, same source on every machine.
  • Prices: what I actually paid in October 2026, next to asking prices for the same parts on eBay Italy/Germany, Subito and Idealo on 23 October 2026. Listings, not completed sales; used unless noted.
  • What I disclose: soft-2 ran with almost no free RAM; the CUDA versions differ; the CPU-versus-PCIe comparison was run before the drive moved to PCIe; the README’s 5070 figure comes from a different engine version, operating system and prompt text.

This article was written with the help of Claude (Anthropic), from my notes, ideas and measurements; I reviewed and edited the text. Every measurement was run on my own machines.

items.title: Tesla gave up the EV crown. Now it wants to win the autonomy race
items.summary: Elon Musk’s “flying” Roadster jumped and flipped through the air this month in a stunt that went viral around the world. But his bigger bet is on changing the way Tesla makes money—and the wider car industry is scrambling to catch up. Five days after the spectacle, made possible by compressed-gas thrusters developed by Musk’s SpaceX, he revealed the companies were exploring a merger that could accelerate his push into autonomous driving. At stake is more than a technological race. Car groups, already grappling with growing Chinese competition, are seeking to move beyond a business model centered on vehicle sales towards one that also generates recurring revenues from software and AI-powered services. Read full article Comments
