items.title: Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder mania has reached lookalike contest levels
items.summary: Dozens gathered for the Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder lookalike contest. Getty Images Dozens gathered in New York for a Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes look-alike contest. A small crowd cheered on the sea of black blazers, blonde buns, and tiny headphones. One of the event's organizers said more than 200 people registered to attend. Washington Square Park on Sunday afternoon looked like a cross between a vigil, a corporate mixer, and a low-budget film set. It was, in reality, an Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder lookalike contest, as fandom about the documentary " You Can See Everything" spilled onto the streets. A small crowd cheered on the gaggle of blazer-donning blondes and graying fans wearing tiny headphones. Holmes wannabes milled around, their heavily lined eyes wide and fingers forming the "okay" hand gesture associated with the Theranos founder. Spotted in Washington Square Park https://t.co/fmyNswZWm1 — Scott Barry Kaufman ⛵ (@sbkaufman) October 25, 2026 Age was no object: One of the Holmeses appeared to be under 10 in a video on X, though she'd already mastered the founders' characteristic stare. The prize ultimately went to two adults, Joe Sivick and Nicole Travolta, the post said. Speaking into a megaphone, Sivick said he lives in New York, is married, and has a cat. Travolta, who identifies as an actress and comedian on Instagram, posted about her unexpected win, showing off a beaded turquoise coin purse that reads "Delulu for life" in a video on her story. Typically a brunette, she appears to have invested in a wig for the big day. The winners of the Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder look-alike contest celebrate in Washington Square Park. https://t.co/IzhuTp8Z22 — Thought Catalog (@ThoughtCatalog) October 26, 2026 WATCH: Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes Lookalike Contest Takes Over Washington Square Park Fans in turtlenecks and blonde wigs packed Washington Square Park in NYC on Sunday for a Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes lookalike contest decided right in front of the crowd. Winners Joe Sivick and Nicole Travolta and organizers Maddy West and Katherine Gehring talk about the day. Video: Ken Lopez | Licensing @FreedomNTV Desk@freedomnews.tv — Oliya Scootercaster 🛴 (@ScooterCasterNY) October 25, 2026 Maddy West, a New York-based comedian and Fielder fan, organized the event with a friend. Look-alike contests rose in popularity a few years ago, with celebrities from Timothée Chalamet to Glen Powell getting the doppelganger treatment. The organizers had about a week to set up the event, from the prizes and the registration to securing the guest judge, Kor Skeete, who starred in an episode of Fielder's series "The Rehearsal." West said more than 200 people responded to a registration form on the event's Partiful invitation . Neither Sivick nor Travolta wanted the $50 cash prize, West said, opting instead to keep a purse made by a local business. West said Sivick's impression was so convincing, she momentarily thought he was Fielder himself. "When he showed up to the event, I saw him from a distance, and he was wearing sunglasses. At first glance, I was like, 'Oh my gosh, did Nathan Fielder actually show?" West said. JUST IN: New Yorkers gather in Washington Square Park for an Elizabeth Holmes lookalike contest. https://t.co/ZeUIM8OvxO — Polymarket (@Polymarket) October 25, 2026 Sunday's contestants aren't the only ones investing in the documentary duo's wardrobe. TikTokers have posted about dressing up as Holmes and Fielder — or Holmes and her " drop of blood ," in at least one case — for Halloween. Fielder's documentary has made waves in the tech and film worlds since it debuted earlier this month. The A24 movie tracks the time the comedian spent with Holmes weeks before she reported to prison for defrauding investors, among other charges. Business Insider's Callie Ahlgrim described it as "part character study, part psychological thriller, part surrealist thought experiment." "You Can See Everything" grossed $15 million in its opening weekend after opening in 855 theaters, doubling producers' expectations. The movie is part of a string of recent releases about wealthy, hubristic tech founders — there's Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning," Elon Musk in "Musk," Sam Altman in "Artificial," and Sam Bankman-Fried in "The Altruists." The on-screen Silicon Valley backlash has coincided with real-life discontent about the AI buildout , which is becoming a more potent issue for tech leaders and politicians alike. This story has been updated with comments from event organizer Maddy West. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Dozens gathered for the Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder lookalike contest.

Getty Images

  • Dozens gathered in New York for a Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes look-alike contest.
  • A small crowd cheered on the sea of black blazers, blonde buns, and tiny headphones.
  • One of the event's organizers said more than 200 people registered to attend.

Washington Square Park on Sunday afternoon looked like a cross between a vigil, a corporate mixer, and a low-budget film set.

It was, in reality, an Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder lookalike contest, as fandom about the documentary "You Can See Everything" spilled onto the streets. A small crowd cheered on the gaggle of blazer-donning blondes and graying fans wearing tiny headphones. Holmes wannabes milled around, their heavily lined eyes wide and fingers forming the "okay" hand gesture associated with the Theranos founder.

Spotted in Washington Square Park https://t.co/fmyNswZWm1

— Scott Barry Kaufman ⛵ (@sbkaufman) October 25, 2026

Age was no object: One of the Holmeses appeared to be under 10 in a video on X, though she'd already mastered the founders' characteristic stare.

The prize ultimately went to two adults, Joe Sivick and Nicole Travolta, the post said. Speaking into a megaphone, Sivick said he lives in New York, is married, and has a cat. Travolta, who identifies as an actress and comedian on Instagram, posted about her unexpected win, showing off a beaded turquoise coin purse that reads "Delulu for life" in a video on her story. Typically a brunette, she appears to have invested in a wig for the big day.

The winners of the Elizabeth Holmes and Nathan Fielder look-alike contest celebrate in Washington Square Park. https://t.co/IzhuTp8Z22

— Thought Catalog (@ThoughtCatalog) October 26, 2026

WATCH: Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes Lookalike Contest Takes Over Washington Square Park Fans in turtlenecks and blonde wigs packed Washington Square Park in NYC on Sunday for a Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes lookalike contest decided right in front of the crowd. Winners Joe Sivick and Nicole Travolta and organizers Maddy West and Katherine Gehring talk about the day. Video: Ken Lopez | Licensing @FreedomNTV Desk@freedomnews.tv

— Oliya Scootercaster 🛴 (@ScooterCasterNY) October 25, 2026

Maddy West, a New York-based comedian and Fielder fan, organized the event with a friend. Look-alike contests rose in popularity a few years ago, with celebrities from Timothée Chalamet to Glen Powell getting the doppelganger treatment.

The organizers had about a week to set up the event, from the prizes and the registration to securing the guest judge, Kor Skeete, who starred in an episode of Fielder's series "The Rehearsal." West said more than 200 people responded to a registration form on the event's Partiful invitation.

Neither Sivick nor Travolta wanted the $50 cash prize, West said, opting instead to keep a purse made by a local business. West said Sivick's impression was so convincing, she momentarily thought he was Fielder himself.

"When he showed up to the event, I saw him from a distance, and he was wearing sunglasses. At first glance, I was like, 'Oh my gosh, did Nathan Fielder actually show?" West said.

JUST IN: New Yorkers gather in Washington Square Park for an Elizabeth Holmes lookalike contest. https://t.co/ZeUIM8OvxO

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) October 25, 2026

Sunday's contestants aren't the only ones investing in the documentary duo's wardrobe. TikTokers have posted about dressing up as Holmes and Fielder — or Holmes and her "drop of blood," in at least one case — for Halloween.

Fielder's documentary has made waves in the tech and film worlds since it debuted earlier this month. The A24 movie tracks the time the comedian spent with Holmes weeks before she reported to prison for defrauding investors, among other charges. Business Insider's Callie Ahlgrim described it as "part character study, part psychological thriller, part surrealist thought experiment." "You Can See Everything" grossed $15 million in its opening weekend after opening in 855 theaters, doubling producers' expectations.

The movie is part of a string of recent releases about wealthy, hubristic tech founders — there's Mark Zuckerberg in "The Social Reckoning," Elon Musk in "Musk," Sam Altman in "Artificial," and Sam Bankman-Fried in "The Altruists." The on-screen Silicon Valley backlash has coincided with real-life discontent about the AI buildout, which is becoming a more potent issue for tech leaders and politicians alike.

This story has been updated with comments from event organizer Maddy West.

items.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash vs. MiniMax M3: One is cheaper, but not faster or better
items.summary: MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on October 19, 2026, and says it cuts the overall cost of agentic tasks by 70% and makes online inference nearly three times faster than M3. MiniMax lists Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens. Those are half M3’s discounted rates of $0.30 and $1.20 for requests with no more than 512K input tokens; cached input and longer M3 requests have separate rates. Online inference speed differs from the time needed to finish a tool-using task. Artificial Analysis independently scored M3.1 Flash at 72.5% on AutomationBench-AA, a test of multi-step work across simulated business apps. That score measures the share of task objectives completed without guardrail violations. It differs from the percentage of entire tasks completed on Zapier’s own AutomationBench leaderboard. I didn’t run AutomationBench myself. Instead, I tested M3.1 Flash against M3 on three smaller agent tasks to see how they behaved in work closer to my own. One run per task is too small a sample to measure a general improvement in accuracy, cost, or speed. The tests I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to MiniMax’s own servers, at default settings. At the time of testing, I used OpenRouter’s free Flash endpoint, so the dollar amounts below for Flash are estimates at MiniMax’s list prices, not charges I paid. I didn’t use the MiniMax API directly because its credit minimum was too high for this small test. I capped the turns each model could use to complete the job. Results through OpenRouter may differ from runs through MiniMax’s API, even when routed to MiniMax’s servers. I used OpenRouter because it let me test both models in one place. Agentic bug fix – A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap. Incident investigation – Logs, metrics, and deploy history for 20 fake services during an outage. The cause is a config change hidden behind two decoy deploys and a server clock that runs slow. Long context – A fake engineering wiki of about 500,000 tokens with three questions about how its services depend on each other. The agentic bug fix test Neither model scored perfectly, both finishing with a 5 of 6, but each missed something different. Flash fixed all three bugs without breaking anything. It then ran out of turns before writing its final answer, so it never reported the wrong test. M3 reported the wrong test but missed one case on the second bug. The tool logs show two different working styles. Flash read 37 files over its first 14 turns before making a single edit. It had every bug fixed by turn 16, then spent its last four turns writing a scratch test to double-check the docs. M3 ran the tests once and made its first fix on turn 4. Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found. Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found. M3 moved faster and missed a case. Flash used more than twice the input tokens and had an estimated cost about 23% lower on this task, helped by discounted cached input. The numbers: Flash: 25 turns, 538,718 in, 7,056 out, $0.017, 129.0 s, 55 tokens/s. M3 17 turns, 203,639 in, 4,327 out, $0.022, 36.8 s, 118 tokens/s. The incident investigation test Both models scored 10 of 10. Each found the config change, ruled out both decoy deploys, caught the slow clock, and listed all nine affected services in order. MiniMax released M3.1 Flash on October 19, 2026, and says it cuts the overall cost of agentic tasks by 70% and makes online inference nearly three times faster than M3. MiniMax lists Flash at $0.15 per million input tokens and $0.60 per million output tokens.

Those are half M3’s discounted rates of $0.30 and $1.20 for requests with no more than 512K input tokens; cached input and longer M3 requests have separate rates. Online inference speed differs from the time needed to finish a tool-using task.

Artificial Analysis independently scored M3.1 Flash at 72.5% on AutomationBench-AA, a test of multi-step work across simulated business apps. That score measures the share of task objectives completed without guardrail violations. It differs from the percentage of entire tasks completed on Zapier’s own AutomationBench leaderboard.

I didn’t run AutomationBench myself. Instead, I tested M3.1 Flash against M3 on three smaller agent tasks to see how they behaved in work closer to my own. One run per task is too small a sample to measure a general improvement in accuracy, cost, or speed.

The tests

I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to MiniMax’s own servers, at default settings. At the time of testing, I used OpenRouter’s free Flash endpoint, so the dollar amounts below for Flash are estimates at MiniMax’s list prices, not charges I paid. I didn’t use the MiniMax API directly because its credit minimum was too high for this small test. I capped the turns each model could use to complete the job.

Results through OpenRouter may differ from runs through MiniMax’s API, even when routed to MiniMax’s servers. I used OpenRouter because it let me test both models in one place.

  • Agentic bug fix – A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
  • Incident investigation – Logs, metrics, and deploy history for 20 fake services during an outage. The cause is a config change hidden behind two decoy deploys and a server clock that runs slow.
  • Long context – A fake engineering wiki of about 500,000 tokens with three questions about how its services depend on each other.
The agentic bug fix test

Neither model scored perfectly, both finishing with a 5 of 6, but each missed something different. Flash fixed all three bugs without breaking anything. It then ran out of turns before writing its final answer, so it never reported the wrong test. M3 reported the wrong test but missed one case on the second bug.

The tool logs show two different working styles. Flash read 37 files over its first 14 turns before making a single edit. It had every bug fixed by turn 16, then spent its last four turns writing a scratch test to double-check the docs. M3 ran the tests once and made its first fix on turn 4. 

Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found.

Flash’s approach got all three bugs right, but it burned through its turns reading and checking and never got to write up what it found. M3 moved faster and missed a case. Flash used more than twice the input tokens and had an estimated cost about 23% lower on this task, helped by discounted cached input.

The numbers: 

  • Flash: 25 turns, 538,718 in, 7,056 out, $0.017, 129.0 s, 55 tokens/s.
  • M3 17 turns, 203,639 in, 4,327 out, $0.022, 36.8 s, 118 tokens/s.
The incident investigation test

Both models scored 10 of 10. Each found the config change, ruled out both decoy deploys, caught the slow clock, and listed all nine affected services in order.

They made the same 63 tool calls, but Flash bundled more calls per turn and finished in 17 turns, compared with M3’s 24. Flash used fewer input tokens and had an estimated cost about 68% lower on this test, close to MiniMax’s 70% claim for agentic tasks. Turn count alone does not explain the difference; cache use and token prices also matter.

Flash used fewer input tokens here, but slightly more output tokens.

The numbers:

  • Flash: 17 turns, 367,401 in, 13,175 out, $0.020, 146.2 s, 90 tokens/s.
  • M3: 24 turns, 592,377 in, 12,061 out, $0.062, 72.2 s, 167 tokens/s.
The long context test

Neither model produced an answer. Flash used the 64,000 output tokens I allowed and ran out before writing anything. M3 also stopped after roughly 29,000 output tokens without an answer. MiniMax lists a roughly 1-million-token context window for M3, but that capacity did not translate into a completed answer in this run.

MiniMax lists a roughly 1-million-token context window for M3, but that capacity did not translate into a completed answer…

I ran one extra round with reasoning set to low and the same 28,000-token output limit for both. Flash answered this time but found only 3 of 33 affected services. M3 again ran out before answering.

Neither model answered this large-document question reliably under my settings. Flash hit the 64,000-token output limit I set on the first run. When I pushed it to answer with less, it missed 30 of the 33 services. I wouldn’t rely on either result for a task like this.

The test results
TestMiniMax M3.1 FlashMiniMax M3Agentic bug fix5 of 65 of 6Incident investigation10 of 1010 of 10Long contextNo answerNo answerTotal tokens in / out1,401,606 / 84,2311,291,477 / 45,214Total cost (Flash estimated)$0.15$0.27Total model time661.6 s465.0 s

Flash’s estimated total cost was lower, even though it used more input and output tokens. Cache use and different token prices affect that comparison, so token totals alone cannot show which model would cost less at identical rates.

What do I think?

I noticed differences between MiniMax M3 and M3.1 Flash, but apart from the lower estimated cost, I wouldn’t call them improvements in these runs. Flash was slower overall, and both models scored the same on the graded tasks.

items.title: Stripe’s AI Shopping Lead Puts Card Giants on Edge
items.summary: As AI assistants like Instinct and Meta Platforms’ Muse start to gain traction in shopping, Stripe has taken a leading position in how the agents pay. That’s putting the credit card giants on edge. The reason for their apprehension: Stripe in many cases is enabling AI agent purchases through virtual cards for one-time use, which can leave card networks with less control over the shopping and payment process, people who work closely with the card firms say. Mastercard and Visa have developed their own payment technology for agent shopping that would use customers’ existing cards, giving the card companies more visibility into who’s making what purchases. That method is still at an early stage, though.

items.title: The sandbox wasn’t enough: Why AI agent governance requires runtime observability
items.summary: Models running an OpenAI cybersecurity evaluation reached the public Internet from an environment designed to be isolated. Package installation through an internal registry proxy and cache was the only intended network path. The models found a previously unknown vulnerability in that proxy. They escalated privileges, moved laterally to a node with Internet access, then used additional vulnerabilities and stolen credentials to intrude into Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. The isolation policy said the public Internet was out of bounds – but the running system proved otherwise. This was not a story about absent monitoring. OpenAI says its security team detected anomalous activity internally. Hugging Face reports that it combined runtime and SIEM signals into an attack signal, but the alert wasn’t critical enough to prompt the on-call team promptly. Hugging Face investigators recovered roughly 17,600 agent actions across several trust boundaries. The signals existed. They didn’t trigger intervention early enough. “A configured boundary does not prove what is reachable at runtime.” Anthropic’s review of 141,006 cybersecurity evaluation runs found three incidents involving six runs, revealing a different failure mode. Those models reached real systems because an evaluation environment had unintended Internet access. That was a configuration failure, not an exploited sandbox escape. These were capability evaluations, not normal production deployments. Both organizations report that they removed or reduced standard deployment safeguards to measure underlying cyber capabilities. But the governance lesson still holds: A configured boundary does not prove what is reachable at runtime. Why AI agents change the containment problem Runtime detection and defense-in-depth are not new. Agents change the execution model. In a fixed workflow, code specifies intermediate steps. A tool-using agent can choose and revise those steps while it runs. It can react to a result, retry a failed path, and use one tool’s output as another tool’s input. That changes what must be governed. A DNS lookup, package download, or credential read may be harmless alone. In the right sequence, the same events can form a path from a sandbox to a production system. Design-time governance sets the conditions: isolation, identities, tool permissions, policies and approvals. Runtime governance measures what happened against those conditions and changes system state when the two diverge. Observability does not replace prevention. It shows when prevention no longer matches reality. Governance frameworks already reflect this distinction. For high-risk systems, the EU AI Act requires automatic event logging, human oversight capable of detecting anomalies and interrupting a system, and post-market monitoring throughout its lifetime. NIST’s Generative AI Profile similarly calls for post-deployment monitoring, escalation, and incident response. “Observability does not replace prevention. It shows when prevention no longer matches reality.” Those frameworks establish the requirement. Agents compress the response window in which it must be met. One deployment-specific measure makes that visible: actions_before_containment = agent_action_rate x detection_to_containment_time This does not measure the severity of those actions. It measures how many can occur before the system intervenes. Four properties that turn telemetry into governance The answer is not simply more logs. A runtime evidence system needs four properties. Coverage: Are the transitions that change authority or create an external effect instrumented? Relevant events include agent and run identity , tool calls, process execution, privilege changes, credential use, network destinations, package retrieval, resource changes, and policy decisions. Log volume cannot compensate for a blind trust boundary. “The answer is not simply more logs. Log volume cannot compensate for a blind trust boundary.” Correlation: Can an external effect be traced to the action that caused it? The evidence should identify the agent run, tool call, policy decision, and descendant actions. A planner trace without process, identity, and network evidence shows the request, not its effect. Process and network evidence without the agent trace shows the effect, not the decision that caused it. Timeliness: Can the system intervene before the action becomes irreversible? Place synchronous gates in front of high-impact actions such as public egress, credential access, code execution, and production writes. Streaming analysis handles patterns that become dangerous only across several events. A separate response service can then suspend the run, isolate the workload, or revoke its credentials. Auditability: Can investigators reproduce the finding without trusting the agent’s account? My earlier article argued that database-backed observations should remain separate from an agent’s interpretation. The same separation applies here. The agent may explain its actions, but its explanation is not the audit record. From evidence to intervention Telemetry becomes containment only when it is connected to a response: agent action + policy decision + infrastructure effect | v correlated evidence | v response Agent actions, policy decisions, and infrastructure effects establish what was attempted, permitted, and changed. Correlating them turns separate events into evidence. Connecting that evidence to a response turns observability into containment. This evidence creates its own analytical workload. Agent runs, tools, identities, policy decisions, processes, and network destinations all add dimensions. Removing those dimensions before analysis can remove the signal that identifies the violating run. The evidence in this feedback loop comes from two instrumentation layers, and the coverage list above spans both. The agent runtime emits run identity, model calls, tool calls, and guardrail checks. The infrastructure emits process execution, credential use, network destinations, and resource changes. Neither layer can reconstruct the other. Infrastructure logs cannot say which run or which tool call opened a connection. An agent trace cannot say what the connection reached. The agent layer is the domain of LLM observability . Langfuse records each step an agent takes as a typed observation , including agent, tool, generation, and guardrail steps, and distinguishes the tools available to an agent from the tools it called. That distinction supports filters for sensitive tool use and looping tool paths, with alerts on the result. Trace context propagates across service boundaries and through MCP calls , so one trace can span a multi-service agent and its tool servers. DKB runs an assistant for roughly 6 million banking customers that can change transfer limits and block cards, with the customer confirming each action. Langfuse traces every interaction, automatically screens for compliance violations, and routes flagged cases to human review. Cresta propagates trace context across a Go agent service, a Python retrieval pipeline and a tool-execution service, so one trace covers the full call tree. ClickStack covers the infrastructure layer. It collects OpenTelemetry logs, metrics, and traces as wide events in ClickHouse, allowing teams to correlate high-cardinality telemetry with SQL during live detection and forensic investigation. The two layers share trace context. An application instrumented with OpenTelemetry can export the same traces to both so that each tool can identify the same request. Logs and metrics continue to flow to ClickStack, where SQL correlates them with those traces. Both store their data in ClickHouse. “Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.” Langfuse and ClickStack complement policy engines, identity systems, and enforcement mechanisms. Policy engines evaluate what is allowed, identity systems establish who or what is acting, and enforcement mechanisms carry out the response. The two observability layers bring their signals together with observed behavior, with ClickHouse serving as the analytical foundation for correlation and investigation. That runtime governance loop should pass four tests: Every critical trust boundary has telemetry coverage. You can trace every high-impact action from agent identity and policy decision to downstream effects. Evidence reaches a policy gate or bounded stop path in time to prevent or contain irreversible effects. The audit record remains independent of the agent’s narrative. Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.

Langfuse traces every interaction, automatically screens for compliance violations, and routes flagged cases to human review. Cresta propagates trace context across a Go agent service, a Python retrieval pipeline and a tool-execution service, so one trace covers the full call tree.

ClickStack covers the infrastructure layer. It collects OpenTelemetry logs, metrics, and traces as wide events in ClickHouse, allowing teams to correlate high-cardinality telemetry with SQL during live detection and forensic investigation.

The two layers share trace context. An application instrumented with OpenTelemetry can export the same traces to both so that each tool can identify the same request. Logs and metrics continue to flow to ClickStack, where SQL correlates them with those traces. Both store their data in ClickHouse.

“Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.”

Langfuse and ClickStack complement policy engines, identity systems, and enforcement mechanisms. Policy engines evaluate what is allowed, identity systems establish who or what is acting, and enforcement mechanisms carry out the response. The two observability layers bring their signals together with observed behavior, with ClickHouse serving as the analytical foundation for correlation and investigation.

That runtime governance loop should pass four tests:

  1. Every critical trust boundary has telemetry coverage.
  2. You can trace every high-impact action from agent identity and policy decision to downstream effects.
  3. Evidence reaches a policy gate or bounded stop path in time to prevent or contain irreversible effects.
  4. The audit record remains independent of the agent’s narrative.

Governance is not the policy document. It is the system’s ability to show whether the policy held, explain what happened when it did not, and stop the consequences from spreading.

The post The sandbox wasn’t enough: Why AI agent governance requires runtime observability appeared first on The New Stack.

items.title: Sophos, Palo Alto Networks retract early claims of PHP2Shell exploitation - but attacks are starting
items.summary: The exploitation of PHP servers/applications OpenAI and the NSA warned about has been slow to start – five days after a pair of critical PHP bugs were disclosed. Indeed both Sophos and Palo Alto Networks have actively retracted claims of exploitation. With frontier models making it far easier to spin up exploits from patch diffs, this suggests that true pre-auth RCE exploits are proving far harder to identify and weaponise than many suspected – even as exploitation of other bugs continues. Sophos, on October 22, reported “exploitation of PHP2Shell in customer environments” but the next day said it was “correcting that assessment.” Its telemetry showed “scanning and a small number of failed exploitation attempts.. there is no evidence of a successful compromise due to these vulnerabilities.” Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said on October 24 it was “unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs” after spotting post-compromise activity “against a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application” — and also retracted its claim of PHP2Shell exploitation. VulnCheck’s Caitlin Condon however said on October 24 that her team had “ got code execution working in on PHP 8.2 and 8.3 today, which rounds out our testing across supported version streams. There won’t be a universal exploit, but exploitability for RCE with ASLR is definitely possible across the affected version range,” she added. And on Saturday (October 24) Adel Karimi, who leads detection and response efforts at Perplexity, said his honeypots showed evidence of RCE “with usable memory disclosure” against an Apache mod_php box running PHP 8.4.26. “The response delivered an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, and a function address derived from that dump using the public exploit's offsets appears in the subsequent execution payload," Karimi said on X – later adding that he had “confirmed more from the same IP, plus a new IP with a different payload that might be a different actor… and this is showing up in multiple regions now.” Attacks appear to be meaningfully starting. Security researcher Marcus Hutchins described Karimi’s write-up as “by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild php2shell exploitation I've seen so far…” He had earlier commented that “The RCEs requires the attacker to obtain memory addresses which are typically protected by ASLR. - I suspect the original author (lcfr_hax) likely has a reliable exploit which leads to stable code execution. “Most of the PoCs being posted are completely non-functional AI slop.” Major Linux distributions like Ubuntu have pushed patches but the potential blast radius if properly functioning pre-auth RCE exploits start circulating more widely is large. Getting attacks up and running thus-far seems to have been far more complex than many anticipated and certainly buys more patching time for the many many organisations that are still working out what’s exposed or what to prioritise.
items.summary_html:
The exploitation of PHP servers/applications OpenAI and the NSA warned about has been slow to start – five days after a pair of critical PHP bugs were disclosed. Indeed both Sophos and Palo Alto Networks have actively retracted claims of exploitation.

With frontier models making it far easier to spin up exploits from patch diffs, this suggests that true pre-auth RCE exploits are proving far harder to identify and weaponise than many suspected – even as exploitation of other bugs continues. 

Sophos, on October 22, reported “exploitation of PHP2Shell in customer environments” but the next day said it was “correcting that assessment.”

 Its telemetry showed “scanning and a small number of failed exploitation attempts.. there is no evidence of a successful compromise due to these vulnerabilities.”

Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said on October 24 it was “unable to confirm that initial access is associated with the specific PHP2Shell CVEs” after spotting post-compromise activity “against a European government agency executed in the context of a vulnerable PHP application” — and also retracted its claim of PHP2Shell exploitation. 

VulnCheck’s Caitlin Condon however said on October 24 that her team had “ got code execution working in on PHP 8.2 and 8.3 today, which rounds out our testing across supported version streams. There won’t be a universal exploit, but exploitability for RCE with ASLR is definitely possible across the affected version range,” she added.

And on Saturday (October 24) Adel Karimi, who leads detection and response efforts at Perplexity, said his honeypots showed evidence of RCE “with usable memory disclosure” against an Apache mod_php box running PHP 8.4.26.

“The response delivered an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, and a function address derived from that dump using the public exploit's offsets appears in the subsequent execution payload," Karimi said on X – later adding that he had “confirmed more from the same IP, plus a new IP with a different payload that might be a different actor… and this is showing up in multiple regions now.” Attacks appear to be meaningfully starting.

Security researcher Marcus Hutchins described Karimi’s write-up as “by far the highest quality confirmation of in-the-wild php2shell exploitation I've seen so far…”

He had earlier commented that “The RCEs requires the attacker to obtain memory addresses which are typically protected by ASLR. - I suspect the original author (lcfr_hax) likely has a reliable exploit which leads to stable code execution. 

“Most of the PoCs being posted are completely non-functional AI slop.”

Major Linux distributions like Ubuntu have pushed patches but the potential blast radius if properly functioning pre-auth RCE exploits start circulating more widely is large. Getting attacks up and running thus-far seems to have been far more complex than many anticipated and certainly buys more patching time for the many many organisations that are still working out what’s exposed or what to prioritise.

items.title: YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS
items.summary: Home » Blog Table of Contents YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS What Is YOLO26? Why YOLO26 Matters for Real-Time Object Detection What Changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 Architecture Configuring Your Development Environment Project Structure Installing the Ultralytics YOLO26 Model on macOS Running YOLO26 Object Detection on Images, Video, and Webcam Streams Understanding YOLO26 Prediction Outputs YOLO26 Benchmarking Methodology on a MacBook YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Benchmark Results on macOS YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Visual Detection Quality Comparison When to Use the YOLO26 Model Summary YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS In this lesson, you will learn what YOLO26 is, what changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 architecture compared to earlier releases, how to run YOLO26 object detection on images, video, and webcam streams on macOS, and how to benchmark YOLO26 against YOLO12n where we measured nearly 30% throughput gains on video. This lesson is the 1st in a 2-part series on YOLO26 : YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS (this tutorial) Lesson 2 To learn what YOLO26 is and how it compares to YOLO12 on macOS, just keep reading. Looking for the source code to this post? Jump Right To The Downloads Section What Is YOLO26? If you have followed the You Only Look Once (YOLO) family over the years, you already know the pattern. Every release promises better speed, better accuracy, or a cleaner deployment story. Sometimes that means small gains. Sometimes it means a meaningful shift in how the detector behaves in production. YOLO26 is interesting because it is not just another checkpoint refresh. Ultralytics presents it as an end-to-end detector with NMS-free inference by default, along with changes aimed at faster central processing unit (CPU) execution and cleaner edge deployment. Those claims matter because many real-world YOLO systems for real-time object detection do not run on large data center graphics processing units (GPUs). They run on laptops, edge boxes, personal computers (PCs), robotics platforms, and embedded devices where simplicity and latency matter. In this lesson, you will answer 4 practical questions: What changed in YOLO26 compared with earlier Ultralytics YOLO releases? How do you run YOLO26 on macOS for images, videos, and webcam streams? What do the YOLO26 model outputs actually look like in Python? How does YOLO26 vs YOLO12 performance stack up on a MacBook? By the end of this lesson, you will have a grounded understanding of what YOLO26 is, a reproducible benchmark workflow, and concrete numbers showing YOLO26 object detection running nearly 30% faster than YOLO12n on video. Why YOLO26 Matters for Real-Time Object Detection The easiest way to misunderstand a new detector release is to treat it like a version number bump and move on. That misses the point. What makes the Ultralytics YOLO26 release worth paying attention to is not just accuracy. It is the combination of 3 practical ideas. End-to-End Detection Traditional real-time detectors usually produce many overlapping candidate boxes and then rely on non-maximum suppression (NMS) to prune duplicates. That works well, but it adds a post-processing stage and a few more tuning knobs. Ultralytics documents YOLO26 as using an end-to-end path by default, which means the standard inference path no longer depends on NMS in the same way earlier pipelines did. In plain English, the model is designed to produce a more direct set of final detections. Why NMS Becomes a Performance Tax NMS sounds simple in theory, but in practice it behaves like an extra tax on every frame. After the model generates candidate boxes, the pipeline still has to filter them, sort them, and suppress overlaps based on intersection over union (IoU). That adds more work after the neural network has already done its main job. On desktop GPUs, that cost may be easy to hide. On CPUs and edge accelerators, it can become much more visible. Even worse, it can complicate deployment because post-processing is not always handled by the same optimized runtime that executes the network itself. Why Latency Variability Matters NMS is also scene-dependent. A sparse image with very few confident detections is cheap to process. A crowded frame with many overlapping candidates demands more sorting and more overlap checks. That means latency can fluctuate based on what the camera sees. For robotics, industrial inspection, and real-time video systems, predictable timing matters. Even if YOLO26 does not make every environment perfectly deterministic, removing NMS from the standard inference path reduces one major source of latency jitter. Faster CPU-Oriented Deployment On paper, the official YOLO26 documentation emphasizes stronger CPU performance, especially for deployment scenarios where a heavy GPU stack is not the main story. That matters on macOS because many of you prototype on Apple laptops and often need a reliable local baseline before thinking about mobile, edge, or cloud deployment. Cleaner Edge Story YOLO26 is also positioned as an edge-first release. That does not mean it is only for edge devices. It means the design decisions try to reduce deployment friction across hardware and export formats. If you are building applications for robotics, industrial inspection, or always-on video analytics, those changes are not academic. They directly affect latency, integration complexity, and operational cost. What Changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 Architecture Now let us make that concrete. End-to-End, NMS-Free Inference by Default According to the public Ultralytics documentation, YOLO26 uses a one-to-one head by default for end-to-end prediction, and this default path does not require NMS. Ultralytics also notes that you can still switch back to a more traditional path by setting end2end=False for workflows that need compatibility with NMS-based post-processing. That distinction is worth understanding. Traditional Detector Pipeline In a traditional pipeline, the detector produces many candidate boxes. Post-processing then removes duplicates and overlapping boxes with NMS. The final detection quality can depend on the confidence score and IoU thresholds. YOLO26 Default Pipeline In the default YOLO26 path, the detector is configured to produce final detections directly enough that NMS is not part of the standard prediction path. This reduces post-processing overhead and simplifies deployment logic. For you as a practitioner, the biggest takeaway is simple: fewer moving parts after the forward pass usually makes inference pipelines easier to reason about and easier to deploy. The One-to-Many Legacy Earlier YOLO-style detectors typically learn through a one-to-many assignment strategy, where multiple predictions may be associated with the same ground-truth object during training. That is useful for optimization and recall, but it also leaves the model with a dense set of redundant candidates that need cleanup afterward. YOLO26 moves the default inference story closer to one-to-one prediction. Instead of asking post-processing to resolve a large pile of overlapping candidates, the deployed model is designed to produce a cleaner final set of object hypotheses. Figure 1: Traditional object detection versus YOLO26 end-to-end detection (source: image by the author). DFL Removal and Export Friendliness Ultralytics also highlights Distribution Focal Loss (DFL) removal as a major change in YOLO26. The practical benefit is not that you need to memorize every detail of the underlying loss formulation. The practical benefit is cleaner export behavior and wider edge compatibility. That matters if you eventually want to move from PyTorch to Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX), Core ML, NCNN, or another deployment target without spending your entire week debugging export quirks. It also matters because older regression heads often require extra decoding logic after the raw network output. By simplifying that path, YOLO26 makes the exported graph easier to deploy and easier to inspect. Training-Side Changes Ultralytics documents several training-related updates for YOLO26, including Progressive Loss (ProgLoss), Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment (STAL), and a MuSGD optimizer. You do not need to dive deep into those right now because this lesson is centered on inference and benchmarking, not custom training. Still, it is useful to know that YOLO26 is not only an inference story. Some of its improvements are tied to how the model was trained in the first place. Why One-to-One Training Is Hard One reason NMS-free detection took time to mature is that strict one-to-one supervision is harder to optimize. If the model is forced to commit to one prediction per object too early, the learning signal can become sparse and unstable. Dual-Head Intuition The broader end-to-end YOLO line addresses that problem by combining rich training supervision with a cleaner deployment path. The key intuition is that the model can still learn from denser training signals internally while using a one-to-one style head for final inference. You do not need every implementation detail in this lesson, but it helps to know that YOLO26 is not simply “YOLO with NMS turned off.” The clean inference behavior is supported by training design. What to Defer to Lesson 2 We should keep the deeper training mechanics for Lesson 2. That is the right place to discuss how label assignment, optimizer choice, and architecture decisions affect custom training results. CPU Speed Improvements Ultralytics specifically claims large CPU-side gains for YOLO26. That is one of the main reasons this lesson focuses on a MacBook workflow. If a detector says it is edge-first and CPU-aware, it should be able to prove that in a benchmark you can reproduce locally. Figure 2: High-level reasons YOLO26 matters in practice: end-to-end inference, CPU speed, and edge deployment (source: image by the author). Configuring Your Development Environment To follow this guide, you need to have the Ultralytics package installed on your system. Luckily, Ultralytics is pip-installable: $ pip install -U ultralytics If you need help configuring your development environment for Ultralytics and YOLO26, we highly recommend creating a fresh virtual environment first. Need Help Configuring Your Development Environment? Having trouble configuring your development environment? Want access to pre-configured Jupyter Notebooks running on Google Colab? Be sure to join PyImageSearch University — you will be up and running with this tutorial in a matter of minutes. All that said, are you: Short on time? Learning on your employer’s administratively locked system? Wanting to skip the hassle of fighting with the command line, package managers, and virtual environments? Ready to run the code immediately on your Windows, macOS, or Linux system? Then join PyImageSearch University today! Gain access to Jupyter Notebooks for this tutorial and other PyImageSearch guides pre-configured to run on Google Colab’s ecosystem right in your web browser! No installation required. And best of all, these Jupyter Notebooks will run on Windows, macOS, and Linux! Project Structure The following is a short directory structure: . ├── benchmark_yolo_macos.py ├── yolo26n.pt ├── yolo12n.pt └── / └── traffic_clip.mp4 The benchmark_yolo_macos.py script is the main workhorse. The model checkpoints are downloaded automatically by Ultralytics the first time you reference them. Installing the Ultralytics YOLO26 Model on macOS Let us move from theory to practice. Create a Clean Python Environment If you already have a computer vision environment on your Mac, resist the temptation to pile more packages into it. Use a fresh environment. python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip Install Ultralytics With the environment active, install the Ultralytics package: pip install -U ultralytics At the time of writing, this is the cleanest way to access YOLO26 through the official Python and CLI interfaces. Verify the Installation You can verify the install in either Python or the command-line interface (CLI). CLI Check yolo version Python Check from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") print(model.task) The first time you load a pretrained checkpoint, Ultralytics will download it automatically if it is not already present on your machine. Optional: Check for Apple Silicon Acceleration If you are on Apple Silicon, it is useful to know whether the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend is available. import torch print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available()) print("MPS built:", torch.backends.mps.is_built()) If MPS is available, you can run predictions with device="mps" . If not, stay on CPU and keep the benchmark methodology consistent. Figure 3: Installing the Ultralytics package and verifying a YOLO26 model on macOS (source: image by the author). Running YOLO26 Object Detection on Images, Video, and Webcam Streams Now you are ready to run the model. First Image Inference The smallest useful example is a single image. from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") results = model("image.jpg") That line performs the entire inference pass and returns a list of Results objects, one per image. If you want to be explicit about the prediction application programming interface (API) and device choice, do this instead: from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") results = model.predict( source="image.jpg", imgsz=640, conf=0.25, device="mps", # use "cpu" if MPS is unavailable ) Figure 4: Running YOLO26 on a single image using the Ultralytics Python API (source: image by the author). Running on a Folder of Images When you pass a directory, Ultralytics will iterate through the media automatically. from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") results = model.predict(source="images/", imgsz=640, conf=0.25, device="mps") This is a fast way to build a qualitative feel for the model before you benchmark it. Running on a Video File For video inference, the API stays almost identical. from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") results = model.predict(source="sample_video.mp4", show=True, device="mps") If you want saved output rather than a live preview window, add save=True . Running Real-Time Webcam Detection Webcam inference is where macOS users get an immediate feel for real-world responsiveness. from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") model.predict(source=0, show=True, device="mps") Figure 5: Real-time webcam detection with YOLO26 on macOS (source: image by the author). Understanding YOLO26 Prediction Outputs Running inference is only half the story. If you are going to build with YOLO26, you also need to understand what comes back. The Results Object A prediction call returns a list of Results objects. In the single-image case, you usually care about results[0] . from ultralytics import YOLO model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt") results = model("image.jpg") result = results[0] Inspect Boxes, Classes, and Confidences The boxes are stored in result.boxes . boxes = result.boxes print("Number of detections:", len(boxes)) print("Classes:", boxes.cls) print("Confidences:", boxes.conf) print("XYXY boxes:", boxes.xyxy) In practice, the most useful fields are the following. boxes.xyxy Bounding boxes in corner format: (x1, y1, x2, y2) . boxes.conf Confidence scores for each detection. boxes.cls Predicted class IDs. Map Class IDs Back to Labels Ultralytics stores class name metadata on the model. names = result.names for box in result.boxes: class_id = int(box.cls.item()) confidence = float(box.conf.item()) label = names[class_id] print(label, confidence) Inspect Preprocessing, Inference, and Postprocessing Time Ultralytics Results objects also expose timing information. print(result.speed) This usually gives you a dictionary with timings for preprocessing, inference, and postprocessing, measured in milliseconds per image. That is very useful for debugging, but for a fair benchmark we still want a consistent, external timing harness around repeated runs. What True End-to-End Export Looks Like One practical way to verify the deployment story is to export the model and inspect the graph. If you export YOLO26 to ONNX and open it in Netron, the goal is not to memorize every operator. The goal is to confirm that the exported graph is much closer to the final inference path used by the application than older detector exports that still depend on heavier post-processing outside the network. Older YOLO-Style Export The exported graph often ends in dense predictions that still need external filtering, decoding, or NMS-like logic before they become a clean set of final detections. YOLO12 vs. YOLO26: ONNX Export Comparison In YOLO12, the ONNX export shown in Figure 6 includes non-maximum suppression (NMS) directly inside the model graph. The graph contains an explicit NonMaxSuppression node followed by a sequence of Gather , Slice , and Concat operations to filter and format the final detections. This design produces ready-to-use outputs but tightly couples post-processing with the model itself. As a result, it becomes harder to customize thresholds, experiment with alternative filtering strategies, or adapt the pipeline for different deployment environments. Additionally, embedding NMS inside the graph introduces extra operations during inference, which can contribute to higher latency depending on the execution backend and hardware. Figure 6: ONNX graph of YOLO12 showing embedded non-maximum suppression (NMS) and associated post-processing operations within the model (source: image by the author). In contrast, YOLO26 removes non-maximum suppression from the model graph entirely. As illustrated in Figure 7 , the exported ONNX graph produces a single consolidated output tensor without any embedded NMS logic. Figure 7: ONNX graph of YOLO26 producing a unified output tensor without embedded NMS, enabling external post-processing (source: image by the author). This design shifts post-processing outside the model, resulting in a cleaner and more modular pipeline. Developers can control filtering, thresholding, and downstream processing explicitly, making the system easier to optimize, debug, and integrate with tracking and analytics systems. In practice, this separation can also improve end-to-end latency, especially when using optimized or hardware-accelerated post-processing outside the model graph. The exported graph is much closer to the final detection representation consumed by the application. This is what is typically meant when describing the model as end-to-end for inference. The key difference is not just the model architecture, but where post-processing is performed inside the graph versus in the surrounding application pipeline. YOLO26 Benchmarking Methodology on a MacBook This is the section that separates a useful lesson from a casual demo. What You Want to Measure For Lesson 1, focus on 4 metrics: Median latency per image Throughput in frames per second (FPS) Model size on disk Parameter count Memory usage is also valuable, but it is easier to measure unreliably. If you include it, document exactly how you measured it. Keep Your Benchmark Honest When people publish model comparisons, they often change too many variables at once. Do not do that. Keep these fixed across both models: Same machine Same device target, either CPU or MPS Same input image size Same batch size Same test image or test image set Same number of warmup iterations Same number of timed iterations If you cannot control those variables, your comparison becomes anecdotal. Figure 8: Benchmark protocol used to compare YOLO26 and the baseline model on a MacBook (source: image by the author). A Practical Benchmark Harness for YOLO Real-Time Object Detection To make this lesson fully reproducible, we have included a companion script called benchmark_yolo_macos.py . You can use it to benchmark any combination of YOLO checkpoints on your own machine. At a high level, the script does the following: Loads one or more Ultralytics YOLO checkpoints Performs warmup runs to stabilize the runtime Measures wall-clock latency over repeated predictions Reports median latency and FPS Extracts parameter counts from the loaded model Reports checkpoint file size on disk Here is the full script: import argparse import statistics import time from pathlib import Path from ultralytics import YOLO def parse_args(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Benchmark YOLO models on macOS.") parser.add_argument("--models", nargs="+", required=True, help="Model weights to benchmark.") parser.add_argument("--source", required=True, help="Image, folder, or video source for inference.") parser.add_argument("--imgsz", type=int, default=640, help="Inference image size.") parser.add_argument("--device", default="cpu", help="Inference device, e.g. cpu or mps.") parser.add_argument("--conf", type=float, default=0.25, help="Confidence threshold.") parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=5, help="Warmup iterations.") parser.add_argument("--runs", type=int, default=30, help="Timed iterations.") parser.add_argument( "--max-items", type=int, default=None, help="Maximum number of frames/items to process per run for videos, folders, or streams.", ) return parser.parse_args() def get_param_count(model): if hasattr(model.model, "parameters"): return sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in model.model.parameters()) return None def format_params(param_count): if param_count is None: return "n/a" return f"{param_count / 1_000_000:.2f}M" def format_size(weights_path): path = Path(weights_path) if path.exists() and path.is_file(): return f"{path.stat().st_size / (1024 * 1024):.2f} MB" return "downloaded/cache-managed" IMAGE_SUFFIXES = {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".bmp", ".tif", ".tiff", ".webp"} VIDEO_SUFFIXES = {".mp4", ".mov", ".m4v", ".avi", ".mkv", ".webm", ".mpg", ".mpeg"} def classify_source(source): source_str = str(source) if source_str.isdigit(): return "stream" path = Path(source_str).expanduser() if path.is_dir(): return "collection" suffix = path.suffix.lower() if suffix in IMAGE_SUFFIXES: return "image" if suffix in VIDEO_SUFFIXES: return "video" return "collection" def timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=None): source_kind = classify_source(source) start = time.perf_counter() if source_kind == "image": model.predict(source=source, imgsz=imgsz, conf=conf, device=device, verbose=False) items_processed = 1 else: items_processed = 0 for _ in model.predict(source=source, imgsz=imgsz, conf=conf, device=device, verbose=False, stream=True): items_processed += 1 if max_items is not None and items_processed >= max_items: break end = time.perf_counter() return { "elapsed_ms": (end - start) * 1000.0, "items_processed": items_processed, "source_kind": source_kind, } def benchmark_model(weights, source, imgsz, conf, device, warmup, runs, max_items=None): model = YOLO(weights) for _ in range(warmup): timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=max_items) timings = [timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=max_items) for _ in range(runs)] elapsed_values = [timing["elapsed_ms"] for timing in timings] items_processed = timings[-1]["items_processed"] if timings else 0 source_kind = timings[-1]["source_kind"] if timings else classify_source(source) median_latency_ms = statistics.median(elapsed_values) fps = 1000.0 / median_latency_ms if median_latency_ms > 0 else 0.0 median_ms_per_item = median_latency_ms / items_processed if items_processed > 0 else None item_rate = (1000.0 * items_processed / median_latency_ms) if median_latency_ms > 0 and items_processed > 0 else 0.0 return { "model": weights, "device": device, "imgsz": imgsz, "source_kind": source_kind, "items_processed": items_processed, "median_latency_ms": median_latency_ms, "median_ms_per_item": median_ms_per_item, "fps": fps, "item_rate": item_rate, "params": format_params(get_param_count(model)), "size": format_size(weights), } def print_results(results): header = ( f"{'Model':<20} {'Device':<8} {'Source':<10} {'Items':<8} {'Median Total (ms)':<20} " f"{'ms/item':<12} {'item/s':<10} {'Params':<12} {'Size':<20}" ) print(header) print("-" * len(header)) for result in results: ms_per_item = f"{result['median_ms_per_item']:.2f}" if result["median_ms_per_item"] is not None else "n/a" print( f"{result['model']:<20} {result['device']:<8} {result['source_kind']:<10} {result['items_processed']:<8} " f"{result['median_latency_ms']:<20.2f} {ms_per_item:<12} {result['item_rate']:<10.2f} " f"{result['params']:<12} {result['size']:<20}" ) def main(): args = parse_args() results = [ benchmark_model( weights=model_name, source=args.source, imgsz=args.imgsz, conf=args.conf, device=args.device, warmup=args.warmup, runs=args.runs, max_items=args.max_items, ) for model_name in args.models ] print_results(results) if __name__ == "__main__": main() Let us walk through the key parts of this script so you understand exactly what is happening. parse_args : sets up the CLI. You pass in one or more models (e.g., yolo26n.pt and yolo12n.pt ), a source image or video, and optional knobs for image size, device, warmup iterations, and timed runs. The max-items flag is especially useful for video benchmarks, it caps how many frames get processed per run so you are not sitting through an entire clip. classify_source : figures out whether your input is a single image, a video, a directory of images, or a live stream. This matters because image inference runs in one shot, while video and streams use Ultralytics’ stream=True generator to process frames lazily. timed_predict : is the core timing function. It wraps a single prediction pass with time.perf_counter() calls. For images, it runs a standard model.predict(...) . For videos and streams, it iterates through the streaming generator and counts frames, optionally stopping early at max_items . The function returns elapsed time, items processed, and source type. benchmark_model : orchestrates the full benchmark for one model. It loads the checkpoint, runs the specified number of warmup iterations (to reduce first-run overhead such as graph compilation and cache effects), then collects timing data over the timed runs. From the raw timings, it computes median latency, FPS, per-item throughput, parameter count, and file size. print_results : formats everything into a readable terminal table so you can eyeball the comparison immediately. Here is the core usage pattern: python benchmark_yolo_macos.py \ --models yolo26n.pt yolo12n.pt \ --source traffic_clip.mp4 \ --imgsz 640 \ --device mps \ --warmup 5 \ --runs 30 \ --max-items 300 In this lesson, we use yolo12n.pt as the baseline because it is the most recent predecessor available through the Ultralytics package before YOLO26. The benchmark methodology matters more than the exact baseline label, as long as the comparison stays controlled, you get an honest picture of where YOLO26 stands. If you want a second benchmark perspective, cite the official Ultralytics CPU ONNX and T4 TensorRT numbers alongside your MacBook measurements. That gives your readers both a vendor-published reference point and a local reproducible benchmark. Why You Should Use Median Latency Always use median latency instead of a single run or a raw average from a tiny sample. Your first run may include checkpoint download, graph setup, cache effects, or backend warmup. Median latency after warmup gives you a more stable number. CPU versus MPS On a MacBook, you should benchmark both if time permits. CPU Benchmark CPU numbers help you evaluate edge-style deployment behavior and align well with Ultralytics’ published CPU ONNX comparisons. MPS Benchmark MPS numbers tell you how the model feels on Apple Silicon in day-to-day local development. Those 2 measurements answer different questions, so it is okay to report both as long as you keep the methodology clear. YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Benchmark Results on macOS Now let us look at the actual numbers. What We Compared For this lesson, we ran the YOLO26 vs YOLO12 comparison on the same MacBook using the companion script. The focus is on the video benchmark because that is where you will see the real difference in a streaming workload. Video Benchmark on MPS (YOLO26 vs YOLO12) Source: the first 300 frames of traffic.mp4 using --max-items 300 so the benchmark reflects a real streaming-style workload. Figure 9: YOLO26 vs. YOLO12 benchmark on the Apple Silicon MPS backend (source: image by the author). This is where the YOLO26 model really shines. Across 300 frames of video, YOLO26n runs at 9.81 ms/frame compared to 12.40 ms/frame for YOLO12n. In throughput terms, that is roughly a 30% advantage for YOLO26n, going from 80.62 FPS to 101.90 FPS on the same Apple Silicon hardware. That is not a rounding error. That is the kind of gain you will actually feel in a real-time object detection pipeline, especially when you are processing continuous video streams. As shown in Figure 10 from Ultralytics , YOLO26 achieves a superior accuracy–latency trade-off, delivering higher mean average precision (mAP) at comparable or lower inference latency than previous YOLO versions. Figure 10: Official YOLO26 benchmark results comparing accuracy and latency across model sizes using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA T4 GPU (source: Ultralytics YOLO26 ). YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Visual Detection Quality Comparison Benchmarks matter, but they do not tell the full story. A fast detector that misses obvious objects is not useful. What to Look For When you inspect predictions, look for the following. Missed Detections Does one model consistently ignore small or partially occluded objects? Duplicate Detections This is especially interesting in the context of end-to-end detection. If the pipeline is NMS-free by default, the model still needs to remain visually clean and stable. Box Tightness Are the boxes reasonably aligned to the target object, or do they feel loose and noisy? Confidence Behavior Are confidence scores calibrated sensibly, or does one model appear overconfident on poor detections? These qualitative observations help readers connect the benchmark table to what they would actually see in a deployment pipeline. Figure 11: Prediction comparison between YOLO12 (top) and YOLO26 (bottom). Both models detect many of the same vehicles, but their class labels and confidence scores differ. The foreground red vehicle is labeled “bus” by YOLO12 and “truck” by YOLO26 (source: image by the author). When to Use the YOLO26 Model By this point, the more important question is not whether YOLO26 is new. It is whether it fits your project. When YOLO26 Is a Strong Fit Edge and On-Device Deployment If you want a detector designed with export and deployment in mind, YOLO26 is a compelling candidate. Simpler Inference Pipelines If reducing post-processing complexity helps your stack, the end-to-end default path is a real advantage. Fast Local Prototyping on macOS If your day-to-day development machine is a MacBook, YOLO26 gives you a practical way to prototype, test, and benchmark without immediately moving to a remote GPU workflow. Figure 12: Where YOLO26 fits best: edge devices, robotics, video analytics, and industrial inspection (source: image by the author). When to Benchmark Carefully Before Committing Your Deployment Backend Is Highly Specialized If your production stack depends on a very specific runtime, export path, or hardware accelerator, always verify real performance on that target rather than assuming the default PyTorch experience will transfer directly. You Already Have a Tuned Baseline If an older YOLO variant is already integrated, optimized, and stable in your stack, YOLO26 should earn its place with measurable gains in speed, simplicity, or accuracy. YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS

In this lesson, you will learn what YOLO26 is, what changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 architecture compared to earlier releases, how to run YOLO26 object detection on images, video, and webcam streams on macOS, and how to benchmark YOLO26 against YOLO12n where we measured nearly 30% throughput gains on video.

This lesson is the 1st in a 2-part series on YOLO26:

  1. YOLO26 Object Detection Tutorial: Benchmarking on macOS (this tutorial)
  2. Lesson 2

To learn what YOLO26 is and how it compares to YOLO12 on macOS, just keep reading.

Looking for the source code to this post? Jump Right To The Downloads Section
What Is YOLO26?

If you have followed the You Only Look Once (YOLO) family over the years, you already know the pattern. Every release promises better speed, better accuracy, or a cleaner deployment story. Sometimes that means small gains. Sometimes it means a meaningful shift in how the detector behaves in production.

YOLO26 is interesting because it is not just another checkpoint refresh. Ultralytics presents it as an end-to-end detector with NMS-free inference by default, along with changes aimed at faster central processing unit (CPU) execution and cleaner edge deployment. Those claims matter because many real-world YOLO systems for real-time object detection do not run on large data center graphics processing units (GPUs). They run on laptops, edge boxes, personal computers (PCs), robotics platforms, and embedded devices where simplicity and latency matter.

In this lesson, you will answer 4 practical questions:

  • What changed in YOLO26 compared with earlier Ultralytics YOLO releases?
  • How do you run YOLO26 on macOS for images, videos, and webcam streams?
  • What do the YOLO26 model outputs actually look like in Python?
  • How does YOLO26 vs YOLO12 performance stack up on a MacBook?

By the end of this lesson, you will have a grounded understanding of what YOLO26 is, a reproducible benchmark workflow, and concrete numbers showing YOLO26 object detection running nearly 30% faster than YOLO12n on video.

Why YOLO26 Matters for Real-Time Object Detection

The easiest way to misunderstand a new detector release is to treat it like a version number bump and move on. That misses the point.

What makes the Ultralytics YOLO26 release worth paying attention to is not just accuracy. It is the combination of 3 practical ideas.

End-to-End Detection

Traditional real-time detectors usually produce many overlapping candidate boxes and then rely on non-maximum suppression (NMS) to prune duplicates. That works well, but it adds a post-processing stage and a few more tuning knobs.

Ultralytics documents YOLO26 as using an end-to-end path by default, which means the standard inference path no longer depends on NMS in the same way earlier pipelines did. In plain English, the model is designed to produce a more direct set of final detections.

Why NMS Becomes a Performance Tax

NMS sounds simple in theory, but in practice it behaves like an extra tax on every frame. After the model generates candidate boxes, the pipeline still has to filter them, sort them, and suppress overlaps based on intersection over union (IoU). That adds more work after the neural network has already done its main job.

On desktop GPUs, that cost may be easy to hide. On CPUs and edge accelerators, it can become much more visible. Even worse, it can complicate deployment because post-processing is not always handled by the same optimized runtime that executes the network itself.

Why Latency Variability Matters

NMS is also scene-dependent. A sparse image with very few confident detections is cheap to process. A crowded frame with many overlapping candidates demands more sorting and more overlap checks. That means latency can fluctuate based on what the camera sees.

For robotics, industrial inspection, and real-time video systems, predictable timing matters. Even if YOLO26 does not make every environment perfectly deterministic, removing NMS from the standard inference path reduces one major source of latency jitter.

Faster CPU-Oriented Deployment

On paper, the official YOLO26 documentation emphasizes stronger CPU performance, especially for deployment scenarios where a heavy GPU stack is not the main story. That matters on macOS because many of you prototype on Apple laptops and often need a reliable local baseline before thinking about mobile, edge, or cloud deployment.

Cleaner Edge Story

YOLO26 is also positioned as an edge-first release. That does not mean it is only for edge devices. It means the design decisions try to reduce deployment friction across hardware and export formats.

If you are building applications for robotics, industrial inspection, or always-on video analytics, those changes are not academic. They directly affect latency, integration complexity, and operational cost.

What Changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 Architecture

Now let us make that concrete.

End-to-End, NMS-Free Inference by Default

According to the public Ultralytics documentation, YOLO26 uses a one-to-one head by default for end-to-end prediction, and this default path does not require NMS. Ultralytics also notes that you can still switch back to a more traditional path by setting end2end=False for workflows that need compatibility with NMS-based post-processing.

That distinction is worth understanding.

Traditional Detector Pipeline

In a traditional pipeline, the detector produces many candidate boxes. Post-processing then removes duplicates and overlapping boxes with NMS. The final detection quality can depend on the confidence score and IoU thresholds.

YOLO26 Default Pipeline

In the default YOLO26 path, the detector is configured to produce final detections directly enough that NMS is not part of the standard prediction path. This reduces post-processing overhead and simplifies deployment logic.

For you as a practitioner, the biggest takeaway is simple: fewer moving parts after the forward pass usually makes inference pipelines easier to reason about and easier to deploy.

The One-to-Many Legacy

Earlier YOLO-style detectors typically learn through a one-to-many assignment strategy, where multiple predictions may be associated with the same ground-truth object during training. That is useful for optimization and recall, but it also leaves the model with a dense set of redundant candidates that need cleanup afterward.

YOLO26 moves the default inference story closer to one-to-one prediction. Instead of asking post-processing to resolve a large pile of overlapping candidates, the deployed model is designed to produce a cleaner final set of object hypotheses.

Figure 1: Traditional object detection versus YOLO26 end-to-end detection (source: image by the author).
DFL Removal and Export Friendliness

Ultralytics also highlights Distribution Focal Loss (DFL) removal as a major change in YOLO26. The practical benefit is not that you need to memorize every detail of the underlying loss formulation. The practical benefit is cleaner export behavior and wider edge compatibility.

That matters if you eventually want to move from PyTorch to Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX), Core ML, NCNN, or another deployment target without spending your entire week debugging export quirks.

It also matters because older regression heads often require extra decoding logic after the raw network output. By simplifying that path, YOLO26 makes the exported graph easier to deploy and easier to inspect.

Training-Side Changes

Ultralytics documents several training-related updates for YOLO26, including Progressive Loss (ProgLoss), Small-Target-Aware Label Assignment (STAL), and a MuSGD optimizer. You do not need to dive deep into those right now because this lesson is centered on inference and benchmarking, not custom training. Still, it is useful to know that YOLO26 is not only an inference story. Some of its improvements are tied to how the model was trained in the first place.

Why One-to-One Training Is Hard

One reason NMS-free detection took time to mature is that strict one-to-one supervision is harder to optimize. If the model is forced to commit to one prediction per object too early, the learning signal can become sparse and unstable.

Dual-Head Intuition

The broader end-to-end YOLO line addresses that problem by combining rich training supervision with a cleaner deployment path. The key intuition is that the model can still learn from denser training signals internally while using a one-to-one style head for final inference.

You do not need every implementation detail in this lesson, but it helps to know that YOLO26 is not simply “YOLO with NMS turned off.” The clean inference behavior is supported by training design.

What to Defer to Lesson 2

We should keep the deeper training mechanics for Lesson 2. That is the right place to discuss how label assignment, optimizer choice, and architecture decisions affect custom training results.

CPU Speed Improvements

Ultralytics specifically claims large CPU-side gains for YOLO26. That is one of the main reasons this lesson focuses on a MacBook workflow. If a detector says it is edge-first and CPU-aware, it should be able to prove that in a benchmark you can reproduce locally.

Figure 2: High-level reasons YOLO26 matters in practice: end-to-end inference, CPU speed, and edge deployment (source: image by the author).
Configuring Your Development Environment

To follow this guide, you need to have the Ultralytics package installed on your system.

Luckily, Ultralytics is pip-installable:

$ pip install -U ultralytics

If you need help configuring your development environment for Ultralytics and YOLO26, we highly recommend creating a fresh virtual environment first.
