All that said, are you:

  • Short on time?
  • Learning on your employer’s administratively locked system?
  • Wanting to skip the hassle of fighting with the command line, package managers, and virtual environments?
  • Ready to run the code immediately on your Windows, macOS, or Linux system?

Then join PyImageSearch University today!

Gain access to Jupyter Notebooks for this tutorial and other PyImageSearch guides pre-configured to run on Google Colab’s ecosystem right in your web browser! No installation required.

And best of all, these Jupyter Notebooks will run on Windows, macOS, and Linux!

Project Structure

The following is a short directory structure:

.
├── benchmark_yolo_macos.py
├── yolo26n.pt
├── yolo12n.pt
└── /
    └── traffic_clip.mp4

The benchmark_yolo_macos.py script is the main workhorse. The model checkpoints are downloaded automatically by Ultralytics the first time you reference them.

Installing the Ultralytics YOLO26 Model on macOS

Let us move from theory to practice.

Create a Clean Python Environment

If you already have a computer vision environment on your Mac, resist the temptation to pile more packages into it. Use a fresh environment.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
Install Ultralytics

With the environment active, install the Ultralytics package:

pip install -U ultralytics

At the time of writing, this is the cleanest way to access YOLO26 through the official Python and CLI interfaces.

Verify the Installation

You can verify the install in either Python or the command-line interface (CLI).

CLI Check 
yolo version
Python Check 
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
print(model.task)

The first time you load a pretrained checkpoint, Ultralytics will download it automatically if it is not already present on your machine.

Optional: Check for Apple Silicon Acceleration

If you are on Apple Silicon, it is useful to know whether the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) backend is available.

import torch

print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available())
print("MPS built:", torch.backends.mps.is_built())

If MPS is available, you can run predictions with device="mps". If not, stay on CPU and keep the benchmark methodology consistent.


Figure 3: Installing the Ultralytics package and verifying a YOLO26 model on macOS (source: image by the author).
Running YOLO26 Object Detection on Images, Video, and Webcam Streams

Now you are ready to run the model.

First Image Inference

The smallest useful example is a single image.

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
results = model("image.jpg")

That line performs the entire inference pass and returns a list of Results objects, one per image.

If you want to be explicit about the prediction application programming interface (API) and device choice, do this instead:

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
results = model.predict(
    source="image.jpg",
    imgsz=640,
    conf=0.25,
    device="mps",  # use "cpu" if MPS is unavailable
)


Figure 4: Running YOLO26 on a single image using the Ultralytics Python API (source: image by the author).
Running on a Folder of Images

When you pass a directory, Ultralytics will iterate through the media automatically.

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
results = model.predict(source="images/", imgsz=640, conf=0.25, device="mps")

This is a fast way to build a qualitative feel for the model before you benchmark it.

Running on a Video File

For video inference, the API stays almost identical.

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
results = model.predict(source="sample_video.mp4", show=True, device="mps")

If you want saved output rather than a live preview window, add save=True.

Running Real-Time Webcam Detection

Webcam inference is where macOS users get an immediate feel for real-world responsiveness.

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
model.predict(source=0, show=True, device="mps")
Figure 5: Real-time webcam detection with YOLO26 on macOS (source: image by the author).
Understanding YOLO26 Prediction Outputs

Running inference is only half the story. If you are going to build with YOLO26, you also need to understand what comes back.

The Results Object

A prediction call returns a list of Results objects. In the single-image case, you usually care about results[0].

from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolo26n.pt")
results = model("image.jpg")
result = results[0]
Inspect Boxes, Classes, and Confidences

The boxes are stored in result.boxes.

boxes = result.boxes

print("Number of detections:", len(boxes))
print("Classes:", boxes.cls)
print("Confidences:", boxes.conf)
print("XYXY boxes:", boxes.xyxy)

In practice, the most useful fields are the following.

boxes.xyxy

Bounding boxes in corner format: (x1, y1, x2, y2).

boxes.conf

Confidence scores for each detection.

boxes.cls

Predicted class IDs.

Map Class IDs Back to Labels

Ultralytics stores class name metadata on the model.

names = result.names

for box in result.boxes:
    class_id = int(box.cls.item())
    confidence = float(box.conf.item())
    label = names[class_id]
    print(label, confidence)
Inspect Preprocessing, Inference, and Postprocessing Time

Ultralytics Results objects also expose timing information.

print(result.speed)

This usually gives you a dictionary with timings for preprocessing, inference, and postprocessing, measured in milliseconds per image. That is very useful for debugging, but for a fair benchmark we still want a consistent, external timing harness around repeated runs.

What True End-to-End Export Looks Like

One practical way to verify the deployment story is to export the model and inspect the graph.

If you export YOLO26 to ONNX and open it in Netron, the goal is not to memorize every operator. The goal is to confirm that the exported graph is much closer to the final inference path used by the application than older detector exports that still depend on heavier post-processing outside the network.

Older YOLO-Style Export

The exported graph often ends in dense predictions that still need external filtering, decoding, or NMS-like logic before they become a clean set of final detections.

YOLO12 vs. YOLO26: ONNX Export Comparison

In YOLO12, the ONNX export shown in Figure 6 includes non-maximum suppression (NMS) directly inside the model graph. The graph contains an explicit NonMaxSuppression node followed by a sequence of Gather, Slice, and Concat operations to filter and format the final detections.

This design produces ready-to-use outputs but tightly couples post-processing with the model itself. As a result, it becomes harder to customize thresholds, experiment with alternative filtering strategies, or adapt the pipeline for different deployment environments.

Additionally, embedding NMS inside the graph introduces extra operations during inference, which can contribute to higher latency depending on the execution backend and hardware.

Figure 6: ONNX graph of YOLO12 showing embedded non-maximum suppression (NMS) and associated post-processing operations within the model (source: image by the author).

In contrast, YOLO26 removes non-maximum suppression from the model graph entirely. As illustrated in Figure 7, the exported ONNX graph produces a single consolidated output tensor without any embedded NMS logic.

Figure 7: ONNX graph of YOLO26 producing a unified output tensor without embedded NMS, enabling external post-processing (source: image by the author).

This design shifts post-processing outside the model, resulting in a cleaner and more modular pipeline. Developers can control filtering, thresholding, and downstream processing explicitly, making the system easier to optimize, debug, and integrate with tracking and analytics systems.

In practice, this separation can also improve end-to-end latency, especially when using optimized or hardware-accelerated post-processing outside the model graph.

The exported graph is much closer to the final detection representation consumed by the application. This is what is typically meant when describing the model as end-to-end for inference.

The key difference is not just the model architecture, but where post-processing is performed inside the graph versus in the surrounding application pipeline.

YOLO26 Benchmarking Methodology on a MacBook

This is the section that separates a useful lesson from a casual demo.

What You Want to Measure

For Lesson 1, focus on 4 metrics:

  • Median latency per image
  • Throughput in frames per second (FPS)
  • Model size on disk
  • Parameter count

Memory usage is also valuable, but it is easier to measure unreliably. If you include it, document exactly how you measured it.

Keep Your Benchmark Honest

When people publish model comparisons, they often change too many variables at once. Do not do that.

Keep these fixed across both models:

  • Same machine
  • Same device target, either CPU or MPS
  • Same input image size
  • Same batch size
  • Same test image or test image set
  • Same number of warmup iterations
  • Same number of timed iterations

If you cannot control those variables, your comparison becomes anecdotal.


Figure 8: Benchmark protocol used to compare YOLO26 and the baseline model on a MacBook (source: image by the author).
A Practical Benchmark Harness for YOLO Real-Time Object Detection

To make this lesson fully reproducible, we have included a companion script called benchmark_yolo_macos.py. You can use it to benchmark any combination of YOLO checkpoints on your own machine.

At a high level, the script does the following:

  • Loads one or more Ultralytics YOLO checkpoints
  • Performs warmup runs to stabilize the runtime
  • Measures wall-clock latency over repeated predictions
  • Reports median latency and FPS
  • Extracts parameter counts from the loaded model
  • Reports checkpoint file size on disk

Here is the full script:

import argparse
import statistics
import time
from pathlib import Path

from ultralytics import YOLO


def parse_args():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Benchmark YOLO models on macOS.")
    parser.add_argument("--models", nargs="+", required=True, help="Model weights to benchmark.")
    parser.add_argument("--source", required=True, help="Image, folder, or video source for inference.")
    parser.add_argument("--imgsz", type=int, default=640, help="Inference image size.")
    parser.add_argument("--device", default="cpu", help="Inference device, e.g. cpu or mps.")
    parser.add_argument("--conf", type=float, default=0.25, help="Confidence threshold.")
    parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=5, help="Warmup iterations.")
    parser.add_argument("--runs", type=int, default=30, help="Timed iterations.")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--max-items",
        type=int,
        default=None,
        help="Maximum number of frames/items to process per run for videos, folders, or streams.",
    )
    return parser.parse_args()


def get_param_count(model):
    if hasattr(model.model, "parameters"):
        return sum(parameter.numel() for parameter in model.model.parameters())
    return None


def format_params(param_count):
    if param_count is None:
        return "n/a"
    return f"{param_count / 1_000_000:.2f}M"


def format_size(weights_path):
    path = Path(weights_path)
    if path.exists() and path.is_file():
        return f"{path.stat().st_size / (1024 * 1024):.2f} MB"
    return "downloaded/cache-managed"


IMAGE_SUFFIXES = {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png", ".bmp", ".tif", ".tiff", ".webp"}
VIDEO_SUFFIXES = {".mp4", ".mov", ".m4v", ".avi", ".mkv", ".webm", ".mpg", ".mpeg"}


def classify_source(source):
    source_str = str(source)
    if source_str.isdigit():
        return "stream"

    path = Path(source_str).expanduser()
    if path.is_dir():
        return "collection"

    suffix = path.suffix.lower()
    if suffix in IMAGE_SUFFIXES:
        return "image"
    if suffix in VIDEO_SUFFIXES:
        return "video"
    return "collection"


def timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=None):
    source_kind = classify_source(source)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    if source_kind == "image":
        model.predict(source=source, imgsz=imgsz, conf=conf, device=device, verbose=False)
        items_processed = 1
    else:
        items_processed = 0
        for _ in model.predict(source=source, imgsz=imgsz, conf=conf, device=device, verbose=False, stream=True):
            items_processed += 1
            if max_items is not None and items_processed >= max_items:
                break
    end = time.perf_counter()
    return {
        "elapsed_ms": (end - start) * 1000.0,
        "items_processed": items_processed,
        "source_kind": source_kind,
    }


def benchmark_model(weights, source, imgsz, conf, device, warmup, runs, max_items=None):
    model = YOLO(weights)

    for _ in range(warmup):
        timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=max_items)

    timings = [timed_predict(model, source, imgsz, conf, device, max_items=max_items) for _ in range(runs)]
    elapsed_values = [timing["elapsed_ms"] for timing in timings]
    items_processed = timings[-1]["items_processed"] if timings else 0
    source_kind = timings[-1]["source_kind"] if timings else classify_source(source)
    median_latency_ms = statistics.median(elapsed_values)
    fps = 1000.0 / median_latency_ms if median_latency_ms > 0 else 0.0
    median_ms_per_item = median_latency_ms / items_processed if items_processed > 0 else None
    item_rate = (1000.0 * items_processed / median_latency_ms) if median_latency_ms > 0 and items_processed > 0 else 0.0

    return {
        "model": weights,
        "device": device,
        "imgsz": imgsz,
        "source_kind": source_kind,
        "items_processed": items_processed,
        "median_latency_ms": median_latency_ms,
        "median_ms_per_item": median_ms_per_item,
        "fps": fps,
        "item_rate": item_rate,
        "params": format_params(get_param_count(model)),
        "size": format_size(weights),
    }


def print_results(results):
    header = (
        f"{'Model':<20} {'Device':<8} {'Source':<10} {'Items':<8} {'Median Total (ms)':<20} "
        f"{'ms/item':<12} {'item/s':<10} {'Params':<12} {'Size':<20}"
    )
    print(header)
    print("-" * len(header))
    for result in results:
        ms_per_item = f"{result['median_ms_per_item']:.2f}" if result["median_ms_per_item"] is not None else "n/a"
        print(
            f"{result['model']:<20} {result['device']:<8} {result['source_kind']:<10} {result['items_processed']:<8} "
            f"{result['median_latency_ms']:<20.2f} {ms_per_item:<12} {result['item_rate']:<10.2f} "
            f"{result['params']:<12} {result['size']:<20}"
        )


def main():
    args = parse_args()
    results = [
        benchmark_model(
            weights=model_name,
            source=args.source,
            imgsz=args.imgsz,
            conf=args.conf,
            device=args.device,
            warmup=args.warmup,
            runs=args.runs,
            max_items=args.max_items,
        )
        for model_name in args.models
    ]
    print_results(results)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Let us walk through the key parts of this script so you understand exactly what is happening.

  • parse_args: sets up the CLI. You pass in one or more models (e.g., yolo26n.pt and yolo12n.pt), a source image or video, and optional knobs for image size, device, warmup iterations, and timed runs. The max-items flag is especially useful for video benchmarks, it caps how many frames get processed per run so you are not sitting through an entire clip.
  • classify_source: figures out whether your input is a single image, a video, a directory of images, or a live stream. This matters because image inference runs in one shot, while video and streams use Ultralytics’ stream=True generator to process frames lazily.
  • timed_predict: is the core timing function. It wraps a single prediction pass with time.perf_counter() calls. For images, it runs a standard model.predict(...). For videos and streams, it iterates through the streaming generator and counts frames, optionally stopping early at max_items. The function returns elapsed time, items processed, and source type.
  • benchmark_model: orchestrates the full benchmark for one model. It loads the checkpoint, runs the specified number of warmup iterations (to reduce first-run overhead such as graph compilation and cache effects), then collects timing data over the timed runs. From the raw timings, it computes median latency, FPS, per-item throughput, parameter count, and file size.
  • print_results: formats everything into a readable terminal table so you can eyeball the comparison immediately.

Here is the core usage pattern:

python benchmark_yolo_macos.py \
  --models yolo26n.pt yolo12n.pt \
  --source traffic_clip.mp4 \
  --imgsz 640 \
  --device mps \
  --warmup 5 \
  --runs 30 \
  --max-items 300

In this lesson, we use yolo12n.pt as the baseline because it is the most recent predecessor available through the Ultralytics package before YOLO26. The benchmark methodology matters more than the exact baseline label, as long as the comparison stays controlled, you get an honest picture of where YOLO26 stands.

If you want a second benchmark perspective, cite the official Ultralytics CPU ONNX and T4 TensorRT numbers alongside your MacBook measurements. That gives your readers both a vendor-published reference point and a local reproducible benchmark.

Why You Should Use Median Latency

Always use median latency instead of a single run or a raw average from a tiny sample. Your first run may include checkpoint download, graph setup, cache effects, or backend warmup. Median latency after warmup gives you a more stable number.

CPU versus MPS

On a MacBook, you should benchmark both if time permits.

CPU Benchmark

CPU numbers help you evaluate edge-style deployment behavior and align well with Ultralytics’ published CPU ONNX comparisons.

MPS Benchmark

MPS numbers tell you how the model feels on Apple Silicon in day-to-day local development.

Those 2 measurements answer different questions, so it is okay to report both as long as you keep the methodology clear.

YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Benchmark Results on macOS

Now let us look at the actual numbers.

What We Compared

For this lesson, we ran the YOLO26 vs YOLO12 comparison on the same MacBook using the companion script. The focus is on the video benchmark because that is where you will see the real difference in a streaming workload.

Video Benchmark on MPS (YOLO26 vs YOLO12)

Source: the first 300 frames of traffic.mp4 using --max-items 300 so the benchmark reflects a real streaming-style workload.

Figure 9: YOLO26 vs. YOLO12 benchmark on the Apple Silicon MPS backend (source: image by the author).

This is where the YOLO26 model really shines. Across 300 frames of video, YOLO26n runs at 9.81 ms/frame compared to 12.40 ms/frame for YOLO12n. In throughput terms, that is roughly a 30% advantage for YOLO26n, going from 80.62 FPS to 101.90 FPS on the same Apple Silicon hardware.

That is not a rounding error. That is the kind of gain you will actually feel in a real-time object detection pipeline, especially when you are processing continuous video streams.

As shown in Figure 10 from Ultralytics, YOLO26 achieves a superior accuracy–latency trade-off, delivering higher mean average precision (mAP) at comparable or lower inference latency than previous YOLO versions.

Figure 10: Official YOLO26 benchmark results comparing accuracy and latency across model sizes using TensorRT FP16 on an NVIDIA T4 GPU (source: Ultralytics YOLO26).
YOLO26 vs YOLO12: Visual Detection Quality Comparison

Benchmarks matter, but they do not tell the full story. A fast detector that misses obvious objects is not useful.

What to Look For

When you inspect predictions, look for the following.

Missed Detections

Does one model consistently ignore small or partially occluded objects?

Duplicate Detections

This is especially interesting in the context of end-to-end detection. If the pipeline is NMS-free by default, the model still needs to remain visually clean and stable.

Box Tightness

Are the boxes reasonably aligned to the target object, or do they feel loose and noisy?

Confidence Behavior

Are confidence scores calibrated sensibly, or does one model appear overconfident on poor detections?

These qualitative observations help readers connect the benchmark table to what they would actually see in a deployment pipeline.

Figure 11: Prediction comparison between YOLO12 (top) and YOLO26 (bottom). Both models detect many of the same vehicles, but their class labels and confidence scores differ. The foreground red vehicle is labeled “bus” by YOLO12 and “truck” by YOLO26 (source: image by the author). When to Use the YOLO26 Model

By this point, the more important question is not whether YOLO26 is new. It is whether it fits your project.

When YOLO26 Is a Strong Fit Edge and On-Device Deployment

If you want a detector designed with export and deployment in mind, YOLO26 is a compelling candidate.

Simpler Inference Pipelines

If reducing post-processing complexity helps your stack, the end-to-end default path is a real advantage.

Fast Local Prototyping on macOS

If your day-to-day development machine is a MacBook, YOLO26 gives you a practical way to prototype, test, and benchmark without immediately moving to a remote GPU workflow.


Figure 12: Where YOLO26 fits best: edge devices, robotics, video analytics, and industrial inspection (source: image by the author).
When to Benchmark Carefully Before Committing Your Deployment Backend Is Highly Specialized

If your production stack depends on a very specific runtime, export path, or hardware accelerator, always verify real performance on that target rather than assuming the default PyTorch experience will transfer directly.

You Already Have a Tuned Baseline

If an older YOLO variant is already integrated, optimized, and stable in your stack, YOLO26 should earn its place with measurable gains in speed, simplicity, or accuracy.

Summary

In this lesson, you moved beyond the standard “pip install and predict” workflow and explored YOLO26 as both a model and an engineering release.

You learned what changed in the Ultralytics YOLO26 architecture compared to its predecessors, why those changes matter for real-time object detection, and how to verify the differences on your own hardware.

You installed the Ultralytics YOLO26 model on macOS, ran inference on images, video, and a live webcam feed, and examined the prediction outputs to understand what the model actually returns.

You also looked at the architectural changes under the hood, including end-to-end NMS-free inference, DFL removal for cleaner exports, and the training-side improvements that contribute to faster CPU deployment.

The central focus of this lesson was reproducible benchmarking. You used a companion script, benchmark_yolo_macos.py, to measure YOLO26n against YOLO12n on the same Apple Silicon hardware under identical conditions.

Over 300 frames of traffic video on MPS, YOLO26n reached 101.90 FPS compared to 80.62 FPS for YOLO12n, a nearly 30% throughput advantage. That gap is not a rounding error. It is the kind of gain you will actually feel in a streaming pipeline.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms

—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab

We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.

A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.

As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.

Here’s why AI safety needs to go further.

Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships

Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.

A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.

The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off?
Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality.

—Robin George Andrews

The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story.

items.title: Bihar Partners with IT Cos to Train Government School Teachers In AI
items.summary: Bihar’s Education Department has partnered with 11 IT firms, including Google Education, to equip government school teachers with skills in artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies. The initiative will receive support from the Union government’s skill development department and include practical IT training. It is part of Bihar’s broader plan to expand digital learning, including making computer education compulsory from Class 6 in government schools from the next academic session and introducing smart classrooms in 700 model schools. Bihar Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the training would prioritise AI, with the aim of improving teaching quality, according to Dainik Jagran. The Education Department is arranging centralised training at the State Council of Educational Research and Training (SCERT) campus. The participating companies will conduct sessions in separate batches, while school principals will nominate teachers for the programme. The training is expected to help educators develop digital skills they can apply in school settings. The state aims to have the training arrangements in place by January, according to Dainik Jagran. However, the report did not specify how many teachers will participate or how long the training will last. Alongside the teacher training initiative, Bihar plans to make computer education compulsory for students from 6th standard and above in all government schools from the next academic session. The move is intended to introduce students to digital learning earlier in their schooling. The department also plans to strengthen IT infrastructure to support the expansion of computer education. The department plans smart classrooms for 700 model schools, with facilities expected to extend to other government schools in phases. The smart classroom rollout, alongside teacher training and compulsory computer education, is part of Bihar’s broader plan to expand technology use in government schools. Its progress will depend on delivering the training and installing the planned infrastructure.

items.title: AI is creating jobs as well as erasing them – but how rewarding are they?
items.summary: Kathryn Conrad & Digit / Isolation / Licenced by CC-BY 4.0 By Akhil Bhardwaj , University of Bath Don’t believe the hype about AI taking over all forms of work . Most of the evidence to date suggests large-scale job losses are limited . But what is changing is the way work is organised. One area of increased employment is in people “cleaning up” after large language models (LLMs), or quality controlling them. The sales pitch is that these AI systems can program code, write reports, analyse data and automate routine decisions faster and better than humans, all at negligible marginal cost. In theory, this should free people to focus on higher-level thinking, and leisure. In practice, AI agents produce vast amounts of “almost right” output – but there are still errors, hallucinations and odd gaps in judgment that a real person has to catch. The resulting jobs, often known as AI remediation , vary in their skill and remuneration levels. Some AI companies are now hiring experienced professionals in many different fields to ensure their agents are producing work of requisite quality – and to help them change that if not. But there is also a more subtle shift in job responsibilities within many organisations. Some white-collar workers in industries such as finance, tech and retail are suggesting that AI can add to, rather than reduce, their workload, because of the need to monitor so-called “workslop” . This can also undermine trust in colleagues who are using AI agents. A 2025 Harvard Business Review report quoted a retail director who lamented spending “more time following up on the information [provided by AI] and checking it with my own research. I then had to waste even more time setting up meetings with other supervisors to address the issue.” Public sector slop The public sector risks being drawn into this “AI repair” logic. The UK government (among many others) is experimenting with AI for tasks such as summarising consultation responses, drafting correspondence and analysing sentiment in citizen feedback. Official guidance for civil servants encourages cautious use of generative AI, while warning that its outputs can be misleading and must be independently verified. This means, if public services start producing large volumes of AI-generated analysis and letters, they will also have to create new positions whose main responsibility is to monitor, check and correct that output before it reaches citizens or feeds into policy. How much of the apparent AI efficiency gain will be consumed by people silently tidying up after systems that are sold as automatic? We already know what can happen when AI automation goes wrong in government. In the Netherlands, tax authorities used algorithms to generate risk scores for supposed fraud and automatically flag families for investigation. Tens of thousands of parents – many from minorities – were wrongly accused of fraud , forced to repay benefits they did not owe, and pushed into debt or bankruptcy. Here, the problem was not just the output but the absence of robust human supervision, able to question the machine’s verdict before lives were destroyed. Any public-sector wave of generative AI adoption will have to invest heavily in exactly that kind of supervision , to avoid repeating the same harms at a larger scale. There is a deeper trap here. The tokens (the basic building blocks of data processed by LLMs) that generate all this output are heavily subsidised by debt-laden AI companies – but the human time needed to check and fix it is not. Many companies are deliberately pricing access below cost to build dependence on their systems. Once enough organisations have reoriented their workflows and services around a particular AI model, the company behind it can start to raise prices, limit free tiers, change terms or segment features. So the cost-benefit analysis of AI today may look very different in the future. Hidden humans There has already long been a global dimension to the “hidden humans” underpinning AI. Some of the most unpleasant aspects of AI work – chatbot moderation, data labelling, low-level annotation of images – has been outsourced to low-wage countries for many years. This work has been found to take a substantial mental toll on some of these workers, because of the disturbing nature of graphic text and images of violence, self-harm and the like. Employees in such sectors and geographies also often lack any legal protection . If AI workslop becomes the norm inside organisations, it is easy to imagine a second wave of outsourcing: the routine checking and correction of AI-generated text shipped to offshore centres – packaged as quality control, but experienced on the ground as endless, underpaid digital piecework. We can already see the work-reorganisation side of this in translation services . In many agencies, the main workflow is now machine translation plus “post-editing”. The AI does a first pass; freelance human translators are paid less money to correct its mistakes. Research suggests that post-editing is often paid worse than traditional translation, requires similar or greater cognitive effort, and is widely perceived as tedious and deskilling. Yet those doing this role simultaneously raise concerns about even that position being replaced in the longer term. How to push back Popular culture shows how workers can try to resist being pushed into low-status AI clean-up roles. In 2023, Hollywood writers went on strike partly because they feared studios would use AI tools to generate first drafts and then hire humans to polish them on the cheap. The resulting agreement with the Writers Guild of America set guardrails : AI cannot be credited as a writer, cannot be forced on writers, and cannot be used in ways that undercut human pay and recognition. In effect, the union fought to stop a slide into AI-janitor work, where creative professionals would spend most of their time tidying up after algorithms rather than originating stories themselves, However, translators, freelancers working in fields such as video-gaming , and other workers have far less collective bargaining power, which makes it easier for AI-driven business models to quietly make repair work as the new normal. In my view, the problem is not only economic – it is also about meaning . Most people would like to feel their work actually contributes something in the world. They want to believe they are solving problems , helping people, or contributing to making something that would not exist without them. But for at least as long as access to powerful AI systems remains cheap (and heavily subsidised), more and more people will be diverted to cleaning up the mess these systems inevitably create. How meaningful these jobs are is, I believe, a question we cannot afford to dodge. Akhil Bhardwaj , Associate Professor (Strategy and Organisation), School of Management, University of Bath This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. items.title: Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now
items.summary: Data center protests, like this one in Pennsylvania, have spread nationwide. AP Photo/Marc Levy It may not be as shocking as rogue AI agents hacking another system, but the current political resistance to data centers has taken a surprising turn: It’s bringing together strange bedfellows , from democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders to right-wing strategist Steve Bannon . Organized opposition to new data centers , made up of a coalition of varied interests, has spread across the nation. Through protests, packed zoning commission meetings, moratoriums and other government action, the resistance has upended dozens of proposed projects. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure , housing the computing resources used to train AI models. They’re also massive facilities that require extraordinary amounts of energy. By 2030, U.S. data center electricity use is expected to reach 12% of the nation’s total consumption. They carry some benefits. At the national level, data centers fuel the computing power seen as critical to U.S. competition with China. Locally, they create an uptick in jobs , especially during the construction phase, and can generate tax revenue. In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, though, the heavy costs associated with them – such as land use , higher household utility bills and environmental degradation – appear to outweigh the benefits, bringing together people who usually find themselves politically at odds. I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of AI in political campaigns is reshaping established practices and power dynamics. I believe data centers may be disrupting some of the partisan issue alignments Americans have grown to expect. Data centers, like these near Social Circle, Ga., require enormous amounts of electricity. AP Photo/Mike Stewart, File Political disruption – AI style Despite ongoing debate about the extent of and reasons for polarization, one thing is for sure: Democrats and Republicans stake out distinct positions on many issues. Pew Research Center data shows , for example, that 63% of Democrats say climate change is a very big problem facing the country, compared with 14% of Republicans, a 49-point gap. By contrast, the partisan gap on data centers is small – and getting smaller: In summer 2026, the Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans whether they support the construction of data centers in their communities. Supporters of both parties were more opposed than supportive, although opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%. That partisan gap had narrowed over the previous four months, moving from 18 to 15 points. A perfect storm This year has been marked by considerable upheaval: political, economic and technological. Americans have been hit hard with surging fuel and energy prices . And with rapid AI development, they witness real-world examples of the sort of lapses in safety that have worried both AI insiders and observers. One “rogue” attack announced in July 2026 involved OpenAI’s AI agents escaping a secure environment and autonomously – without human direction or assistance – breaking into the system of Hugging Face, another AI company. Shortly after, news broke that out-of-control AI agents were not just a one-off limited to that hack. Polling shows that majorities of both parties feel that AI technology is developing too fast, though Democrats’ levels of concern are 22 points higher than Republicans’. The gap is much smaller – 4 points – on support for government keeping AI under human control and on protecting U.S. workers. Backing for each is very high, hovering around 80%. This bipartisanship on attitudes about AI and data centers appears also to show up in alliances on the ground and, in some cases, in new organizations with a focus on thwarting data centers. For example, New York’s No Data Center FLX has organized protests, sued the local zoning board of appeals and collected almost 23,000 petition signatures in opposition to a proposed data center. Allies and adversaries Government makes decisions about data centers at all levels. In cities and counties, zoning fights draw a disparate resistance : environmentalists, folks reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests. Some bipartisanship has extended to Congress. In mid-September, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a wide margin: 417-3. The bill requires states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill, which would establish a voluntary structure, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Comparable sentiment killed the Senate version , a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change. Politics as usual As midterm elections approach, candidates up and down the ballot are blanketing the airwaves and digital channels with ads against data centers . President Donald Trump , for his part, has weighed in, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” It’s a fine line for some Republican candidates between responding to voter concerns and not alienating the president. If data center politics seem familiar, it may be because this isn’t the first issue to bring together such a diverse coalition: In the 1990s, opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement did the same, uniting organized labor and environmentalists , frequent adversaries, over concerns about job losses and pollution. That alliance never extended beyond the boundaries of its singular focus on trade agreements, though. Similarly, don’t expect data centers to permanently reshape the U.S. political landscape. Barbara A. items.title: Building Custom TypeScript Extensions and Lifecycle Hooks for Pi Agent
items.summary: Most developer teams adopting minimalist coding loops quickly discover that an off-the-shelf harness fails the moment it hits legacy monorepos. Standard runtimes rely on an immutable set of four core tools and expect flat directory structures, leaving engineers blind when custom security boundaries or pre-commit validations are required. Writing custom TypeScript extensions and lifecycle hooks for pi agent bridges this gap, letting teams inject deterministic checks directly into the agent runtime without bloating the system prompt. By hooking into the DAG execution loop, developers gain surgical control over tool arguments, state persistence, and output validation while keeping token expenditure flat. Working through production deployments revealed that relying on standard event emitters causes race conditions during multi-file refactoring tasks. This deep-dive details how to construct stateful, type-safe extensions that survive asynchronous interruptions and maintain strict execution guarantees in production. Generated by AI Infrastructure and Setup Configuring a robust extension environment starts with pinning the core runtime dependencies and establishing strict TypeScript compilation rules. Because extensions execute inside the agent’s main event loop, loose typing or unhandled promise rejections will crash the entire session state tree. Setting up the project requires importing the exact typings from @earendil-works/pi-agent-core to ensure that custom hook signatures align with the runtime's internal dispatcher. Avoid loose any declarations on hook payloads; the event context objects carry stateful references that mutate across tool execution phases. import { AgentRuntime, HookContext, ToolExecutionEvent } from '@earendil-works/pi-agent-core'; import { promises as fs } from 'node:fs'; import * as path from 'node:path'; export interface SecurityConfig { allowedPaths: string[]; blocklistPatterns: RegExp[]; } Initializing the extension harness inside an enterprise repository demands an explicit configuration loader that validates path boundaries before the runtime initializes its first tool call. Skipping this validation phase invites arbitrary file modifications during unsupervised background refactoring runs. Core Implementation Strategy Registering lifecycle hooks involves attaching middleware functions to specific interception points within the agent execution lifecycle. The core runtime exposes hooks such as beforeToolCall, afterToolExecution, and agentStart, each designed to inspect or mutate runtime parameters synchronously or asynchronously. Implementing a production-grade file modification guard requires intercepting the write and edit tool calls before they hit the disk. The following pattern inspects incoming arguments and strips out unauthorized path traversal attempts. export function registerSecurityExtension(runtime: AgentRuntime, config: SecurityConfig) { runtime.hook('beforeToolCall', async (context: HookContext) => { if (context.toolName === 'write' || context.toolName === 'edit') { const targetPath = path.resolve(context.args.path); const isAllowed = config.allowedPaths.some(p => targetPath.startsWith(path.resolve(p))); if (!isAllowed) { throw new Error(`Security violation: Modification of ${targetPath} is prohibited by runtime extension.`); } } }); } Managing state across multiple tool iterations requires leveraging the context store attached to the session DAG. Instead of relying on module-scoped global variables — which fail during concurrent worker threads — extensions must read and write state directly through the provided telemetry context object. Handling the Edge Cases Asynchronous steering messages and concurrent tool dispatches introduce subtle race conditions that break naive extension implementations. When an agent triggers multiple parallel read operations alongside a disruptive write hook, promise resolution order can cause state desynchronization. Debugging these timing failures requires wrapping hook bodies in explicit serialization blocks or utilizing atomic lock mechanisms within the extension state store. Standard runtimes rely on an immutable set of four core tools and expect flat directory structures, leaving engineers blind when custom security boundaries or pre-commit validations are required.

Writing custom TypeScript extensions and lifecycle hooks for pi agent bridges this gap, letting teams inject deterministic checks directly into the agent runtime without bloating the system prompt. By hooking into the DAG execution loop, developers gain surgical control over tool arguments, state persistence, and output validation while keeping token expenditure flat.

Working through production deployments revealed that relying on standard event emitters causes race conditions during multi-file refactoring tasks. This deep-dive details how to construct stateful, type-safe extensions that survive asynchronous interruptions and maintain strict execution guarantees in production.

Generated by AIInfrastructure and Setup

Configuring a robust extension environment starts with pinning the core runtime dependencies and establishing strict TypeScript compilation rules. Because extensions execute inside the agent’s main event loop, loose typing or unhandled promise rejections will crash the entire session state tree.

import { promises as fs } from 'node:fs';
import * as path from 'node:path';

export interface SecurityConfig {
  allowedPaths: string[];
  blocklistPatterns: RegExp[];
}

Initializing the extension harness inside an enterprise repository demands an explicit configuration loader that validates path boundaries before the runtime initializes its first tool call. Skipping this validation phase invites arbitrary file modifications during unsupervised background refactoring runs.

Core Implementation Strategy

Registering lifecycle hooks involves attaching middleware functions to specific interception points within the agent execution lifecycle. The core runtime exposes hooks such as beforeToolCall, afterToolExecution, and agentStart, each designed to inspect or mutate runtime parameters synchronously or asynchronously.

Implementing a production-grade file modification guard requires intercepting the write and edit tool calls before they hit the disk. The following pattern inspects incoming arguments and strips out unauthorized path traversal attempts.

export function registerSecurityExtension(runtime: AgentRuntime, config: SecurityConfig) {
  runtime.hook('beforeToolCall', async (context: HookContext) => {
    if (context.toolName === 'write' || context.toolName === 'edit') {
      const targetPath = path.resolve(context.args.path);
      const isAllowed = config.allowedPaths.some(p => targetPath.startsWith(path.resolve(p)));
      
      if (!isAllowed) {
        throw new Error(`Security violation: Modification of ${targetPath} is prohibited by runtime extension.`);
      }
    }
  });
}

Managing state across multiple tool iterations requires leveraging the context store attached to the session DAG. Instead of relying on module-scoped global variables — which fail during concurrent worker threads — extensions must read and write state directly through the provided telemetry context object.

let activeOperations = new Map>();

export function wrapAsyncHook(runtime: AgentRuntime) {
  runtime.hook('afterToolExecution', async (context: ToolExecutionEvent) => {
    const lockKey = `${context.sessionId}-${context.toolName}`;
    if (activeOperations.has(lockKey)) {
      await activeOperations.get(lockKey);
    }

    }

items.title: The neocloud stock rout continues as Elon Musk warns of 'guppy-level death'
items.summary: Elon Musk said that many neocloud companies face "guppy-level death." Bloomberg/Getty Images Shares in neocloud companies are falling over concerns about their levels of debt. CoreWeave and Nebius, two major public neoclouds, have seen their stocks drop sharply in recent weeks. On Sunday, Elon Musk questioned the sector, saying that "some will make it through, but not many." Neocloud companies are sliding even lower. Shares dropped further on Monday after Elon Musk warned that many of them face "guppy-level death." CoreWeave and Nebius have both fallen more than 30% over the past month, largely due to growing concerns about the debt they've taken on to build more data centers. Soon after Monday's open, shares in both companies were down a further 4%, while Iren, another publicly traded neocloud, fell 2%. The declines follow a string of X posts from Musk on Sunday evening questioning the neocloud business model. "As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," he said. "That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation," he added. "Some will make it through, but not many." Musk said that while SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, his company makes money through Starlink and rocket launches. Meanwhile, investors are worried that a slowing AI boom could leave debt-heavy neoclouds struggling to service their loans. After one X user posted arguing that Musk was trying to drive down the share prices of neocloud companies to acquire them, Musk replied: "SpaceX is not buying any neoclouds. Pointless." Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang remains bullish about the sector. "The demand for the neoclouds is off the charts," he told CNBC last Thursday. Nvidia holds significant stakes in CoreWeave, Nebius, and other cloud-computing companies. A CoreWeave spokesperson said: "The AI cloud market is not a monolith," and that lenders distinguish between speculative capacity and businesses with contracted revenue and a record of delivery. They added that the company is "already a market leader operating at scale" with expertise, which it sees as key for opportunities to finance further growth. A recent Bernstein Research report analyzed thousands of planned US data centers and estimated that only about 35% of the announced capacity will be built. "Press releases are cheap … concrete is not," Bernstein analysts wrote in a research note. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The AI observability race will be won on interoperability
items.summary: The AI race is often measured by model quality, speed, and token cost. For business leaders, those measures contribute to a larger question: Can an organization deliver useful AI outcomes reliably, at the right cost, and with a level of risk it can defend? To answer that question, organizations need comparable evidence and data across changing models, frameworks, and providers. OpenTelemetry helps by giving teams a common way to capture and describe AI behavior. That can reduce the need to maintain a separate data model for each integration. Shared AI conventions can reduce duplicate integration work, make providers and models easier to compare, and support decisions about quality, cost, and risk. Consistent data also gives teams a stronger basis for scaling AI applications. Interoperability reduces the cost of change AI applications have many parts: model providers, orchestration frameworks, retrieval systems, tools, and evaluation services, to name a few. Each may handle a conversation or agent action differently. Teams spend time normalizing those differences before they can investigate failures or compare results. These subtle differences slow product improvement and make switching observability providers more expensive. “Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters.” That distinction matters to businesses. Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions describe common conversation and message concepts while accounting for the limits of representing complex data in telemetry. They also allow large content to be stored externally, with references retained in telemetry. Splunk’s Agent Observability work illustrates the practical value of this approach: it’s built on OpenTelemetry and AGNTCY standards to provide vendor-neutral monitoring across AI agents and applications. The aim is to give teams a way to correlate agent behavior with performance, quality, cost, and risk — even as the underlying stack changes. Measure the outcome, not just the tokens Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value. A less expensive model can consume more tokens or require more retries to complete a task. A higher-cost model may be more efficient if it reaches the desired result reliably on the first attempt. That makes cost per outcome a more useful business measure than cost per token alone. A successful outcome might be a completed workflow or an accurate answer that meets an agreed quality bar. OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data about model calls, latency, errors, usage and tool interactions, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use. The organization still needs to define success and measure it against the cost and use of these tools. “Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value.” Evaluation can help. An instrumentation-side evaluator can provide quick feedback close to the application, while platform-side evaluation can compare models and releases across workloads. With consistent telemetry, teams can use evaluation results to decide which model fits a task, whether a release improved performance, and where spending is driving value. They can do this regardless of changes to models, providers, or tool calls. Build for change without reinstrumenting In addition, telemetry quality needs to be visible before production. Open source tools like Observability Studio provide a development-time example: teams can inspect local telemetry and validate whether it follows OpenTelemetry conventions. They can even use the tool to help add instrumentation that is compliant from the start. Catching missing or inconsistent data earlier can reduce rework and give operators stronger evidence when they need to troubleshoot or assess a release. “OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use.” The business benefit is a quicker path from adopting a new AI capability to understanding how it behaves in connection with the organization’s business priorities and customers. Observability provides control for agent behavior AI agents can select tools, retry operations, and trigger actions on behalf of users. An AI SRE agent , for example, might detect that customers can’t check out on a retail site, investigate the problem, restart a failing service, and confirm that purchases are working again. Teams need to know not just whether the agent responds, but whether it takes useful actions, follows safety rules, and knows when to stop and ask for help. A mistaken action can make an outage worse and damage customer trust, while repeated retries or endless troubleshooting can drive unexpected costs. This is where observability starts to provide operational control. Agent observability can help teams evaluate behavior and track performance and cost. When connected to enforcement systems, it can also support guardrails that block harmful actions or outputs. Shared telemetry collected through OpenTelemetry can connect those controls to evidence about the agent’s steps, tool calls, and ultimately its business impact. The standard should make evidence portable; the business should define the policy to apply that evidence. Which actions require approval? What quality bar is acceptable? When should a request be routed to a person or a different model? OpenTelemetry doesn’t need to answer those questions. Instead, it gives teams the power to make those decisions using consistent information. Upstreaming is an investment in scale For businesses, upstreaming their changes to open source can mean broader coverage and less duplicated engineering—but only when projects have clear ownership and sustained community maintenance. AI instrumentation faces a similar challenge. Third-party libraries can support new frameworks and providers before the broader ecosystem catches up. Upstream proposals show the value of reusing mature instrumentation, along with the need to settle code scope, contribution rights, and long-term maintenance. For example, the OpenInference proposal covers instrumentation code, while leaving its specification and semantic conventions outside the proposed scope. “The prize is not more data. It is the ability to scale AI with clearer decisions about value, reliability, and risk.” For OpenTelemetry, the challenge is to agree on common evidence. Shared conventions can make model behavior easier to compare, reduce the cost of integrating new providers, and help teams connect AI performance to spend, customer experience, and business outcomes. Adopting OpenTelemetry’s standards also helps to minimize potential rework in the future. The prize is not more data. The AI race is often measured by model quality, speed, and token cost. For business leaders, those measures contribute to a larger question: Can an organization deliver useful AI outcomes reliably, at the right cost, and with a level of risk it can defend?

To answer that question, organizations need comparable evidence and data across changing models, frameworks, and providers. OpenTelemetry helps by giving teams a common way to capture and describe AI behavior. That can reduce the need to maintain a separate data model for each integration.

Shared AI conventions can reduce duplicate integration work, make providers and models easier to compare, and support decisions about quality, cost, and risk. Consistent data also gives teams a stronger basis for scaling AI applications.

Interoperability reduces the cost of change

AI applications have many parts: model providers, orchestration frameworks, retrieval systems, tools, and evaluation services, to name a few. Each may handle a conversation or agent action differently. Teams spend time normalizing those differences before they can investigate failures or compare results. These subtle differences slow product improvement and make switching observability providers more expensive.

“Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters.”

That distinction matters to businesses. Standardization doesn’t require every system to store every detail in the same way. It does require enough shared meaning to compare what matters. OpenTelemetry’s GenAI conventions describe common conversation and message concepts while accounting for the limits of representing complex data in telemetry. They also allow large content to be stored externally, with references retained in telemetry.

Splunk’s Agent Observability work illustrates the practical value of this approach: it’s built on OpenTelemetry and AGNTCY standards to provide vendor-neutral monitoring across AI agents and applications. The aim is to give teams a way to correlate agent behavior with performance, quality, cost, and risk — even as the underlying stack changes.

Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value. A less expensive model can consume more tokens or require more retries to complete a task. A higher-cost model may be more efficient if it reaches the desired result reliably on the first attempt.

That makes cost per outcome a more useful business measure than cost per token alone. A successful outcome might be a completed workflow or an accurate answer that meets an agreed quality bar. OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data about model calls, latency, errors, usage and tool interactions, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use. The organization still needs to define success and measure it against the cost and use of these tools.

“Token counts help explain spend, but they don’t tell you whether that AI spend was tied to useful work or added business value.”

Evaluation can help. An instrumentation-side evaluator can provide quick feedback close to the application, while platform-side evaluation can compare models and releases across workloads. With consistent telemetry, teams can use evaluation results to decide which model fits a task, whether a release improved performance, and where spending is driving value. They can do this regardless of changes to models, providers, or tool calls.

Build for change without reinstrumenting

In addition, telemetry quality needs to be visible before production. Open source tools like Observability Studio provide a development-time example: teams can inspect local telemetry and validate whether it follows OpenTelemetry conventions. They can even use the tool to help add instrumentation that is compliant from the start. Catching missing or inconsistent data earlier can reduce rework and give operators stronger evidence when they need to troubleshoot or assess a release.

“OpenTelemetry provides the framework for collecting consistent data, regardless of what model, backend, provider, or tools are in use.”

The business benefit is a quicker path from adopting a new AI capability to understanding how it behaves in connection with the organization’s business priorities and customers.

Observability provides control for agent behavior

AI agents can select tools, retry operations, and trigger actions on behalf of users.  An AI SRE agent, for example, might detect that customers can’t check out on a retail site, investigate the problem, restart a failing service, and confirm that purchases are working again. Teams need to know not just whether the agent responds, but whether it takes useful actions, follows safety rules, and knows when to stop and ask for help. A mistaken action can make an outage worse and damage customer trust, while repeated retries or endless troubleshooting can drive unexpected costs.

This is where observability starts to provide operational control. Agent observability can help teams evaluate behavior and track performance and cost. When connected to enforcement systems, it can also support guardrails that block harmful actions or outputs. Shared telemetry collected through OpenTelemetry can connect those controls to evidence about the agent’s steps, tool calls, and ultimately its business impact.

The standard should make evidence portable; the business should define the policy to apply that evidence. Which actions require approval? What quality bar is acceptable? When should a request be routed to a person or a different model? OpenTelemetry doesn’t need to answer those questions. Instead, it gives teams the power to make those decisions using consistent information.

Upstreaming is an investment in scale

For businesses, upstreaming their changes to open source can mean broader coverage and less duplicated engineering—but only when projects have clear ownership and sustained community maintenance.

AI instrumentation faces a similar challenge. Third-party libraries can support new frameworks and providers before the broader ecosystem catches up. Upstream proposals show the value of reusing mature instrumentation, along with the need to settle code scope, contribution rights, and long-term maintenance. For example, the OpenInference proposal covers instrumentation code, while leaving its specification and semantic conventions outside the proposed scope.

“The prize is not more data. It is the ability to scale AI with clearer decisions about value, reliability, and risk.”

For OpenTelemetry, the challenge is to agree on common evidence. Shared conventions can make model behavior easier to compare, reduce the cost of integrating new providers, and help teams connect AI performance to spend, customer experience, and business outcomes. Adopting OpenTelemetry’s standards also helps to minimize potential rework in the future.

The prize is not more data. It is the ability to scale AI with clearer decisions about value, reliability, and risk.

items.title: Meta looks to raise up to $95 billion from stock sales to fund its huge AI build-out
items.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is among the most prominent figures in the AI race. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Meta is seeking a major cash injection to fund its AI ambitions. The tech giant said on Monday it is looking to raise up to $95 billion from stock offerings. Tech firms are spending big on AI infrastructure as they try to win the superintelligence race. Meta is tapping investors for up to $95 billion to fund its huge AI build-out. The tech giant said in a Monday filing that it has launched about $35 billion in equity offerings, comprising around $22.5 billion of Class A common stock, and $12.5 billion in depositary shares representing preferred stock. The parent company of Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram also said it was planning a $60 billion at-the-market offering once its Class C shares begin trading in the first quarter of 2027. In an at-the-market offering, a company sells shares gradually into the market at the prevailing market price, instead of as a large block at a fixed price. Meta said last week that it would introduce the new share class to help founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg access the liquidity he may need to pay California's proposed wealth tax without having to sell existing shares and erode his voting control over the company. "AI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services," the company said in a press release. "Meta is investing to expand the infrastructure and compute capacity needed to support these opportunities and to bring personal superintelligence to billions of people and businesses," it added. Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom have each expressed an interest in buying up to $5 billion of the common stock being offered, but those indications aren't binding, so they might buy more or less, Meta said. Meta stock swung during Monday's premarket from 2% in the green to 0.4% in the red. Meta is spending heavily on AI infrastructure as it develops consumer AI products and pursues Mark Zuckerberg’s goal of "personal superintelligence." The company said it expects to incur $135 billion to $145 billion of capital expenditures this year. It highlighted $97 billion of operating cash flow for the first nine months of this year, and the roughly $82 billion of cash and other liquid assets it held at the end of September. Meta's revenue jumped by 26% to around $65 billion last quarter , but its operating income shrank by 37% to $13 billion as costs surged from about $31 billion to $52 billion. Meta said last week that it would introduce the new share class to help founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg access the liquidity he may need to pay California's proposed wealth tax without having to sell existing shares and erode his voting control over the company.

"AI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services," the company said in a press release.

"Meta is investing to expand the infrastructure and compute capacity needed to support these opportunities and to bring personal superintelligence to billions of people and businesses," it added.

Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom have each expressed an interest in buying up to $5 billion of the common stock being offered, but those indications aren't binding, so they might buy more or less, Meta said.

Meta stock swung during Monday's premarket from 2% in the green to 0.4% in the red.

Meta is spending heavily on AI infrastructure as it develops consumer AI products and pursues Mark Zuckerberg’s goal of "personal superintelligence."

The company said it expects to incur $135 billion to $145 billion of capital expenditures this year. It highlighted $97 billion of operating cash flow for the first nine months of this year, and the roughly $82 billion of cash and other liquid assets it held at the end of September.

Meta's revenue jumped by 26% to around $65 billion last quarter, but its operating income shrank by 37% to $13 billion as costs surged from about $31 billion to $52 billion.

items.title: Meta Wants $95 Billion Through Stock Sales to Fund AI Infrastructure
items.summary: Meta Platforms plans to raise up to $95 billion through equity offerings. This includes $35 billion in immediate public offerings of common and convertible preferred stock and a separate programme to sell up to $60 billion in shares. The company said the financing would support investments in AI infrastructure, computing capacity and personal superintelligence as it expands its AI products and services. Meta Investor NVIDIA, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Broadcom have indicated an interest in purchasing up to $5 billion collectively in the Class A offering. Their indications are non-binding, meaning the companies are not committed to buying the shares. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs are leading the offerings, said Meta . The initial $35 billion offering comprises $22.5 billion in Class A common stock and approximately $12.5 billion in depositary shares representing mandatory convertible preferred stock. Meta also plans to establish a $60 billion at-the-market (ATM) share sale programme in the first quarter of 2027, following the commencement of trading in its new Class C common stock. The proposed programme is not finalised, and Meta said it is not guaranteed to proceed on the announced terms, or at all. The fundraising comes as Meta prepares to spend $135 billion to $145 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, primarily to expand its AI infrastructure and computing capacity. The company said it operates data centres across 23 US states and is building four superclusters, each with more than one gigawatt of capacity. It expects to nearly double its total infrastructure capacity in 2026 compared with the previous year. Meta generated $97 billion in operating cash flow in the first nine months of 2026 and held about $82 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and marketable securities at the end of September. The company said it would fund its investments through a combination of operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, strategic partnerships and equity capital. Meta's third-quarter results show the scale of investment required. Revenue rose 26% year-on-year to $64.6 billion, while net income increased to $9.86 billion from $2.71 billion a year earlier. However, operating income fell 37% to $13 billion, partly reflecting a $9.89 billion charge related to an agreement with 52 US state attorneys general over litigation concerning teen mental health and social media.

items.title: India’s GCCs to Add 1.4 Million Jobs, Drive 170 Million Sq. Ft. Office Demand by 2031
items.summary: India’s Global Capability Centres (GCCs) are projected to grow from approximately 2.3 million employees today to 3.3–3.7 million by 2031. They are expected to add 1–1.4 million net jobs during this period, generating 150–170 million sq. ft. of incremental office demand, according to a new report by Embark, a fully integrated service provider. Released on October 23, 2026, the report draws on a survey of 100 Indian GCC leaders, executive interviews and market data to examine how AI adoption, evolving business priorities and changing workplace models will shape the sector through 2031. Most surveyed leaders said their centres had moved beyond selective AI adoption. However, productivity gains r emain below 15%, suggesting AI benefits have yet to translate into substantial productivity improvements. Meanwhile, 71% of respondents expect their centres to take on broader functional ownership, while relatively few anticipate global leadership roles moving to India. Existing GCCs are expected to account for around 80% of incremental workforce additions. “India’s opportunity is to turn AI adoption into measurable business value, driving demand for specialist talent and supporting continued workforce and office growth through 2031,” said Aravind Maiya, CEO and co-founder of Embark. AI to reshape GCC workforce composition The report identifies a shift in workforce composition rather than headcount growth alone. Automation, slower backfilling and role consolidation are expected to moderate demand for routine roles by 0.4–0.5 million jobs. This is expected to be offset by expanded mandates, adding 1.2–1.5 million jobs, and the creation of around 0.3 million AI-led roles. As GCCs take on more complex responsibilities, demand for specialised capabilities is expected to grow, including platform engineering, cybersecurity, solution architecture, and domain-specific expertise. India also has scope to attract new GCCs. According to the report, about 3,144 viable Global 5000 companies have not yet established a GCC in India, potentially leading to 590–640 new setups by 2031. Tier 1 cities, including Bengaluru and Hyderabad, are expected to account for 90% of new GCC setups. These cities already account for 67% of GCC leasing across India’s Tier 1 markets, the report states. “Tier 2 and 3 cities will add targeted capacity through hub-and-spoke models, particularly for cost-sensitive delivery, specialised talent access, and operational resilience,” the report states. GCC expansion to reshape office demand As GCCs assume greater responsibility for global functions, products and platforms, their workplace requirements are also expected to change. Collaboration and shared spaces are projected to increase from 27% to 55% of workplace allocation by 2031. Hybrid working models, peak-day attendance, and specialist infrastructure requirements are expected to shift planning from seat-led to purpose-led workspaces designed for collaboration, innovation, security, and complex work. Office demand is expected to remain concentrated in a few sectors. Banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), along with technology, media and telecommunications (TMT), are projected to account for around 54% of incremental GCC office demand. Retail and consumer packaged goods (CPG) are expected to be among the fastest-growing sectors for office space, with a projected compound annual growth rate of 17–21%. The report expects India’s GCC expansion to support office demand through 2031. While existing office capacity may absorb some near-term growth, available capacity is expected to tighten as attendance increases, mandates deepen, and specialist infrastructure requirements rise. This could make expansion flexibility, secure infrastructure and faster operational readiness important considerations for landlords and developers. “For landlords and developers, expansion optionality, secure and specialist-ready infrastructure, and speed to operational readiness will become increasingly important differentiators. Flexible and managed spaces are likely to remain relevant for pilot setups and smaller entry models, while larger and regulated GCCs will increasingly require dedicated, secure, and customised premises,” the report states. Established GCCs are expected to remain the primary drivers of near-term growth, with mature centres expanding beyond delivery-oriented mandates to take ownership of entire functions, products, platforms and business outcomes. As their responsibilities evolve, the report suggests office infrastructure must keep pace with changing workforce requirements and the growing need for specialised, secure work environments.

items.title: Pronto Founder Enters Physical AI Space With Provision Labs
items.summary: Anjali Sardana, founder and chief executive of Indian household services startup Pronto, has launched Provision Labs, a San Francisco-based venture focused on data infrastructure for artificial intelligence (AI) systems that perform physical tasks. Sardana will continue to lead Pronto while also serving at Provision Labs. Provision Labs lists Lachy Groom, General Catalyst, Bain Capital Ventures and Glade Brook Capital among its backers, according to its website. The company has not disclosed its funding amount , valuation or initial customers. The launch comes as Pronto develops a separate initiative to record household service sessions for AI training. It remains unclear whether Provision Labs will use that data or establish its own collection arrangements. According to The Economic Times , Provision Labs will collect data to train and test AI systems that use robots and other machines to perform tasks in real-world environments. The report, which cited people familiar with the venture, said the startup will work with developers building models for robotics and other applications. Pronto has introduced Pronto Verified, an opt-in programme that records household service sessions using wearable cameras. The company said it can anonymise the recordings and use them to train AI systems for robotics . Provision Labs' stated focus on physical AI data makes the relationship between the two businesses a key unanswered question. Neither company has publicly confirmed that Provision Labs will access Pronto's recordings or that a data-sharing agreement exists. The startup has not announced any commercial partnerships or explained how it will source data across industries. Its website describes its focus as the data, evaluation and deployment layer for physical AI.
