items.title: HCLTech Taps NVIDIA Simulation Tools to Automate Software-Defined Vehicle Testing
items.summary: HCLTech has launched an AI-powered vehicle software testing offering that uses NVIDIA’s simulation tools and AI models to validate software-defined vehicles. The offering targets vehicle manufacturers and tier-1 suppliers. The Verification and Validation (V&V) offering uses virtual simulation and AI agents to automate parts of the validation process, including test creation, execution, failure investigation and compliance reporting, HCLTech said. As vehicles receive more over-the-air software updates, automakers must validate increasingly complex systems across different configurations. HCLTech identified fragmented toolchains, manual testing and compliance work as challenges that can slow software releases. The offering uses NVIDIA Omniverse, Cosmos, Alpamayo, Omniverse NuRec and Isaac Sim to generate and test scenarios in virtual environments. HCLTech said this approach could reduce reliance on physical testing and expand coverage of rare and safety-critical conditions. NVIDIA's simulation technologies are also being applied to autonomous vehicle development and testing, including work discussed at NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 . The system also uses the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit to coordinate multiple AI agents, with reasoning powered by NVIDIA Nemotron open models. HCLTech said it is designed to link requirements with test results and compliance records across the validation process. Pankaj Tagra, Chief Growth Officer and Global Head of Mobility at HCLTech, said frequent software updates and increasingly complex vehicle systems had made traditional validation processes difficult to scale. “Automotive software is evolving faster than traditional validation processes were designed to handle,” Tagra said. He said the offering was designed to move automakers toward continuous validation, using simulation and AI to support decisions about software releases. NVIDIA’s EMEA Industry Lead for Automotive Enterprise, Sebastian Scheurle, said simulation could help automakers test safety-critical scenarios earlier in development. “Validation now sets the pace for software-defined vehicles,” Scheurle said. On October 12, HCLTech announced a partnership with Anthropic to integrate Claude and Claude Code into its engineering workflows and selected enterprise software products. The HCLTech–Anthropic partnership uses a separate technology stack from the NVIDIA-powered automotive validation offering. HCLTech did not name automotive customers using the offering or quantify any reductions in testing time or costs.

items.title: Week in AI Careers: Who Gets the AI Jobs, and Who Doesn’t
items.summary: Two data releases last week put numbers on who the AI labor market is lifting and who it is passing over. The Pew Research Center found that men have captured almost all of the job growth in AI-exposed occupations since generative AI arrived, while women’s employment in those roles has stayed flat. Goldman Sachs economist Joseph Briggs estimated that up to 9 percent of workers could be displaced during the AI transition, though he expects the cuts to cluster in a recession rather than arrive at a steady pace. Governments moved too: New York committed 10 million dollars to train 40,000 residents for AI work at a new Queens institute, and Italy’s workplace AI rules took effect requiring a human to make the final call on hiring and firing. Quick Hits cover a federal AI-workforce grant, a manufacturing training partnership, and new research on AI hiring tools, followed by the two ODSC events. Surveys and research Pew finds men capturing nearly all job growth in AI-exposed work What happened: The Pew Research Center reported on October 22 that employment growth in AI-exposed occupations has gone almost entirely to men since generative AI became widely available. Comparing 2017 through 2019 against 2023 through 2026, using Current Population Survey data and the Department of Labor’s O*NET task ratings across 480 occupations, Pew found that for each one-point rise in a job’s AI-exposure score, men’s employment grew 6.3 percent while women’s grew 0.2 percent. The split was widest at lower education levels, where men without more than a high school education saw employment in more exposed jobs rise 8.8 percent as women’s fell 9.5 percent, per Pew’s analysis . Why it matters: The finding points to a distributional split inside the AI labor market that headline job-growth numbers hide, with gains concentrated among men and among roles men already hold. Pew cautions that the link between exposure and employment is not necessarily causal, since other forces moved these occupations over the same years. For workers and employers tracking AI’s effect on hiring, the question is shifting from how many jobs to which workers. Goldman Sachs estimates up to 9 percent of workers could be displaced in the AI transition What happened: Goldman Sachs economist Joseph Briggs estimated in an October 22 research note that as many as 9 percent of workers could be displaced during the shift to AI, with slower hiring trimming employment by roughly another 3 percent, a combined figure the firm rounds to about one in 11 workers. The estimate assumes AI eventually raises productivity by about 15 percent in the United States and other developed economies, and it revises up a 6-to-7 percent estimate the same desk published in August 2025. Briggs argued that AI-related job losses are likely to cluster during recessions rather than arrive at a steady pace, and noted that AI-attributed layoffs have fallen from their spring 2026 peak, as Fortune reported . Why it matters: A displacement figure from a major bank’s economics desk carries weight with the executives and investors who set hiring budgets, even as a forecast resting on an assumed productivity gain. The claim that the damage waits for a downturn reframes the timing debate, since a healthy economy can absorb automation while a slowdown can turn deferred cuts into a wave. For workers, the practical signal is that AI exposure and cyclical risk now compound each other. Reskilling and upskilling New York commits 10 million dollars to a Queens AI jobs institute What happened: Governor Kathy Hochul announced on October 22 a 10 million dollar public investment in a new AI Jobs Institute in Long Island City, Queens, created and run by the workforce nonprofit Pursuit, with a goal of training up to 40,000 New Yorkers by 2032. Empire State Development is contributing about 3.06 million dollars of the total, and the institute’s partners include Google.org, OpenAI, Anthropic, Wells Fargo, and the New York Jobs CEO Council. Construction begins this winter, with the center expected to open in mid-2027, per the Governor’s office . Why it matters: A state putting public money behind AI workforce training, rather than leaving it to employers and bootcamps, signals that governments now treat AI skills as public infrastructure. The 40,000-person target over roughly six years is modest against New York’s tech workforce, so the program’s value will rest on whether its pathways lead to jobs rather than certificates. The lineup of frontier-lab partners also ties a public training effort to the companies whose tools are reshaping the work. Worker sentiment and workplace policy Italy’s workplace AI rules require a human to make the final employment call What happened: Italy’s workplace provisions on AI took effect on October 23 under Legislative Decree 179/2026, which aligns national law with the EU AI Act and was published in the Official Gazette on October 8. Article 41 bars recruitment, dismissals, disciplinary measures, contract changes, and performance assessments from being made solely by automated systems, requiring a final decision by a person with real and independent authority. The decree also entitles employees to clear information about the AI systems in use and the extent to which they shape employment decisions, per DLA Piper’s analysis . Why it matters: A national rule placing a named person between an algorithm and a firing decision sets a compliance baseline that multinational employers operating in Italy will have to meet, and it previews how the EU AI Act lands in day-to-day HR. The transparency duty may prove as consequential as the human-in-the-loop requirement, since it forces employers to document where AI already influences hiring and reviews. For HR and people-analytics teams, the near-term work is mapping which systems touch employment decisions before regulators ask. Quick hits Reskilling and upskilling Davenport University won a 3 million dollar federal grant to build AI-workforce training, working with regional employers and its workforce advisory boards to identify the AI skills needed across industries, per the university . The Manufacturing Institute and Texas State Technical College launched a free AI training program for manufacturing workers in Texas, part of the Institute’s effort to close AI skills gaps on the shop floor, per the Manufacturing Institute . Worker policy The Vera Institute of Justice warned that AI hiring tools can screen out applicants with conviction histories, flagging a fair-chance-hiring risk as more employers automate resume screening, per Vera’s research . ODSC updates ODSC AI West 2026 returns October 27 to 29 at the Hyatt Regency San Francisco Airport in Burlingame, with more than 250 speakers across hands-on training in machine learning, LLMs, agentic AI, and AI engineering. Registration and schedule are at odsc.ai/west . ODSC AI NYC, the AI for Work Summit, runs December 2 to 3 at the Jay Conference Center at Bryant Park, focused on applied enterprise AI: agents and copilots, deployment, evaluation, governance, and production workflows. Details are at summit.ai . Originally published at https://opendatascience.com on October 26, 2026.

The decree also entitles employees to clear information about the AI systems in use and the extent to which they shape employment decisions, per DLA Piper’s analysis .

Why it matters: A national rule placing a named person between an algorithm and a firing decision sets a compliance baseline that multinational employers operating in Italy will have to meet, and it previews how the EU AI Act lands in day-to-day HR. The transparency duty may prove as consequential as the human-in-the-loop requirement, since it forces employers to document where AI already influences hiring and reviews. For HR and people-analytics teams, the near-term work is mapping which systems touch employment decisions before regulators ask.

Quick hitsReskilling and upskilling

Davenport University won a 3 million dollar federal grant to build AI-workforce training, working with regional employers and its workforce advisory boards to identify the AI skills needed across industries, per the university.

The Manufacturing Institute and Texas State Technical College launched a free AI training program for manufacturing workers in Texas, part of the Institute’s effort to close AI skills gaps on the shop floor, per the Manufacturing Institute.

Worker policy

The Vera Institute of Justice warned that AI hiring tools can screen out applicants with conviction histories, flagging a fair-chance-hiring risk as more employers automate resume screening, per Vera’s research.

ODSC updates

ODSC AI West 2026 returns October 27 to 29 at the Hyatt Regency San Francisco Airport in Burlingame, with more than 250 speakers across hands-on training in machine learning, LLMs, agentic AI, and AI engineering. Registration and schedule are at odsc.ai/west.

ODSC AI NYC, the AI for Work Summit, runs December 2 to 3 at the Jay Conference Center at Bryant Park, focused on applied enterprise AI: agents and copilots, deployment, evaluation, governance, and production workflows. Details are at summit.ai.

Here's what luxury homebuyers are looking for in 2026.

Westend61/Getty Images

  • Home sales may be sluggish, but the luxury segment of the market is thriving.
  • Sotheby's International Realty highlighted four things motivating luxury homebuyers in 2026.
  • Some are buying homes in Milan, while others are moving to San Francisco to take part in the AI boom.

While many Americans are sitting on the sidelines, waiting for the real-estate market to become more affordable, ultrawealthy buyers are still snapping up homes.

Sotheby's International Realty's 2026 Mid-Year luxury outlook survey found that 55% of its real-estate affiliated professionals worldwide who specialize in properties priced at $10 million and above saw an increase in luxury homebuyers in their local markets over the previous 12 months. Respondents also said they expect strong demand for the remainder of 2026.

"The affluent remain engaged and confident in the luxury housing market. They are deliberate but not deterred," Philip A. White Jr., president and CEO of Sotheby's International Realty, said in the brokerage's report.

Here are four trends gaining traction among ultrawealthy homebuyers according to Sotheby's report, from a revival in San Francisco's real estate market to a growing demand for homes that allow buyers to age in place.

Luxury buyers want a home where they can age in place
Wealthy homebuyers want homes with health and wellness amenities, such as saunas.

sl-f/Getty Images

Americans are increasingly focusing on health and wellness, transforming not only how they live but also what they want in their homes.

Sotheby's International Realty found that luxury buyers — many of whom already invest in products and routines that help them stay healthy — are less likely to downsize or move into senior housing. Instead, they are opting to buy homes that better allow them to age in place.

Sotheby's International Realty's survey shows that nearly 40% of real estate professionals said aging in place is a growing priority among homebuyers.

"Increasing life expectancy, coupled with affluent homebuyers' desire to 'age in place,' is reshaping everything from home design and location choice to how inventory circulates in prime real estate markets," Tammy Fahmi, senior vice president of global servicing and strategy at Sotheby's International Realty, said in the report.

For luxury buyers, a home's ability to support a high quality of life is a top priority. Sotheby's found that they want spa-like amenities, including saunas, cold plunges, and red-light therapy; advanced air and water filtration, and easy access to the outdoors through nearby hiking or walking trails. Those who can afford it are also interested in integrated health-monitoring technology or in-home staff.

2. Miami remains a hot spot for ultrawealthy homebuyers
Downtown Miamit

benedek/Getty Images

While home sales are still down across the country, Sotheby's International Realty's report suggests that the luxury end of the real-estate market is doing well.

"There's a little more inventory that has helped keep that property market moving," Lawrence Yun, chief economist and senior vice president of research at the National Association of Realtors, said in Sotheby's report. "The stock market has helped, plus the ability of upper-end homebuyers to pay with cash and not be concerned about mortgage rates."

In the US, several markets continue to attract luxury buyers, especially Miami. In recent years, celebrities and billionaires, including Jeff Bezos and Mark Zuckerberg, have purchased multimillion-dollar homes in the Miami area.

"The ultra-luxury property market in Miami is on particularly solid ground," Yun said. "They had a little oversupply, but with their infrastructure development and new luxury condominium construction, it's becoming an even bigger city."

3. Ultrawealthy buyers want to live where their money goes further.
Milan.

undefined undefined/Getty Images

Global uncertainty is prompting many people to reconsider both where they invest their money and where they live. For ultra-high net worth individuals, that often means looking to cities that offer stability and greater value.

Among those places, Milan is becoming an increasingly attractive destination for luxury homebuyers, according to a Sotheby's report.

Milan's appeal is also tied to Italy's tax incentives and residency-by-investment program, which provides access to the Schengen Area, which includes countries such as the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, Portugal, and Greece.

"That has attracted a lot of ultra-high-net-worth individuals," Diletta Giorgolo, a global real estate advisor at Italy Sotheby's International Realty, said in the report. "More people were coming to Italy for not only residency, but their fiscal regime. We were always used to international buyers, but they came for second homes. The big difference is that now many are buying primary homes."

4. AI is breathing new life into the Bay Area and reviving its real estate market
AI is causing a revival in San Francsizo's luxury market.

halbergman/Getty Images

As the AI industry booms in the Bay Area, younger affluent buyers who left for cities like New York and Los Angeles are being drawn back by job opportunities.

"San Francisco thrives on innovation and new technology, and now the AI boom is real," Alex Hachiya, a San Francisco-based senior global real estate advisor at Sotheby's International Realty, said in Sotheby's report. "Wealth flooded back into the city in 2025, and we saw 84% more sales of homes priced at $7.5 million and up that year, compared to 2024."

Hachiya said it is typical for younger luxury buyers, many of whom work in tech, are entrepreneurs, or come from family wealth, to buy homes in San Francisco before later purchasing a second property in the suburbs, where they plan to raise their children.

He added that when it comes to homes, these buyers want move-in-ready homes with flexible living spaces and walkable neighborhoods.

items.title: Tata Communications Plans $450 Mn Investment to Build 10,000 Km AI Network
items.summary: Tata Communications plans to invest $400 million to $450 million to build around 10,000 kilometres of fibre infrastructure connecting India’s data centres and AI hubs. The network will provide high-speed, low-latency connectivity between data centres and link them to the company’s global network backbone. The three-phase project will target hyperscalers, AI platforms, neocloud providers and enterprises as demand for data centre capacity and AI infrastructure grows in India. The first phase will cover the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor. Subsequent phases will extend the network to data centre hubs in eastern and western India, including Visakhapatnam, Bhubaneswar, Jamnagar and GIFT City. Tata Communications expects the data centre-to-data centre connectivity market in India to exceed $1 billion over the medium term. “We are excited about the opportunity in the India data centre-to-data centre connectivity, which we believe could evolve into a market exceeding USD 1 billion over the medium term,” said Ganesh Lakshminarayanan, MD and CEO of Tata Communications. He added that anchor customer commitments and contracted demand are driving a growing share of the company’s expansion, providing a basis for capital deployment. The network will connect data centre clusters with international cable landing stations, linking Indian AI infrastructure to global markets. The company plans to expand its national long-distance and metro networks alongside the project to meet existing enterprise and data centre connectivity requirements. “The AI economy needs more than compute. It needs a network built for speed, scale and resilience,” said Rupesh Chokshi, Chief Product and Technology Officer and Executive Vice President and Global Business Head of network services at Tata Communications. The network, which the company calls its AI Network Fabric, will provide connectivity for AI workloads that require high bandwidth, low latency and network resilience. India’s data centre industry is expanding amid growing cloud adoption, AI deployment and demand for local data storage. As operators add capacity, connectivity between facilities is becoming an important part of the infrastructure required to run AI workloads. Tata Communications operates more than 500,000 kilometres of subsea optical fibre and over 200,000 kilometres of terrestrial fibre, according to the company. In June, it announced plans for a new subsea cable system between Mumbai and Singapore. It has also invested as a consortium member in a cable system connecting Chennai and Singapore, which is expected to be ready for service in the fourth quarter of 2029. The company integrated its TGN IA2 submarine cable in 2025 to improve latency, reliability and network diversity across the Asia-Pacific region. The planned AI network will build on this infrastructure to connect India’s data centre clusters with international AI and cloud hubs.

items.title: When Traction Becomes Personal Exposure: What The Joonko Guilty Plea Means For Founders
items.summary: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently. Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts. Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably. Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck. Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math. Kyle Jeziorski is the market-facing and client leader at Founder Shield, the innovation arm of The Baldwin Group , with eight years invested in the boutique broker and more than a decade in the insurance industry. Before Founder Shield, he worked at Marsh on the FINPRO team focusing on management liability in the large private and public space. A graduate of Saint Joseph’s University ’s risk management and insurance program, Jeziorski has focused his entire career helping clients navigate through an ever-changing risk environment. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research. The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction.

Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield.

The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability.

Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred:

  • LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.”
  • Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth.
  • Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue.
  • Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own.

Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest?

Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims.

An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout.

Where D&O coverage may stop

Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends.

As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage.

Three policy provisions deserve attention:

  • The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions.
  • Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted.
  • Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances.

D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced.

Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics

Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently.

Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts.

Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably.

Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck.

Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math.

Kyle Jeziorski is the market-facing and client leader at Founder Shield, the innovation arm of The Baldwin Group, with eight years invested in the boutique broker and more than a decade in the insurance industry. Before Founder Shield, he worked at Marsh on the FINPRO team focusing on management liability in the large private and public space. A graduate of Saint Joseph’s University’s risk management and insurance program, Jeziorski has focused his entire career helping clients navigate through an ever-changing risk environment.

items.title: California Startups Have Raised More So Far In 2026 Than The Entire US Ever Has In A Single Year
items.summary: California companies have scooped up more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding this year. That, per Crunchbase data, is an apparent record share. But that’s not all. As investment hit unprecedented levels in 2026, Golden State companies alone raised more than all U.S. startups in any prior year on record. Most of that stems from a handful of megarounds for San Francisco-based AI pioneers. And keep in mind: This year still has a couple months left. Yet California companies have already pulled in an unparalleled $385 billion in seed- through growth-stage rounds. That’s more than double last year’s tally. California’s share of U.S. startup funding also has been trending higher for the past three years. Much of this is due to San Francisco AI unicorns, but we’re also seeing strength in the broader Silicon Valley region as well as Southern California. Where the money went Flabbergasting financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic account for more than half of this year’s California statewide tally. But even without those, California companies 1 still secured a disproportionate share of the largest U.S. equity funding rounds. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 next-largest California funding rounds this year. Some of these are familiar names and involve fairly mature companies. For instance Waymo , which launched inside Google in 2009 and spun out as an independent company 10 years ago, picked up $16 billion in February. Another old-timer is Databricks , which picked up $5 billion in August. It’s now 13 years old and has raised over $30 billion in debt and equity funding to date. Still, we’re also seeing younger companies secure megarounds. Prometheus , the physical AI startup co-founded and led by Jeff Bezos and launched last year, pulled in $12 billion in new funding this spring. And AI model startup Safe Superintelligence landed $5 billion in a Nvidia -led round this summer. Early-stage funding That brings us to our next point. California’s startup funding windfall isn’t only about late-stage and pre-IPO companies bagging enormous rounds. Early- and seed-stage companies are also attracting big checks from investors. Per Crunchbase data, California companies have secured nearly $62 billion in seed- and early-stage financings so far in 2026. That’s roughly 57% of all U.S. funding at these stages. It’s also far above prior year tallies, as charted below, and appears to be a record funding level. Don’t bet against California If there’s a lesson to be learned in these numbers, it’s one that savvy startup investors ought to have learned a long time ago: Don’t bet against California. Whatever the year, whatever the technology cycle, California, and Silicon Valley in particular, have a knack for being home to the leading companies of the era. Today, however, it is part of SpaceX, which is headquartered in Texas. ↩

items.title: Article: The Evolution of Agentic Harnesses: From Chains to Graph to Code
items.summary: Agentic LLM systems have moved from linear prompt chains to graph-based workflows and, more recently, code-executing harnesses. Chains are simple but fragile, graphs add branching, retries, and validation, and code harnesses verify outputs through execution. The article advises validating model outputs and choosing the least complex design that meets reliability, speed, and cost needs. By Karthik Ramgopal

The Rundown: Canva just launched Craft, the company’s first in-house AI image model, debuting at No. 4 on DesignArena’s crowdsourced leaderboard behind only three OpenAI models.

The details:

  • Craft was trained on millions of designer-made templates like menus, slides, and posters from the company’s own library.

  • The model plans each layout before drawing it with a two-step architecture, so images convert easily into editable designs via a Magic Layers feature.

  • Craft’s 1340 score on the DesignArena beats the top models from Microsoft, Google, and xAI, while also landing No. 1 overall in portrait and nature categories.

  • Craft is live for all Canva platform users and via public API, with MCP access for external assistants and agents also on the way.

Why it matters: Canva has an endless supply of training data, and Craft’s strong results show how powerful that can be for building an in-house model. While legacy competitors have been reeling amid the AI boom, Canva’s integrations and now its own AI model put near frontier-level image capabilities in front of 250M+ users on its own terms.

“Every Friday at 10 a.m. ET, a scheduled Claude agent refreshes a living 'Hevy Workout Log' document with that week's strength-training data, body measurements, and a progress photo. The automation runs fully unattended, with no human in the loop after the owner sets it up.

The agent pulls information from three independent systems: the Hevy fitness-tracking API, a Google Drive photo folder, and the living document. It reconciles those sources against a date range, determines what's new versus already recorded, and writes structured, formatted updates in the correct places. This requires more judgment than a simple script or webhook.

Claude Docs, through a Claude Artifact, is the living document: it has one tab for each weekday and a Weekly Summary tab. There is no custom backend, database, or glue code. items.title: AI helped me automate some of my wealth advisor job. Here's why I'm not worried about it stealing my edge.
items.summary: Rick Nott, Senior Managing Director at Angeles Investments Angeles Investments Rick Nott has used AI to save himself a lot of tedious work as a wealth advisor. He said new AI products may help other advisors save time too, but they won't replace humans. Nott spoke to Business Insider about how he uses the technology to save him time now. Rick Nott is a senior managing director and private wealth advisor at Santa Monica, California-based Angeles Investments. He spoke to Business Insider about how he uses AI, and why he's excited and afraid when looking at AI-native financial planning platforms. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. When Claude first rolled out its solution for financial advisors , I felt fear and excitement. How complicated will it be? How will it work? I'm not a software developer, but I have some basic tech skills. LLMs have allowed me to dig into coding, which I'd been avoiding learning because it's a lot of work. I know enough to know what I want, how it should look, and how to check the outputs, and now I can automate more of my process. AI has become the glue between the various systems we use and the different workflows we have. I've shown some colleagues how I operate. One told me that I basically have another full-time employee's worth of output through the technology, by automating data collection processes and making it easier to analyze my clients' portfolios. What AI unlocks I started my career while still in college in the late 2000s doing data reporting work for a wealth firm. Between all of the software advisors use, there's a lot of manual work, typically done in Excel, to connect it together. Previously, I could only provide balance sheet reporting for clients with more than $100 million because it took so much manual work. Now I can do it with someone with significantly less. As a family's net worth grows, so does complexity. For many, understanding their overall financial system is their biggest pain point. Banks and brokerage accounts are the easy part, but trusts, business ownership structures, and private investments, which all report differently and require cash on hand to make capital calls, can take huge amounts of manual work to analyze. Imagine a wealth advisory business serving 30 families, each holding about 10 private investments. Each investment generates about 10 documents a year, including quarterly reports, capital calls, distribution notices, and tax documents. Each of these 3,000 documents takes a skilled analyst 15 to 30 minutes to analyze and distill into our reports. That's 750 to 1,500 hours a year, most of it crammed into the few weeks after each quarter closes. With AI, that data is extracted and mapped as it arrives, and one analyst reviews the work instead of a team racing against a deadline. Our goal is to create a one-page document or report on their phone that's as close to real-time as possible. There's a lot you can do with all of your data in one place. For example, a two- or three-sentence prompt could expand into a full email to a client, with all relevant and accurate information already populated. You can then personalize that to fit the right tone for your client. How AI changes the job AI tools like Claude for financial advisors will be disruptive, and others will gain access to the same connectivity I've built. I think of it as part of a dynamic that's been going on for years in my industry. Vanguard, ETFs, lower costs, and robo-advisors have all put a squeeze on financial advisors. But if you believe a lawyer's only job is writing contracts, or a financial advisor's only job is putting together a portfolio, there's a fundamental kind of misunderstanding of what the actual job is. As long as investing involves human judgment, financial advisors will have a job. AI doesn't improve investment decisions or results. I tell my clients that my role is to be the architect of their financial operating system, and, as with an actual operating system, a centralized source of data is essential. When you have a big-picture view of what your family's mission is, you can avoid getting distracted by market noise and news. From there, you can go a layer down to make strategic plans and ask if we're moving in the right direction, and what opportunities we may have. Another layer down, we work with a CPA to save money on taxes. A full picture of a balance sheet makes it possible to actually know what liquidity you have available. Now I can spend more time developing relationships, the thing that runs our business. I get to know anything and everything about the clients I'm working with and those I'd like to work with. The future of financial advisors and AI I have a natural excitement around tech, and watching the Anthropic webinar was incredible. My main concern is that it's not a subscription-based plan; it's token-based, which could lead to surprise bills for users who don't yet know how to manage their token usage. At small RIAs without the expertise, people will be uploading 100-page PDF documents just to ask basic questions, like the ages of kids in a trust. That will rip through tokens. We priced it out internally, and we would have to pay significantly more for a token-based plan instead of the subscription-based licenses we have now. Maybe eventually everyone will have to pay for tokens that way, and the cost of tokens is going down. We learn to do things faster and at lower cost, but in this industry, we do that for a particular reason: to spend more time with the people we serve. The primary way that our clients give us information is still by talking. There's a significant amount of nuance. You may be able to understand something and infer what's really being said. But note-taking software is still wrong all the time. You have to review it. Money is emotional, and I seriously question whether AI can replace our need to connect with another human being. Do I see someone sitting across the table from AI on a speakerphone? Probably not. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Rick Nott, Senior Managing Director at Angeles Investments

Angeles Investments

  • Rick Nott has used AI to save himself a lot of tedious work as a wealth advisor.
  • He said new AI products may help other advisors save time too, but they won't replace humans.
  • Nott spoke to Business Insider about how he uses the technology to save him time now.

Rick Nott is a senior managing director and private wealth advisor at Santa Monica, California-based Angeles Investments. He spoke to Business Insider about how he uses AI, and why he's excited and afraid when looking at AI-native financial planning platforms. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

When Claude first rolled out its solution for financial advisors, I felt fear and excitement. How complicated will it be? How will it work?

I'm not a software developer, but I have some basic tech skills. LLMs have allowed me to dig into coding, which I'd been avoiding learning because it's a lot of work. I know enough to know what I want, how it should look, and how to check the outputs, and now I can automate more of my process. AI has become the glue between the various systems we use and the different workflows we have.

I've shown some colleagues how I operate. One told me that I basically have another full-time employee's worth of output through the technology, by automating data collection processes and making it easier to analyze my clients' portfolios.

What AI unlocks

I started my career while still in college in the late 2000s doing data reporting work for a wealth firm. Between all of the software advisors use, there's a lot of manual work, typically done in Excel, to connect it together.

Previously, I could only provide balance sheet reporting for clients with more than $100 million because it took so much manual work. Now I can do it with someone with significantly less.

As a family's net worth grows, so does complexity. For many, understanding their overall financial system is their biggest pain point.

Banks and brokerage accounts are the easy part, but trusts, business ownership structures, and private investments, which all report differently and require cash on hand to make capital calls, can take huge amounts of manual work to analyze.

Imagine a wealth advisory business serving 30 families, each holding about 10 private investments. Each investment generates about 10 documents a year, including quarterly reports, capital calls, distribution notices, and tax documents. Each of these 3,000 documents takes a skilled analyst 15 to 30 minutes to analyze and distill into our reports.

That's 750 to 1,500 hours a year, most of it crammed into the few weeks after each quarter closes. With AI, that data is extracted and mapped as it arrives, and one analyst reviews the work instead of a team racing against a deadline.

Our goal is to create a one-page document or report on their phone that's as close to real-time as possible.

There's a lot you can do with all of your data in one place. For example, a two- or three-sentence prompt could expand into a full email to a client, with all relevant and accurate information already populated. You can then personalize that to fit the right tone for your client.

How AI changes the job

AI tools like Claude for financial advisors will be disruptive, and others will gain access to the same connectivity I've built.

I think of it as part of a dynamic that's been going on for years in my industry. Vanguard, ETFs, lower costs, and robo-advisors have all put a squeeze on financial advisors.

But if you believe a lawyer's only job is writing contracts, or a financial advisor's only job is putting together a portfolio, there's a fundamental kind of misunderstanding of what the actual job is.

As long as investing involves human judgment, financial advisors will have a job. AI doesn't improve investment decisions or results.

I tell my clients that my role is to be the architect of their financial operating system, and, as with an actual operating system, a centralized source of data is essential.

When you have a big-picture view of what your family's mission is, you can avoid getting distracted by market noise and news. From there, you can go a layer down to make strategic plans and ask if we're moving in the right direction, and what opportunities we may have. Another layer down, we work with a CPA to save money on taxes.

A full picture of a balance sheet makes it possible to actually know what liquidity you have available. Now I can spend more time developing relationships, the thing that runs our business. I get to know anything and everything about the clients I'm working with and those I'd like to work with.

The future of financial advisors and AI

I have a natural excitement around tech, and watching the Anthropic webinar was incredible. My main concern is that it's not a subscription-based plan; it's token-based, which could lead to surprise bills for users who don't yet know how to manage their token usage.

At small RIAs without the expertise, people will be uploading 100-page PDF documents just to ask basic questions, like the ages of kids in a trust. That will rip through tokens.

We priced it out internally, and we would have to pay significantly more for a token-based plan instead of the subscription-based licenses we have now. Maybe eventually everyone will have to pay for tokens that way, and the cost of tokens is going down.

We learn to do things faster and at lower cost, but in this industry, we do that for a particular reason: to spend more time with the people we serve.

The primary way that our clients give us information is still by talking. There's a significant amount of nuance. You may be able to understand something and infer what's really being said. But note-taking software is still wrong all the time. You have to review it.

Money is emotional, and I seriously question whether AI can replace our need to connect with another human being.

Do I see someone sitting across the table from AI on a speakerphone? Probably not.

The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

items.title: Student-loan borrowers are facing a key issue ahead of the midterms: affording their new monthly payments
items.summary: iStock; BI Over 10 million student-loan borrowers are behind on payments. Some borrowers said they're hopeful the midterms will prompt policy to protect those in default. States with closely contested Senate races, like Texas and Ohio, have high rates of nonpayment, per an Urban Institute analysis. Sarah Bundy has been in and out of default on her student loans for nearly three decades. She borrowed for college in the mid-1990s, but dropped out as her loan balance became unaffordable. At the time, it was $39,000. Now, it's $60,000. The 55-year-old is hoping a "blue wave" will pave the way for Democratic legislation to shield borrowers at risk of default. "At my age, I can never get ahead of this," Bundy said. "So I'm just trying to scooch under the wire as long as I can." Roughly one of every six adult Americans has federal student loan debt, according to Federal Student Aid. And some 16% of federal and private borrowers were 60 or more days late on their payments in 2026, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute. Student-loan payments add to the squeeze from groceries and housing in an election increasingly centered on the cost of everyday life . High utility bills and gas prices are an added strain, especially as inflation is outpacing pay hikes. Economic concerns are also reshaping debates over AI, with politicians reconsidering their support for data centers amid a backlash. For borrowers, the pressure is particularly acute, and elevated student-loan delinquency rates overlap with some of the country's most competitive races. Texas and Ohio, home to closely-contested Senate races, both had higher-than-average non-payment rates. In the House, nine battleground districts as identified by the Cook Political Report as of Friday afternoon had worse nonpayment rates than the national average — some 28% of borrowers are delinquent in Texas's 34th District, and 25% in North Carolina's 1st. Meanwhile, federal student-loan defaults, which typically occur after 270 days of nonpayment, are at a record high. While involuntary collections on defaults, including wage and federal benefit garnishment, have been paused for over a year , Democratic lawmakers have been pushing for legislation to protect borrowers once those consequences resume. Still, even a strong election for Democrats would likely leave them without sufficient numbers to override a presidential veto. As of June 30, 9.3 million borrowers were in default, and an additional 1.5 million were in late-stage delinquency, according to Federal Student Aid. Roughly 14% of the $1.7 trillion student-debt load in the US is in default, or $234 billion. Republican lawmakers have expressed support for President Donald Trump's student-loan changes, which they said will help borrowers repay their loans. Sen. Roger Marshall, who is up for reelection in Kansas, previously said that Trump's "big beautiful" spending legislation "made transformational reforms to student loans." Student-loan borrowers have told Business Insider that they're worried about the consequences of defaulting, primarily through losing a chunk of their paycheck, Social Security payments, and tax refunds. Those concerns are exacerbated by the anticipated higher monthly bills under Trump's repayment overhaul. "All we can do is keep pushing for every little bit of progress we can get on this," Bundy said. A student-loan default wave Luke Helton, a student-loan borrower in Tennessee, previously told Business Insider that the only way he can afford his expected $600 payment increase is by digging into his retirement. While he voted for Trump because he believed in the administration's campaign promise to put America first, his student loan challenges have him second-guessing his vote. "They talked a big game about caring about the little people, and they just haven't," Helton said. The defaulted student-loan portfolio itself is undergoing changes. The Department of Education is moving forward with its plan, announced in March, to transfer defaulted student-loan accounts to the Treasury Department. The transfer will occur in phases, with the most recent step being the launching of a new online portal to help borrowers return to good standing and access default resources. Education Secretary Linda McMahon said that the department "was never intended to serve as the fifth largest bank in America, and that's exactly why we partnered with the Treasury Department to improve the administration of federal student aid programs that millions of American students, families, and borrowers rely on." Democratic lawmakers have raised concerns about the Treasury's capability to manage federal student loans. Over 60 of them pushed to halt the transfer and continue the pause on involuntary collections to continue giving borrowers relief as they navigate Trump's repayment overhaul. Sen. Bernie Sanders also led some of his colleagues in introducing a bill to prevent older borrowers and borrowers with disabilities from facing Social Security garnishment if they default. Bundy recently went to Washington, DC, to urge New York lawmakers to support Sanders' bill. She's one of the millions of borrowers transitioning off the Biden-era SAVE plan, which offered lower monthly payments. She said she's not sure how she'll afford payments once they resume, and she's worried that she — and millions of other borrowers — could fall behind. "When these garnishments start back up, it's really going to throw us pretty far back down," Bundy said. "I don't think people realize just how brutal it really is out there." Have a story to share about student loans? Contact this reporter at asheffey@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Technology has changed. So should the conversation.
items.summary: I’ve spent more than 20 years talking about technology and how it can improve people’s lives. For most of that time, I was optimistic about the future. I still believe tech can make our lives better. But I’m increasingly concerned that companies building technology have stopped asking whether it actually does. I think it’s time we started asking harder questions. My column for Network World (2000-2018) aimed to explain the benefits of new devices and software to business and personal users. This same optimism carried over to my podcasting and video career, where Today in Tech (on Computerworld) and DEMO (on CIO.com) continued the technology conversation with industry thought leaders. Somewhere along the way, the relationship between technology companies and their customers changed. The tech industry now seems more interested in telling us what we need than listening to what we want. New technologies are being pushed into our workplaces, devices, and daily lives, often without clear explanations of how they make things better. Often, there are hidden benefits for the tech companies themselves (personal data, algorithms that exploit users’ emotions, etc.) We’re expected to embrace the future simply because the companies building it tell us we should. items.title: Hexaware Certified as Best Firm for Forward-Deployed Engineers by AIM
items.summary: Hexaware has received the Best Firm for Forward-Deployed Engineers certification from Analytics India Magazine (AIM) under its workplace recognition programme. The certification is based on direct feedback from engineering professionals at the organisation and assesses how well companies prepare and support technical teams to deliver outcomes in live client environments. AIM's Best Firm for Forward-Deployed Engineers programme surveys employees across dimensions including workplace culture, leadership accessibility, cross-functional collaboration, learning and development, and the character of engineering work being delivered. Results are assessed independently to gauge how well organisations back their forward-deployed engineering talent on the ground. Hexaware's certification reflects the experience of engineers working at the intersection of enterprise client needs and emerging technology. Hexaware's forward-deployed engineers are embedded in client settings, building and shipping AI-powered solutions where the stakes are real and the pace of delivery is set by client priorities, not internal timelines. Engineering From the Client Frontline Hexaware's forward-deployed engineering approach places capable technical professionals directly inside client organisations. These engineers are not liaisons or coordinators; they are hands-on builders who work within the client's environment, understand its constraints, and deliver solutions that are shaped by that context from the outset. Employees describe a working model where they have the freedom to make meaningful technical decisions, access to the right tools, and the backing of a broader team when needed. Hexaware's history of early adoption of technologies such as agentic AI means engineers enter client environments with current, relevant capabilities rather than approaches already being superseded. “Working at Hexaware Technologies has always been rewarding. It has always been at the forefront of adopting new technologies quickly, while empowering employees to upskill and contribute to its growth,” said Ajoy Maitra, Senior Software Engineer, Hexaware Technologies. Supporting Engineers Who Deliver at Scale Forward-deployed engineering means Hexaware technical professionals gain experience that goes well beyond what standard delivery roles offer. Working directly with enterprise clients on AI-powered implementations exposes engineers to the full complexity of production environments, stakeholder management, and iterative problem-solving under real conditions. Senior employees at Hexaware point to the organisation's understanding of what it takes to sustain forward-deployed excellence as a defining feature of working there. Leadership visibility and access to mentors are cited as important factors, particularly for engineers who are building their capabilities in leadership as well as in technical domains. “At Hexaware, we are equipped with freedom, tools and the team to deliver high-impact outcomes for our clients. I am incredibly proud to be part of, and contribute to, a firm that understands how to support, celebrate, and scale forward-deployed engineering excellence,” said Yogamurugan Prabhakaran, Technical Architect, Hexaware Technologies. Upskilling as an Organisational Commitment One theme that consistently emerges from employee feedback is that Hexaware treats upskilling not as a programme that runs separately from daily work, but as something woven into how engineers develop on the job. Opportunities to deepen expertise in areas such as agentic AI and other emerging fields arise through active client engagements, not only through formal training pathways. For forward-deployed engineers, this matters considerably. Their value to clients depends on the relevance of their technical knowledge, so an organisation's commitment to keeping its engineers current directly affects how effective those engineers can be in the field. At Hexaware, we treat that commitment as a competitive priority. Certification and What It Signals for Engineering Talent Companies across every sector compete for engineers who can operate effectively in client environments, not just within internal product teams. The skills required for forward-deployed engineering — technical depth combined with the ability to deliver under client conditions — are uncommon and tend to develop only in organisations that deliberately create the conditions for them. Hexaware's certification as a Best Firm for Forward-Deployed Engineers by AIM signals to the engineering community that the firm has built and maintained those conditions. For engineers who want their work to have direct, visible client impact while continuing to grow technically, this recognition speaks to what working at Hexaware genuinely looks like. The Best Firm for Forward-Deployed Engineers certification by Analytics India Magazine (AIM) is a benchmark for organisations building credible, high-performance forward-deployed engineering teams. Companies participate in the programme to gather employee-led insights and review internal practices that support long-term technical capability development.

items.title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
items.summary: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide . A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl . These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling. We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another. A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines. A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms. Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states . The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable. We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar , anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka , and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war . The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world. AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place. Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own. We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline. Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list. Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

items.title: Nvidia's sales and marketing leadership is seeing a changing of the guard — and new faces are gaining influence
items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Bloomberg/Getty Images Nvidia's sales and marketing leadership is changing as its sales pitch evolves. Veterans are retiring, opening the door to internal succession and outside hires. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's daughter Madison is also gaining influence. Nvidia's sales and marketing organizations are seeing a changing of the guard as the AI boom reshapes demands on leadership. Veterans at Nvidia are retiring , opening the door for longtime employees. And CEO Jensen Huang is tapping talent from outside the company — and outside the chip industry — to meet new challenges. Nvidia's sales pitch has evolved. It has already convinced companies to choose its chips. To keep growing, it has to convince more businesses to adopt AI. These customers care less about hardware specifications than how Nvidia's AI can be put to work. Leadership changes are most visible in sales and marketing, said former vice president of corporate marketing Greg Estes, while other areas of the company, such as finance, legal, operations, and software and hardware engineering, have remained relatively stable. In marketing, Nvidia tapped Google Cloud executive Alison Wagonfeld to become its first chief marketing officer earlier this year, while Microsoft veteran Nick Parker became its new sales chief in August. Neither comes from the chip industry, though both bring years of experience helping businesses adopt software and cloud services. Nick Parker, Nvidia's EVP of worldwide field operations. Bloomberg/Getty Images At the same time, Huang's daughter Madison has gained influence beyond her formal marketing role, two former employees said. Huang regularly reshapes Nvidia as the business evolves, said Scott Baker, a sales VP who retired in July after 26 years. "It's truly a battleship spinning on a dime, and everyone gets aligned," he said. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. A 'deep bench' of younger Nvidia talent Retirees this year include former sales EVP Jay Puri, VP of enterprise marketing Laura Fay , SVP of enterprise business Shanker Trivedi, and sales VP Kevin Connors. Fay said Huang doesn't want to lose longtime executives , many of whom he personally recruited. But as they move on, the next generation is getting a chance. Before leaving in April after 17 years, Trivedi made mentorship part of his mission. He was ready to pass the baton after years of grueling travel and seven-day workweeks. "Time stops for nobody," the 69-year-old said. Trivedi said Nvidia has a "deep bench" of younger sales and marketing talent who know its culture, market, and partners inside out, including Raj Mirpuri in AI cloud infrastructure, Kimberly Powell in healthcare, and Kari Briski in AI software. When he retired, the company divided Trivedi's responsibilities among multiple leaders. As Nvidia's revenue soared during the AI boom, his job had ultimately become too big for one person. "Better to flatten the structure and gain velocity," he said. Another Huang is gaining influence One insider bringing an unconventional background to Nvidia's marketing ranks is Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang. Madison formerly worked at French luxury conglomerate LVMH in hospitality marketing before joining Nvidia as an MBA intern in 2020. She has quickly ascended to senior director of product marketing for physical AI. One former employee said Madison's experience working on luxury brands brought a fresh perspective to a marketing team traditionally staffed by semiconductor veterans. Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia. Bloomberg/Getty Images Job titles can be fluid at Nvidia, and a second former employee said Madison's remit extends beyond physical AI marketing. They said she exerts authority across multiple parts of the company and directs teams at all levels on strategy and business decisions. Madison is also among a small circle of executives known to travel with her father. And their close relationship gives her the ability to anticipate his needs during high-level meetings and appearances, the first former employee said. "She 'speaks Jensen' very well," the former employee said, "so he doesn't have to explain himself to her." Have a tip? Contact this reporter via email at gweiss@businessinsider.com or Signal at @geoffweiss.25. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely. Read the original article on Business Insider

Huang regularly reshapes Nvidia as the business evolves, said Scott Baker, a sales VP who retired in July after 26 years.

"It's truly a battleship spinning on a dime, and everyone gets aligned," he said.

Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment from Business Insider.

A 'deep bench' of younger Nvidia talent

Retirees this year include former sales EVP Jay Puri, VP of enterprise marketing Laura Fay, SVP of enterprise business Shanker Trivedi, and sales VP Kevin Connors.

Fay said Huang doesn't want to lose longtime executives, many of whom he personally recruited. But as they move on, the next generation is getting a chance.

Before leaving in April after 17 years, Trivedi made mentorship part of his mission. He was ready to pass the baton after years of grueling travel and seven-day workweeks.

"Time stops for nobody," the 69-year-old said.

Trivedi said Nvidia has a "deep bench" of younger sales and marketing talent who know its culture, market, and partners inside out, including Raj Mirpuri in AI cloud infrastructure, Kimberly Powell in healthcare, and Kari Briski in AI software.

When he retired, the company divided Trivedi's responsibilities among multiple leaders. As Nvidia's revenue soared during the AI boom, his job had ultimately become too big for one person.

"Better to flatten the structure and gain velocity," he said.

Another Huang is gaining influence

One insider bringing an unconventional background to Nvidia's marketing ranks is Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang.

Madison formerly worked at French luxury conglomerate LVMH in hospitality marketing before joining Nvidia as an MBA intern in 2020. She has quickly ascended to senior director of product marketing for physical AI.

One former employee said Madison's experience working on luxury brands brought a fresh perspective to a marketing team traditionally staffed by semiconductor veterans.

Madison Huang, senior director of product marketing for physical AI at Nvidia.

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Job titles can be fluid at Nvidia, and a second former employee said Madison's remit extends beyond physical AI marketing. They said she exerts authority across multiple parts of the company and directs teams at all levels on strategy and business decisions.

Madison is also among a small circle of executives known to travel with her father. And their close relationship gives her the ability to anticipate his needs during high-level meetings and appearances, the first former employee said.

"She 'speaks Jensen' very well," the former employee said, "so he doesn't have to explain himself to her."
