items.title: Micro1 is making a $1 billion bet on AI's latest data craze
items.summary: A San Francisco Muni bus emblazoned with Micro1 advertising drives on Mission Street. Stephen Council/BI Micro1 pledged to spend $1 billion on licensing companies' data for AI developers. The startup snags Slack messages, Canva files, Google Docs, and as much other data as it can get. By selling company data, CEOs have a new revenue stream that popped up this year. As AI labs go on the hunt for real-world data , Micro1 is throwing everything at getting it for them. The startup is one in a new class of fast-moving data brokers, gobbling up companies' internal data and packaging it for the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic , and other model developers. The executives who sell their companies' data to Micro1 find themselves suddenly participating in a new sector of the economy, where terabytes of mundane workplace interactions can be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Ilya Brotzky, the CEO and cofounder of the recruiting startup VanHack, told Business Insider he was shocked when he filled out a Micro1 survey about his company's data and received a "substantial" offer. "I didn't believe it, to be honest," he said. "I felt like it was a little too good to be true." Micro1 says it pays $100,000 to $2 million for a single midsize company's data. It recently announced plans to spend $1 billion on the project over the next year. Brotzky and the other executives Business Insider spoke to for this story wouldn't share the exact amounts their companies received. For Micro1, the new focus on workplace data matches a broader evolution in the industry, as Business Insider has written about in The AI Data Grab , a series about how tech giants are increasingly turning to workers, users, and the physical world to get data to train AI . First, AI companies gobbled up text from the internet and corpora of old books. Then they realized that humans grading AI responses could improve their models. And now, companies are using complex simulations, built on real-world data, to improve the tenacity and skill of their AI. Micro1 CEO Ali Ansari. Micro1 Gartner estimated that spending on AI data is likely to surge from less than $1 billion last year to almost $6.5 billion in 2027. Micro1's chief revenue officer, William Almeida, told Business Insider in September that his company has been explaining to prospective customers why their data is suddenly so valuable for those simulations. "Every time I talk to companies, I tell them, 'Hey, I see this as a booming business,'" Almeida said. Slack DMs, Google Docs, Canva files: Micro1 wants all it can get Micro1 has three ways of working with AI model developers. First, it can take a company's raw data, transform it to protect privacy, and license it to a lab. In addition, Micro1 provides an in-progress AI agent to companies and gets feedback on how it works. The third route is the simulation: Micro1 takes a company's data up to a certain timestamp, freezes it, and then provides that "environment" to a model developer trying to teach its AI how to work from existing context. Micro1 pays more for larger, more complex datasets, as well as for data that represents a unique type of work or knowledge. It usually wants to license a company's entire data corpus, so that an AI model can replicate what it would be like to be a human employee. "The connection, the diversity, the traceability of all of these data points, they matter a lot when you think about model training," Almeida said. Brotzky also received an offer from AI data startup Mercor to buy his company's data, though he opted for Micro1. Once Brotzky dug into Micro1's privacy process, he said he felt comfortable sharing all the data they requested. That included VanHack's Google suite, Confluence data, Slack messages, and customer relationship management software. Grant Gooley, the CEO of the marketing agency MyPortal Marketing, also views his deal with Micro1 as an innovation. He has sold internal design files from Figma and Canva, as well as checklists from Monday.com. "When we were building these processes years ago, I didn't think that we would be using it to support AI learning," Gooley said. "But doing that, it's very fulfilling." CEOs pitch the deals to their workers Micro1 and its rivals are full steam ahead. Still, there are open questions. Former and current employees aren't likely to get any compensation from — or a voice in — their work becoming AI fodder. Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University, previously told Business Insider that data sales are an "ethically gray area." When pitching to potential customers, Almeida tells them this business is in the early days. "If you wait too much, you won't get the premium that the first companies are getting," he said. VanHack's team got a confidence boost from the Micro1 deal, Brotzky said, because of the additional revenue stream it represents Gooley said he's kept MyPortal Marketing's employees in the loop about the deal with Micro1 and hasn't heard any complaints. "I told my team that this is something that you're going to tell your grandchildren about one day, because we are literally supporting the future growth of marketing agencies," Gooley said. items.title: Want to land a legal job at Google or Nvidia? These law firms could be your ticket.
items.summary: Google has a thing for Big Law lawyers. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images Big Law has plenty of competition for its best lawyers. Some of the most ambitious lawyers want to work for clients in their legal departments. New Pirical data shows which law firms have the most alumni working in Big Tech. Big Law has a hard time keeping its lawyers. It's not just rival firms dangling basketball-player salaries, extra vacation, and branded merch to lure away top talent. Big Tech is competing for those lawyers, too. New data shared with Business Insider reveals which firms send the most lawyers to the biggest names in tech. Pirical, a legal people-analytics company, tracked lawyers who previously worked at the 200 largest law firms by revenue in the United States and now hold legal roles at seven tech companies: Google, Meta , Microsoft, Nvidia, OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX. Pirical filtered out summer associates and interns. Morrison Foerster and Wilson Sonsini tied for the top spot, each with 40 alumni working in legal roles across the seven companies. Both firms regularly represent tech startups and the investors backing them. Latham & Watkins followed with 33 former lawyers. Kirkland & Ellis, the industry's revenue leader, ranked 11th with 21 former lawyers working at those companies, tied with Paul Hastings and Sidley Austin. Pirical's analysis may have missed lawyers whose job titles fell outside its search criteria, said Craig Savitzky, its insights and content editor. He said newer companies, particularly Anthropic , are also likely undercounted because their legal teams are growing faster than public profiles are updated. Big Law-Big Tech pipeline For attorneys hoping to land a coveted job at a tech giant , a stint at a white-shoe law firm can be a stepping stone. They can trade billable-hour quotas for a seat closer to the business, attractive pay, and just one client to keep happy instead of dozens. That combination makes these roles "some of the most highly desirable and sought-after positions" for law firm associates, said Casey Sullivan, a recruiter with CMW Legal Search. There's another draw, Sullivan said. The companies at the forefront of artificial intelligence are wrestling with some of the thorniest legal questions of the day, from intellectual property to regulation. "That's where the most interesting work is for lawyers," he said. Not all law firms are equally effective launch pads. Pirical's Savitzky noted that the firms near the top of the list have deep ties to the tech industry, if not the deepest pockets. Cooley brought in $2.4 billion in revenue last fiscal year, placing it 29th on The American Lawyer's ranking of top law firms by revenue. But it tied fourth on Pirical's list, with 29 alumni working at the seven tech companies, including nine at Nvidia, a longtime client. Davis Wright Tremaine, which has represented Microsoft in antitrust and employment lawsuits, has 13 alumni working in the software giant's legal department. Fenwick, which advised Wiz and Fitbit on their sales to Google, has 13 lawyers at the search giant. Business Insider also sliced the data another way, looking at which of the seven tech giants employ the most alumni from the top 25 firms on Pirical's list. Big Law is effectively a feeder school for Google's legal team . The company employs 322 alumni of the top 25 law firms on Pirical's list, more than any other tech company studied. That doesn't necessarily mean Google is the most desirable location for lawyers leaving Big Law. Savitzky said the numbers likely reflect the sheer size of Google's legal department and the decades it has had to recruit from top firms. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Telangana Unveils AI-Powered Digital Twin of IT Minister at DevFest 2026
items.summary: Telangana has unveiled an AI-powered digital twin of IT Minister D. Sridhar Babu, designed to interact with citizens in English and Telugu, as the state explores new ways to use AI for public engagement and governance. During the Google Developer Group (GDG) Hyderabad’s DevFest 2026 on October 24, the "pre-AGI" AI Minister avatar debuted live on stage. Developed on TensorGo’s HumAIn platform under the direction of IT Advisor Sai Krishna, the AI avatar engaged Gen Z attendees by answering questions about Telangana’s strategic vision and tech-driven development. The initiative is planned in phases. The first phase involved the public launch and demonstration, while the second aims to let citizens interact with the AI Minister, share feedback and submit grievances, according to Sai Krishna. “The AI Minister is a Digital twin of the IT Minister, powered by HumAIn, helping him reach more people and gain deeper insights into governance and the issues citizens face at the grassroots level,” Krishna said. The government has not detailed when it will roll out the proposed citizen-facing service or how it will handle grievances, verify responses, protect personal data, and ensure AI-generated answers accurately reflect the minister’s positions. The launch signals Telangana’s interest in applying AI beyond technology demonstrations to public-facing services. However, the initiative’s broader impact will depend on how the system is deployed and whether citizen interactions translate into actionable responses from government departments. TensorGo describes HumAIn as an enterprise-grade platform that lets organisations deploy AI teammates for real-time, interactive, multilingual engagement. The launch comes as Telangana seeks to position Hyderabad as a global technology and AI hub. The state has highlighted initiatives including AI City, AIKAM, global capability centres (GCCs) and the Quantum District as part of its wider technology strategy.

items.title: Verifiable AI: Proving What Happened Behind the Black Box
items.summary: When you call a cloud AI API, you get an answer and a model name. You get no proof that the named model produced it. A Berkeley study found that outside testing mostly cannot tell whether a provider swapped in a cheaper model. zkML produces a mathematical proof that a specific committed model produced a specific output, without revealing the weights. It works today for small models and is far too slow for large language models. opML skips the proof and lets anyone challenge a result. It is cheap and scales to large models, but it offers no privacy and needs a waiting period. Hardware attestation (TEEs) is the only approach practical for large models right now, at the cost of trusting a chip maker. A proof shows which model ran. It does not show that the model is accurate or fair. Regulated sectors need both. Read All

items.title: Tsinghua AI Open-Sources AKV, a Cache Engineering Server for LLM Agents on SGLang
items.summary:
Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV , a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7% . Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang . TL;DR What it is: Serving system plus policy library, no weights. Tested on GPT-OSS-120B (5.1B active), MiniMax-M2.7 (230B total, 10B active) and MiroThinker-1.7-Mini (30B total, 3B active). Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang. Paper used 8 A800-80GB GPUs in BF16. Quick start serves GPT-OSS-120B on 2 GPUs (tensor parallel 2). Performance: 27.7% lower average cost and +1.7 points average score versus threshold summarization. Best: GPT-OSS-120B on SWE-bench Verified: cost per task 20.0 to 9.7 cents, score 40.0 to 43.2. Worst: MiniMax-M2.7 on BrowseComp-Plus scores 58.9, 3.4 points below Text Engineering’s 62.3. What is cache engineering, and how is it different from context engineering? AKV is a Tsinghua serving system that lets LLM agents drop and reposition their own KV cache. Context engineering trims or summarizes the text history. Editing that prefix invalidates every later KV state. The retained suffix must then be re-prefilled. Harnesses therefore summarize late and aggressively, which can lose details from middle rounds. Cache engineering leaves the text trajectory untouched. It only changes which KV entries stay visible to attention. Retained entries are reused without recomputation. They can still carry information from dropped messages. In the research paper’s cost analysis, KV cache reads made up 82.4% of total API cost. How does AKV work? AKV defines 3 cache operations. Append is the standard update for new tokens. Drop removes selected entries from future attention without changing positions. Repos rewrites retained keys to positions 0 through r-1 using a RoPE rotation . Values stay unchanged, so no hidden states are recomputed. In ablations, adding Repos raised GPT-OSS-120B’s BrowseComp-Plus pass rate from 55% to 62%. The hard part is serving. Identical tokens can produce different cache states under different operation histories. Plain prefix matching could reuse the wrong states. AKV extends SGLang’s radix tree with drop and reposition nodes. It frees dropped KV only when no active request still needs it. Segment-batch attention restores evicted states in 1 prefill pass. What does the AKV API look like? The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible . Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. drop_message maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. reposition lists the indices after which positions get compacted. A CachePolicy builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A CacheTool lets the model call drop_context itself. How does AKV perform on agent benchmarks? The main policy is a tool-response rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses. The Standard baseline summarizes at 96K tokens (192K for MiroThinker). Text Engineering summarizes at 48K. Benchmarks are BrowseComp-Plus , GAIA-Text , SWE-bench Verified and xbench-DeepSearch-2510 . Model Standard score / cost Text Eng. score / cost AKV score / cost MiniMax-M2.7 52.4 / 5.0 52.8 / 5.7 53.7 / 4.4 GPT-OSS-120B 51.0 / 11.2 48.3 / 10.2 53.1 / 7.3 MiroThinker-1.7-Mini 44.1 / 20.4 37.1 / 18.1 45.8 / 14.8 Average pass rate (%) and cost (US cents per task) across 4 benchmarks. Source: Table 1 of the paper . AKV also cuts cost 21.9% versus Text Engineering. The accuracy gap opens on long runs. On BrowseComp-Plus at 96K tokens and above, GPT-OSS-120B scores 37% with AKV. Standard scores 24% and Text Engineering 32%, per the project page . Costs are API-equivalent estimates from published rates. Repositioned tokens are charged at the cache-hit rate, a deliberately conservative choice. AKV explainer

items.summary_html:
Tsinghua University and CUHK researchers open-sourced AKV, a serving system for KV cache engineering in LLM agents. Instead of summarizing old history, agents drop selected KV cache entries and keep reusing the rest. Across 3 models and 4 agent benchmarks, average cost falls 27.7%. Average task score rises 1.7 points. The code is Apache-2.0 licensed and builds on SGLang.

TL;DR
  • What it is: Serving system plus policy library, no weights. Tested on GPT-OSS-120B (5.1B active), MiniMax-M2.7 (230B total, 10B active) and MiroThinker-1.7-Mini (30B total, 3B active).
  • Runs on: NVIDIA GPUs via SGLang. Paper used 8 A800-80GB GPUs in BF16. Quick start serves GPT-OSS-120B on 2 GPUs (tensor parallel 2).
  • Performance: 27.7% lower average cost and +1.7 points average score versus threshold summarization.
  • Best: GPT-OSS-120B on SWE-bench Verified: cost per task 20.0 to 9.7 cents, score 40.0 to 43.2.
  • Worst: MiniMax-M2.7 on BrowseComp-Plus scores 58.9, 3.4 points below Text Engineering’s 62.3.
What is cache engineering, and how is it different from context engineering?

AKV is a Tsinghua serving system that lets LLM agents drop and reposition their own KV cache.

Context engineering trims or summarizes the text history. Editing that prefix invalidates every later KV state. The retained suffix must then be re-prefilled. Harnesses therefore summarize late and aggressively, which can lose details from middle rounds.

Cache engineering leaves the text trajectory untouched. It only changes which KV entries stay visible to attention. Retained entries are reused without recomputation. They can still carry information from dropped messages. In the research paper’s cost analysis, KV cache reads made up 82.4% of total API cost.

How does AKV work?

AKV defines 3 cache operations. Append is the standard update for new tokens. Drop removes selected entries from future attention without changing positions. Repos rewrites retained keys to positions 0 through r-1 using a RoPE rotation. Values stay unchanged, so no hidden states are recomputed. In ablations, adding Repos raised GPT-OSS-120B’s BrowseComp-Plus pass rate from 55% to 62%.

The hard part is serving. Identical tokens can produce different cache states under different operation histories. Plain prefix matching could reuse the wrong states. AKV extends SGLang’s radix tree with drop and reposition nodes. It frees dropped KV only when no active request still needs it. Segment-batch attention restores evicted states in 1 prefill pass.

What does the AKV API look like?

The interface is stateless and OpenAI-compatible. Clients send the full message history and two optional fields. drop_message maps a trigger message index to the messages to drop. reposition lists the indices after which positions get compacted.

A CachePolicy builds those fields from a trigger, a selector and a reposition rule. Built-in policies are turn-based, token-based or model-based. A CacheTool lets the model call drop_context itself.

How does AKV perform on agent benchmarks?

The main policy is a tool-response rolling drop that keeps the latest 12 tool responses. The Standard baseline summarizes at 96K tokens (192K for MiroThinker). Text Engineering summarizes at 48K. Benchmarks are BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA-Text, SWE-bench Verified and xbench-DeepSearch-2510.

ModelStandard score / costText Eng. score / costAKV score / costMiniMax-M2.752.4 / 5.052.8 / 5.753.7 / 4.4GPT-OSS-120B51.0 / 11.248.3 / 10.253.1 / 7.3MiroThinker-1.7-Mini44.1 / 20.437.1 / 18.145.8 / 14.8

Average pass rate (%) and cost (US cents per task) across 4 benchmarks. Source: Table 1 of the paper.

AKV also cuts cost 21.9% versus Text Engineering. The accuracy gap opens on long runs. On BrowseComp-Plus at 96K tokens and above, GPT-OSS-120B scores 37% with AKV. Standard scores 24% and Text Engineering 32%, per the project page.

Costs are API-equivalent estimates from published rates. Repositioned tokens are charged at the cache-hit rate, a deliberately conservative choice.

How fast is AKV in serving benchmarks?

Serving tests ran GPT-OSS-120B on 80 long-context SWE-bench Verified tasks. At each method’s peak setting, AKV delivers 1.18x output throughput and 1.53x input throughput. P95 request latency is 1.51x faster.

At concurrency 16, Standard’s P95 latency hits 229.90 seconds versus 30.63 for AKV. KV pressure pushes Standard into repeated re-prefill. Per decode step, full-attention time falls from 7.082 to 2.849 ms.

On 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks under a GPU budget, AKV reached about 47% pass rate. Standard reached 40.7% and Text Engineering 32.3%.

Can agents tune their own cache policy?

MiniMax-M2.7 refined policies on 20 BrowseComp-Plus tasks, then ran 100 held-out tasks. The iteration-6 policy cut cost 17.8% versus Standard at baseline accuracy. The abstract reports 7.1% savings beyond the expert-designed policy.

Exposing cache control as a tool also helped accuracy. GPT-OSS-120B rose from 52.1 to 61.0 on a 100-task subset. MiniMax-M2.7’s cost rose, though, from 5.4 to 5.9 cents.

Key Takeaways
  • AKV lets agents drop and reposition KV cache instead of rewriting history.
  • Average cost falls 27.7% and score rises 1.7 points across 3 models.
  • Repos lifts GPT-OSS-120B on BrowseComp-Plus from 55% to 62%.
  • At concurrency 16, P95 latency drops from 229.90 to 30.63 seconds.
  • Support covers only Qwen, GPT-OSS and MiniMax-M2 text models today.

items.title: Jev Isn’t An Overnight Fix For Your Lack of AI Fundamentals
items.summary: Whenever a new open-source AI framework is released that claims to outperform existing AI models in efficiency or speed, developers are hailed as heroes on X, Hacker News, and Reddit. And soon, the big AI labs release their own projects based on the framework and its idea. A year ago, MCP sparked a similar wave of industry-wide adoption; more recently, OpenClaw did the same. Now, Jev , an AI model developed by TypseSafe AI, is in the spotlight. Led by Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI engineer instrumental in building ChatGPT, the company is now valued at $7.5 billion weeks after launch. Such cycles bring a lot of hype. Almost as if the pitfalls and shortcomings of LLMs and AI models vanished overnight, developers seem free of their challenges. And thus, Jev also needs close examination of what its capabilities truly amount to and what it takes for developers and engineering teams to integrate it into production. What is Jev? Jev is not a departure from the transformer architecture that ChatGPTs and the Claudes of the world are based on—it uses the same architecture. But it does not generate language. It provides specific decision options, or in TypeSafe AI’s words, ‘calibrated decisions’ for a user query, each backed by a confidence score. It essentially behaves like a machine-learning classifier that evaluates a query against predefined options and assigns each a probability. “Decision models are specialised AI models that pick a single, pre-defined answer based on a confidence score rather than generating a free-form response,” Sathya AG, a Principal Architect at Google, tells AIM. “Deploying an LLM for simple deterministic workflows and tasks such as sorting support tickets or financial transactions is equivalent to using a smartphone exclusively for its flashlight capability.” This has been the highlight of Jev's launch. TypeSafe claims its model is up to 193.6 times faster and 444.6 times cheaper than conventional LLMs for structured decision-making workflows. Take customer support tickets, for example. Each ticket needs to be assigned to the right department, assessed for urgency, and evaluated for the need for human intervention. LLMs can perform these tasks, but Jev can return those decisions directly—language processing is overkill. It can assign a department category, an urgency score, and a probability indicating whether human review is needed. “LLMs introduce unnecessary costs for deep reasoning and linguistic fluency, when the task demands nothing more than a fast, reliable, binary signal,” says Sathya. Moreover, Jev is attractive when teams need a general-purpose model that can handle changing classification tasks without training and maintaining a separate classifier for each one. TypeSafe AI reports that hiring marketplace Jack & Jill replaced Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite with Jev for candidate scoring, reporting 88% lower costs and roughly half the median processing time, with no statistically significant change in measured quality. Developers have already put Jev to work on everything from Claude Code skill selection to agents playing soccer and Super Mario. And it didn’t take long for everyone to hop into the benchmark fight and claim they’re better than the others. The Shipping Wars Have Begun Liquid AI made one of the month's more specific competitive claims when it introduced d1, saying the model was the first to rival Jev on text-based decisions while extending the approach to images. In its own tests across six applications, d1 matched or beat GPT-6.1 Sol on four, at 19 to 200 times lower cost and with significantly lower latency across all six. The applications ranged from filtering customer-support tickets to inspecting circuit boards for defects and managing the context retained by coding agents. Two days later, Liquid released open-weight versions of the model, including a 3-billion-parameter variant designed to run on hardware ranging from data-centre GPUs to edge devices. At its DevDay in late September, OpenAI announced a Decisions API, bringing its Luna model's capabilities to structured decision-making tasks such as classifying inputs, routing requests, and selecting an AI agent's next action. Cloudflare released Clef and Clef-flash as open-source decision models. AWS released Strands Decider 2B through its Strands Labs initiative, with the company’s distinguished engineer Marc Brooker beginning to develop the model after encountering Jev Microsoft joined the party most recently, with Microsoft-Decision-1, a model post-trained from Qwen3.5-9B. The company claims the model scores higher on average accuracy and has lower median latency than Jev in tests, and also outperforms OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna Decisions and AWS Strands-Decider 2B. So options for developers and engineering teams are plenty. But what does it take to deploy them in the real world so developers, enterprises, and engineering teams can start experiencing the advantages? The Bottlenecks to Deployment “In my opinion, the adoption of decision models today will not look like a one-to-one replacement of generative models,” says Sathya. “Instead, it will mirror a smart factory assembly line where specialised machines route complex work to human experts. We are moving toward a strict division of labour between two distinct tiers.” With this ‘factory assembly line’ analogy, he explains that decision models will behave like a high-speed sorting machine that intercepts incoming traffic, instantly analyses every request, and handles routine sorting. “Generative models sit at the end of the line, and are activated when the sorting machine flags a highly complex, custom piece of cargo that requires deep reasoning,” he says. Adoption is picking up beyond hobby projects and developer experiments. For instance, Vercel reported that Jev reached nearly 13% of paid teams on its AI Gateway within 24 hours of launch, making it the fastest-adopted model in the platform's history. Vercel's own agent framework, eve, has also made Jev its default evaluation model. “But it is still too early to call this established enterprise adoption,” Pratik Ambhore, Head of Data Engineering at RSI, tells AIM. “The real bottleneck is evaluation, as organisations need labelled historical data, meaningful thresholds, and a clear understanding of the cost of a false positive versus a false negative.” Like Sathya, Ambhore also points ot a cascade model where the decision model handles the high-confidence majority and ambiguous cases go to a more capable model or a human. “But those thresholds have to be validated on the organization’s own data rather than taken at face value from a model’s confidence score.” Thus, telemetry data and trust deficit are the other two challenges to large-scale deployment of decision models. A common challenge engineering teams and enterprises continue to grapple with is the lack of granular, factual, structured data these models rely on. “While generative models can pull answers out of the general internet or unstructured data, a decision model requires highly specific, historical logs of past enterprise choices and exact outcomes to function accurately,” tells Sathya. “Because companies lack this underlying factual data, they cannot confidently predict how a model will behave. Without proper telemetry to audit and prove a model's logic, enterprises are wary of downstream system failures.” But Jev’s constrained outputs do not eliminate the need to validate its decisions. TypeSafe AI has touted a “0% hallucination rate”, but the figure concerns whether Jev's outputs conform to predefined schemas, not whether its decisions are correct. The model may not invent a new option, but it can still choose the wrong one. An independent evaluation by developer Will Kelly illustrates this problem. Kelly ran nine experiments, specified 28 predictions before collecting data, and made 123,805 API requests. In one experiment, he tested whether misleading text embedded in support tickets could influence Jev's routing decisions. A direct instruction to ignore the question changed the decision in just one of 200 tickets. But a subtler claim that a support lead had already made the decision changed the result in 147 of 200 tickets. Confidence scores offered some warning, but not a reliable safeguard. When the subtler attacks succeeded, Jev's average confidence score was 0.680, compared with 0.983 on clean tickets. But confidence also fell when the attacks failed, meaning a low score could flag a suspicious case without reliably indicating whether Jev had been misled. The findings come from one evaluation of a single model version, not a measure of Jev's general failure rate. But they illustrate a fundamental limitation: a decision can be perfectly valid in format and still be wrong. “The model can still choose the wrong answer, and a confidence score is not automatically a calibrated probability,” says Ambhore. “So I see decision models reducing the cost and complexity of making decisions, not eliminating the need to validate those decisions.”

items.title: Building a Synthetic Data Pipeline
items.summary: Why Teams Start Building a Synthetic Data Pipeline Most teams arrive at building a synthetic data pipeline the same way: a dataset is collected, a model is trained, the metrics look acceptable, and then the model fails in production on inputs nobody thought to collect. The usual response is to collect more data, and that works until it does not. It helps organizations make better use of limited real-world datasets where they matter most. If data availability is slowing your AI initiatives, connect with the CapeStart team to explore how synthetic data can support your goals. items.summary_html:
Why Teams Start Building a Synthetic Data Pipeline

Most teams arrive at building a synthetic data pipeline the same way: a dataset is collected, a model is trained, the metrics look acceptable, and then the model fails in production on inputs nobody thought to collect. The usual response is to collect more data, and that works until it does not. Collection takes weeks, annotation takes longer, and the scenarios that break a model appear least often in the real world. Three pressures make the case:

  • Privacy and restricted data. Much real data cannot leave the environment it came from, and principles such as GDPR data minimization limit how widely it can be copied. Public datasets rarely match production conditions. Generated examples let a team work without circulating sensitive originals.
  • Not every task needs a proprietary model. Routing every frame to a proprietary model such as GPT -6 Astra bills per call, and over a product’s life that exceeds the one-time cost of fine-tuning a smaller deep learning model for the same job, especially with methods such as LoRA.
  • Fine-tuning needs rich data. The varied examples a fine-tune depends on were exactly what teams could not collect for uncommon conditions. Synthetic data removes that constraint.

Synthetic data gets discussed as though the interesting part is image generation, when generation is the easy part. The difficult part is producing examples that are realistic, varied in the right ways, and checked for quality within an automated synthetic data pipeline. That is a dataset engineering problem.

What Does Synthetic Data Mean?

Synthetic data is data that was produced rather than captured: images or video frames generated by a model, carrying the same visual properties as the real data a model will eventually see. NVIDIA’s overview of synthetic data generation covers the wider field. Two properties make it useful for model training.

You control the distribution. You decide what the dataset contains: how many examples in difficult lighting, at an awkward viewpoint, or against an unfamiliar background. The dataset reflects known weaknesses rather than whatever a capture campaign happened to record.

Labels come with the data. You already know what is in each example and where, so there is no separate annotation pass and no disagreement between annotators over an ambiguous frame. That removes the labeling cost rather than just reducing it.

Models learn from data representative of production conditions, not necessarily data that was physically captured. Representative is the operative word, and it has to be earned through validation, a point a recent review of synthetic data best practices reinforces by stressing factuality, fidelity, and unbiasedness.

Where Real-World Data Collection Breaks Down

A typical collection effort involves field capture, infrastructure, storage, manual annotation, a quality review of those annotations, and repeat trips when the first round proves incomplete. The cost is dominated by human time rather than technical work, which is why many teams turn to dedicated data annotation services.

Collection also carries a structural bias. Teams capture what is convenient, so common conditions get oversampled and uncommon ones get undersampled. The dataset ends up mirroring the easy part of the problem.

The two approaches have different cost curves, and a sensible strategy uses each where its curve is favorable. Real collection defines what production looks like, and generation fills the gaps collection reaches slowly.

Reference Images and Reference Videos as the Starting Point

The biggest quality difference between synthetic data that helps and synthetic data that quietly hurts is whether generation starts from something real. Generating from a text description alone gives an image that looks plausible and behaves nothing like production input: geometry subtly wrong, environments generic, the capture device’s visual character missing.

Reference-image-based and reference-video-based generation avoid that. You take real media you already have, describe the change you want, and let generation vary that one aspect while the rest of the scene stays as captured. This also narrows the gap early domain randomization research had to bridge with purely simulated images.

This works better when the instruction is derived from the reference rather than written once and reused. The reference tells you what is in the frame, the configuration tells you what should change, and keeping those separate is what reference image- or video-based prompting means. Keeping it config-driven means a newly discovered weakness becomes a configuration change rather than a development task.

Inside a Working Pipeline

The pipeline is organized into five stages, with a feedback loop that lets failures correct themselves rather than accumulate. Each stage can reject the work of the one before it.

Stages of the Synthetic Data Pipeline
  1. Inputs. Real reference media, images or video, paired with a configuration describing the desired change and any structural guidance.
  2. Prompt generation and scene understanding. A captioning step describes the reference media, and a prompt-generation step turns that plus the configuration into a scene-aware edit instruction.
  3. Generation. The engine applies the instructed edit, with structural guidance such as edges or depth supplied alongside it, as in ControlNet, so results stay geometrically consistent.
  4. Automated verification. Two independent, model-driven checks inspect every sample before it proceeds.
  5. Feedback loop and dataset assembly. Failed samples route back for automatic correction. Samples that pass are assembled, with automatic labels, into the training-ready dataset.

Every sample carries a full history: the original reference media, each regeneration attempt, and its final verified form. One detail matters more than it seems: editing a real photo directly risks smoothing away the authentic visual character that makes training data realistic, so the edit is generated cleanly and composited back onto the original.

How Automated Verification Keeps the Dataset Honest

Generative models fail quietly. An edit can look plausible while being subtly wrong, or the model can invent content that was never requested. Unverified output degrades model quality without any visible error. Even the checking models can hallucinate, as research on object hallucination in vision-language models shows, so every generated sample, not a spot-checked subset, passes two independent checks driven by vision-language and language models.

  • Unexpected content detection inspects the sample for objects or details that were not in the source material and not requested, and flags fabricated content.
  • Attribute and quality verification confirms the targeted attribute was applied correctly, and that everything outside it remained unchanged.

A sample must pass both checks. A failed sample is not discarded: it routes back with its failure reason attached, an adjusted instruction is produced, and it is regenerated and re-verified automatically. That closed loop turns generation from produce-and-hope into a self-correcting process, and a confidence score next to each decision keeps borderline cases distinguishable from clear failures.

Using Synthetic Data for Model Training and Fine-Tuning

For object detection and similar tasks, the most reliable use of synthetic data is targeted rather than general: you are raising the count of conditions the dataset barely covers. A survey of synthetic data augmentation in computer vision maps the wider set of techniques, but the conditions that typically need help are these:

  • Uncommon environments the original capture campaign never visited
  • Difficult lighting, including strong backlighting and night scenes
  • Lower-quality imagery from devices or distances that reduce available detail
  • Unusual viewpoints and steep angles
  • Objects that are only partially visible in the frame
  • Unfamiliar backgrounds, so the model stops using background as a shortcut
  • Challenging object appearances, including worn, damaged, or reflective surfaces
  • Rare scenarios that appear a handful of times across months of real footage

Fine-tuning is mechanical once the pipeline exists: mix real data with synthetic examples weighted toward the weak conditions, fine-tune, and evaluate on a real holdout split by condition. Overweighting one condition can cost performance elsewhere, and if synthetic examples share a visual signature, a model learns the signature instead of the condition.

Quality and Realism: What Has to Be Checked

Volume is the easiest thing to produce and the least valuable. Ten thousand images carrying a consistent structural error teach a model to expect that error, while a few hundred validated examples covering a genuine gap move a metric. What is worth checking on every sample:

  • Visual realism. Does it look like something a device in the target environment would produce?
  • Correct object structure. Real geometry and proportions, with no invented or missing parts.
  • Consistency. Lighting direction, shadows, and perspective agree with the reference scene.
  • Realistic environments. Grounded in the reference rather than replaced with something generically pleasant.
  • Preservation of important characteristics. Whatever the model keys on survives the variation intact.
  • No fabricated content. Anything invented that was not requested is a defect, even when it looks good.
  • Comparison against real examples. Generated samples should not stand out beside real ones.

Human review keeps a smaller, more deliberate role. Reviewing part of each batch against real examples catches systematic problems the automated checks were never configured to find, much like the quality-controlled review used in professional AI data services.

Cost, Scalability, and Privacy

The economics differ structurally from manual collection. Collection spends on field time, equipment, travel, storage, annotation, and governance, most of it scaling with human hours. Generation runs on cloud compute and scales through parallel processing, so cost tracks compute minutes rather than headcount.

In practice, a synthetic data pipeline of this shape produces hundreds of verified samples per hour, with compute cost in the tens of dollars for a batch that would otherwise take days to collect and label. Under collection, a new requirement means a new campaign. Under generation, it means a new configuration and a run.

On privacy, synthetic data limits how much sensitive material has to circulate, without removing the concern, and the caveats matter. Reference media is still real data under whatever governance applies; generative models can reproduce elements of their training data, and a dataset built from few references can carry more identifying information than its label suggests.

Combining Synthetic Data With Real Data

Treating synthetic data as a replacement for collection is where most projects go wrong. It is good at coverage and control, and poor at telling you what the real world looks like, because it only knows what you told it. Real data anchors the distribution and remains the only credible basis for evaluation. A reasonable working pattern:

  • Train on real data first and establish a baseline you trust.
  • Analyze errors by condition rather than in aggregate.
  • Generate synthetic examples for the conditions that are underrepresented.
  • Fine-tune on a mix, keeping enough real data to hold the distribution steady.
  • Evaluate on a real holdout set, broken down by condition.
  • Repeat, aiming the next round of generation at whatever is still weak.

The loop matters more than the ratio. Anyone quoting a universal synthetic-to-real ratio is guessing, because the right mix depends on the task, the gap, and how close the examples are to production. Settling that mix is often an early question in an AI consulting engagement.

Where This Applies

The same synthetic data pipeline serves a range of work, much of it computer vision inspection where rare defects drive model quality, as in CapeStart’s work on AI-powered surface defect detection and machine vision in medical device manufacturing. Typical applications include:

  • Computer vision model training for detection and recognition
  • Video model training where temporal consistency matters
  • Targeted augmentation for underrepresented scenarios
  • Privacy-conscious dataset expansion when real samples are restricted
  • Prototyping a new model capability before committing to collection
  • Regression testing existing models against systematically varied inputs

What Changes Across the Machine Learning Lifecycle

The last change matters most. The response to a production failure shifts from scheduling a collection effort to generating examples of that condition within the week, which shortens the slowest loop most organizations have. Closing that loop in production is as much AI integration work as modeling.

Impact of Synthetic Data

This synthetic data pipeline reduced data-acquisition cost per sample by an order of magnitude compared to manual collection, and cut turnaround time for new dataset variations from weeks to hours. It established a repeatable, auditable process where quality is enforced automatically rather than assumed. In practical terms:

  • Restricted problems become workable, without distributing sensitive originals
  • A fine-tuned model replaces ongoing per-call spend on a proprietary model
  • Rare conditions get coverage without waiting for them to occur
Conclusion

Synthetic data does not remove the need for a data strategy. It gives a team a practical way to execute one. Generation is the visible part, but the value sits in everything around it: knowing which conditions need examples, validating every sample, and measuring against real data.

The problems it solves are ordinary ones: data that cannot be shared, conditions too rare to wait for, and the running cost of a proprietary model where a fine-tuned one would do. A reliable synthetic data pipeline addresses all three.

Final thought: Synthetic data is not a replacement for real-world data. It helps organizations make better use of limited real-world datasets where they matter most. If data availability is slowing your AI initiatives, connect with the CapeStart team to explore how synthetic data can support your goals.

items.title: Why I Started Talking to My Computer Instead of Typing at It
items.summary: Reading Is a 5,000-Year-Old Hack. Speaking Is a 200,000-Year-Old Operating System. Before any human could read a single word, every human could tell a story, and anyone within earshot could receive it. That asymmetry is close to 200,000 years old on one side and roughly 5,000 years old on the other. Spoken language, as far as the fossil and genetic evidence can tell us, is old enough to be load-bearing in our neurology. Writing is a tool we bolted on afterward: a clever hack that happens to work, not a native capacity we were born wired for. I have spent the better part of three decades building software at the intersection of biology and computing, so I am not anti-text. I am typing this sentence, after all. But I think we have quietly confused the accelerant for the engine. The printing press, the paperback, the inbox, the feed: all of them move information faster than a human voice ever could across distance and time. None of them changed what kind of animal we are. We are, underneath the literacy, still a species built to speak and to listen. The current wave of voice technology, dictation that replaces typing, text-to-speech that reads to us in our own cloned voice, real-time translation that erases language barriers mid-sentence, looks to me less like a novelty and more like a return trip. Speech Is Older Than the Species Doing the Speaking Modern Homo sapiens is roughly 300,000 years old. The best estimates for the emergence of complex spoken language, built on genes like FOXP2 The evolutionary history of genes involved in spoken and written … and a vocal tract capable of the fine articulatory control speech requires, put the capacity somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 years ago. Writing, by contrast, is about 5,000 years old, invented independently a handful of times, first in Sumer for keeping track of grain and beer. Proto-cuneiform tablet recording the allocation of beer, southern Iraq, about 3100 to 3000 BC. Writing began as bookkeeping. British Museum. That gap matters because of how each capacity is acquired. A child raised in a normal linguistic environment acquires spoken language without being taught, on a predictable developmental timetable, using dedicated neural architecture (Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas) that specialized for exactly this job over evolutionary time. Reading has no dedicated brain region. The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has described literacy as a case of ‘neuronal recycling’ Inside the Letterbox: How Literacy Transforms the Human Brain — PMC , in which circuitry built for object and face recognition gets repurposed, late in each individual’s development and only with years of explicit instruction, to decode strings of symbols. That is why learning to read takes a classroom and a curriculum, and learning to talk takes a crib and a few thousand hours of ambient exposure. Dyslexia is, in a sense, the tell. It is not a defect in a dedicated reading organ, because there isn’t one to be defective. It is friction in the retrofit. The Printing Press Was an Accelerant, Not a New Engine None of this is an argument against writing. Gutenberg’s press, somewhere around 1440, did something genuinely extraordinary: it took knowledge that used to travel at the speed of a human voice, one copied manuscript at a time, and let it propagate at the speed of a printing run. Literacy rates climbed. The Reformation happened. Modern science, which depends on claims being checked, cited, and reproduced across distance and time, becomes possible at a scale that oral transmission alone could never support. A replica of Gutenberg’s press. But notice what the press actually did. It did not change the brain doing the reading. It built a faster delivery mechanism on top of the same repurposed visual circuitry, and it asked more of that circuitry, earlier in life, more universally, than had ever been asked before. The printing press is fire: an external technology that extends a biological capacity (vision, in this case) far past its native range, without ever becoming part of our biology. We are now layering large language models and AI writing assistants on top of that same stack, accelerating text production and editing yet again. Each layer increases the speed of knowledge transfer. None of them touches the underlying wiring, which is still built for sound. Voice as the Great Leveler Here is the practical consequence of treating speech as the default and literacy as the add-on: almost everyone, barring specific pathology, acquires spoken language. Global literacy, even after a century of universal schooling as a stated policy goal, still sits in the high 80s as a percentage Literacy — UNESCO , and that number drops sharply in regions with limited access to education, and historically has always been lower for women and the poor than for the groups who got to decide what counted as literate. Literacy has always been a gate, and gates have always had gatekeepers. Voice does not require a gate in the same way. A toddler in Lagos and a toddler in Oslo both learn to talk before either learns the alphabet of their own language, let alone anyone else’s. Modern voice technology is starting to exploit that shared substrate: real-time speech translation that lets two people in different languages have an actual conversation, dictation tools that let someone who struggles with a keyboard or a spelling system get their ideas into a document anyway, text-to-speech that opens a book to someone who cannot or does not read print fluently. None of these tools are workarounds for a deficiency. They are routing information through the channel we were actually built to use, instead of insisting everyone first learn the 5,000-year-old hack. Why Reading Right Before Bed Might Be Fighting You Here is the part I expect some pushback on. During REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming and with consolidating emotional and declarative memory The REM Sleep — Memory Consolidation Hypothesis — PMC — NIH , your eyes move rapidly and more or less at random: no fixed target, no task, no line to track. Sleep researchers have spent decades trying to pin down exactly what those movements are doing, but the correlation between REM-stage eye activity and memory consolidation is well established in the sleep science literature. Separately, and for different reasons, therapists using EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) have people move their eyes left and right, sometimes up and down or in slow circles, while they process difficult memories, reporting that the bilateral movement itself seems to lower arousal and ease distress. People have independently stumbled onto versions of this as a pre-sleep ritual: deliberate slow eye movements, left-right, up-down, clockwise, meant to settle the nervous system before the lights go off. Now put reading next to that. Reading is the opposite of free eye movement. Your eyes move in short, fast jumps called saccades, each one landing on a word for roughly a quarter of a second, almost entirely left to right if you read English, backtracking only to fix comprehension errors. It is a tightly controlled, goal-directed, linear ocular task: the mechanical inverse of the loose, undirected movement associated with REM and with the calming techniques above. I don’t have a controlled study that proves reading-before-bed undermines rest (if you know of one, send it my way), but the directionality is suggestive enough that I have started treating ‘read a book to wind down’ as a less obviously correct piece of advice than it’s usually presented as. Listening to a story, by contrast, asks nothing of your eyes at all. You can close them. Eye-tracking record of a reader: each circle is a fixation, each line a saccade. Reading is a tightly controlled, left-to-right ocular task. Humanistlaboratoriet, Lund University, 2005 Typing Is a Very Small Movement for a Very Big Brain There is good reason to believe that fine motor dexterity, the manipulation of objects, tool use, the fingers doing something skilled and varied, played a real role in the expansion of the brain regions we now use for planning and language Research progress on the relationship between fine motor skills and … . Hand-brain co-evolution is a serious line of research, not a folk theory: the same cortical real estate that handles complex finger movement sits immediately next to, and appears to have scaffolded, language production areas. Which makes it a little strange that our main daily interface with information now asks almost nothing of the body. Typing is dexterous, technically, but it is also narrow: the same small, repeated finger movements, hour after hour, torso still, eyes locked on a screen twenty inches away. Compare that to what an oral storyteller’s body is doing: standing or pacing, gesturing with both arms, modulating pitch and pace and volume, making eye contact, responding to a listener’s face in real time. Walking itself has a measurable effect on idea generation. A frequently cited Stanford study found that walking, compared to sitting, reliably boosted creative output on divergent-thinking tasks, with the effect persisting even after the person sat back down Stanford study finds walking improves creativity . Oral storytelling was never a seated, finger-only activity. It used a body. Reading Is a 5,000-Year-Old Hack. Speaking Is a 200,000-Year-Old Operating System.

Before any human could read a single word, every human could tell a story, and anyone within earshot could receive it. That asymmetry is close to 200,000 years old on one side and roughly 5,000 years old on the other. Spoken language, as far as the fossil and genetic evidence can tell us, is old enough to be load-bearing in our neurology. Writing is a tool we bolted on afterward: a clever hack that happens to work, not a native capacity we were born wired for.

I have spent the better part of three decades building software at the intersection of biology and computing, so I am not anti-text. I am typing this sentence, after all. But I think we have quietly confused the accelerant for the engine. The printing press, the paperback, the inbox, the feed: all of them move information faster than a human voice ever could across distance and time. None of them changed what kind of animal we are. We are, underneath the literacy, still a species built to speak and to listen. The current wave of voice technology, dictation that replaces typing, text-to-speech that reads to us in our own cloned voice, real-time translation that erases language barriers mid-sentence, looks to me less like a novelty and more like a return trip.

Speech Is Older Than the Species Doing the Speaking

Modern Homo sapiens is roughly 300,000 years old. The best estimates for the emergence of complex spoken language, built on genes like FOXP2 The evolutionary history of genes involved in spoken and written … and a vocal tract capable of the fine articulatory control speech requires, put the capacity somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 years ago. Writing, by contrast, is about 5,000 years old, invented independently a handful of times, first in Sumer for keeping track of grain and beer.

Proto-cuneiform tablet recording the allocation of beer, southern Iraq, about 3100 to 3000 BC. Writing began as bookkeeping. British Museum.

That gap matters because of how each capacity is acquired. A child raised in a normal linguistic environment acquires spoken language without being taught, on a predictable developmental timetable, using dedicated neural architecture (Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas) that specialized for exactly this job over evolutionary time. Reading has no dedicated brain region. The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has described literacy as a case of ‘neuronal recycling’ Inside the Letterbox: How Literacy Transforms the Human Brain — PMC, in which circuitry built for object and face recognition gets repurposed, late in each individual’s development and only with years of explicit instruction, to decode strings of symbols. That is why learning to read takes a classroom and a curriculum, and learning to talk takes a crib and a few thousand hours of ambient exposure.

Dyslexia is, in a sense, the tell. It is not a defect in a dedicated reading organ, because there isn’t one to be defective. It is friction in the retrofit.

The Printing Press Was an Accelerant, Not a New Engine

None of this is an argument against writing. Gutenberg’s press, somewhere around 1440, did something genuinely extraordinary: it took knowledge that used to travel at the speed of a human voice, one copied manuscript at a time, and let it propagate at the speed of a printing run. Literacy rates climbed. The Reformation happened. Modern science, which depends on claims being checked, cited, and reproduced across distance and time, becomes possible at a scale that oral transmission alone could never support.

A replica of Gutenberg’s press.

But notice what the press actually did. It did not change the brain doing the reading. It built a faster delivery mechanism on top of the same repurposed visual circuitry, and it asked more of that circuitry, earlier in life, more universally, than had ever been asked before. The printing press is fire: an external technology that extends a biological capacity (vision, in this case) far past its native range, without ever becoming part of our biology. We are now layering large language models and AI writing assistants on top of that same stack, accelerating text production and editing yet again. Each layer increases the speed of knowledge transfer. None of them touches the underlying wiring, which is still built for sound.

Voice as the Great Leveler

Here is the practical consequence of treating speech as the default and literacy as the add-on: almost everyone, barring specific pathology, acquires spoken language. Global literacy, even after a century of universal schooling as a stated policy goal, still sits in the high 80s as a percentage Literacy — UNESCO, and that number drops sharply in regions with limited access to education, and historically has always been lower for women and the poor than for the groups who got to decide what counted as literate. Literacy has always been a gate, and gates have always had gatekeepers.

Voice does not require a gate in the same way. A toddler in Lagos and a toddler in Oslo both learn to talk before either learns the alphabet of their own language, let alone anyone else’s. Modern voice technology is starting to exploit that shared substrate: real-time speech translation that lets two people in different languages have an actual conversation, dictation tools that let someone who struggles with a keyboard or a spelling system get their ideas into a document anyway, text-to-speech that opens a book to someone who cannot or does not read print fluently. None of these tools are workarounds for a deficiency. They are routing information through the channel we were actually built to use, instead of insisting everyone first learn the 5,000-year-old hack.

During REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming and with consolidating emotional and declarative memory The REM Sleep — Memory Consolidation Hypothesis — PMC — NIH, your eyes move rapidly and more or less at random: no fixed target, no task, no line to track. Sleep researchers have spent decades trying to pin down exactly what those movements are doing, but the correlation between REM-stage eye activity and memory consolidation is well established in the sleep science literature.

Separately, and for different reasons, therapists using EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing) have people move their eyes left and right, sometimes up and down or in slow circles, while they process difficult memories, reporting that the bilateral movement itself seems to lower arousal and ease distress. People have independently stumbled onto versions of this as a pre-sleep ritual: deliberate slow eye movements, left-right, up-down, clockwise, meant to settle the nervous system before the lights go off.

Now put reading next to that. Reading is the opposite of free eye movement. Your eyes move in short, fast jumps called saccades, each one landing on a word for roughly a quarter of a second, almost entirely left to right if you read English, backtracking only to fix comprehension errors. It is a tightly controlled, goal-directed, linear ocular task: the mechanical inverse of the loose, undirected movement associated with REM and with the calming techniques above. I don’t have a controlled study that proves reading-before-bed undermines rest (if you know of one, send it my way), but the directionality is suggestive enough that I have started treating ‘read a book to wind down’ as a less obviously correct piece of advice than it’s usually presented as. Listening to a story, by contrast, asks nothing of your eyes at all. You can close them.

items.title: Musk Says SpaceX Closed $40 Bn GPU Debt Deal, Warns Most Neoclouds Won’t Survive
items.summary: SpaceX closed a $40 billion debt financing deal to buy graphics processing units (GPUs) for AI infrastructure, CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X. He further warned that tighter credit conditions could trigger widespread consolidation among AI cloud providers. “SpaceX closed $40B of debt for GPUs, but we’re investment grade and have Starlink & launch revenue,” Musk wrote. He attributed the company’s ability to secure the financing to its investment-grade status and revenue streams beyond AI data centres. His comments come as technology companies borrow heavily to fund the chips, data centres and computing infrastructure needed to develop and run AI models. Musk’s comments also point to growing pressure on specialised AI cloud providers, commonly known as neoclouds, which rent GPU computing capacity to AI developers and businesses. He said debt markets had become increasingly difficult for companies that lack revenue from businesses outside AI infrastructure. “As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres,” Musk wrote. He predicted that more than 200 neocloud providers would fail or consolidate as access to financing tightens. “Some will make it through, but not many.” Musk also ruled out SpaceX acquiring neocloud companies, describing such a move as “pointless”. Companies such as CoreWeave and Nebius supply computing capacity for AI workloads. Scaling their operations requires substantial investment in GPUs and data centres, making access to debt crucial to their growth. SpaceX’s financing comes as the company ramps up spending on AI infrastructure. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen said the company expects capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company’s revenue rose 161% year-on-year to $14.58 billion in the third quarter ended September 30. Revenue from AI grew nearly tenfold to $7.56 billion. Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet business, and its rocket launch operations have historically been key revenue sources. The company is also investing in AI computing and plans to manufacture its own GPUs. Separately, SpaceX and Tesla are working on Terafab, a chip manufacturing joint venture in Austin. The project is expected to produce its first test chip around May or June 2027, with volume production targeted for the third quarter of 2028.

items.title: Migrating Semantic Kernel Agents to Microsoft Agent Framework in ASP.NET Core
items.summary: Semantic Kernel has been the default .NET agent toolkit for years. In April 2026 Microsoft shipped Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) 1.0 as the unification of Semantic Kernel’s enterprise features and AutoGen’s orchestration patterns. As of October 2026 the package sits at 1.26, Semantic Kernel is in maintenance mode (critical fixes only), and every new capability—graph workflows, native MCP/A2A, durable execution, better middleware—lands only in MAF. Teams that already have working Semantic Kernel agents are not forced to rewrite overnight, but the longer you wait the larger the gap becomes. This article shows a concrete, incremental migration of a tool-using agent into an ASP.NET Core application using current package names and APIs. MAF splits those responsibilities: Model access lives on an IChatClient (from Microsoft.Extensions.AI). Agent behavior lives on AIAgent (most commonly a ChatClientAgent ). Callable capabilities are plain AIFunction s created with AIFunctionFactory.Create . Conversation continuity is an AgentSession created by the agent itself. Cross-cutting concerns move to middleware. There is no longer a mandatory Kernel. You create a chat client for your provider, then call the extension method .AsAIAgent(...) . When to Stay on Semantic Kernel a Little Longer If the existing SK agent is stable, has no need for new orchestration features, and the team is mid-release, there is no emergency. Semantic Kernel still receives critical fixes and security patches, so check Microsoft's current support statement and plan around it. Plan the migration for the next feature cycle rather than forcing it into a hotfix window. Conclusion Migrating a Semantic Kernel agent to Microsoft Agent Framework removes the Kernel as the center of gravity, simplifies tool registration, and puts you on the package that receives all new investment. The surface area is smaller than many teams expect: most of the work is mechanical once the chat client is in place. Start with one agent (a support-reply agent like the one in my open-source SupportAgent.NET project is a good candidate), keep the old path behind a feature flag if needed, and move the rest when the first migration is proven in production. items.summary_html:
Semantic Kernel has been the default .NET agent toolkit for years. In April 2026 Microsoft shipped Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) 1.0 as the unification of Semantic Kernel’s enterprise features and AutoGen’s orchestration patterns. As of October 2026 the package sits at 1.26, Semantic Kernel is in maintenance mode (critical fixes only), and every new capability—graph workflows, native MCP/A2A, durable execution, better middleware—lands only in MAF.

Teams that already have working Semantic Kernel agents are not forced to rewrite overnight, but the longer you wait the larger the gap becomes. This article shows a concrete, incremental migration of a tool-using agent into an ASP.NET Core application using current package names and APIs.

What Actually Changes

The biggest shift is architectural. Semantic Kernel centered everything on a Kernel object that owned the chat service, plugins, filters, and memory. MAF splits those responsibilities:

  • Model access lives on an IChatClient (from Microsoft.Extensions.AI).
  • Agent behavior lives on AIAgent (most commonly a ChatClientAgent).
  • Callable capabilities are plain AIFunctions created with AIFunctionFactory.Create.
  • Conversation continuity is an AgentSession created by the agent itself.
  • Cross-cutting concerns move to middleware.

There is no longer a mandatory Kernel. You create a chat client for your provider, then call the extension method .AsAIAgent(...).

Packages

For a typical ASP.NET Core migration:

dotnet add package Microsoft.Agents.AI
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.AI
# Provider-specific (examples)
dotnet add package Azure.AI.OpenAI
dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.AI.OpenAI  # AsIChatClient() for OpenAI/Azure OpenAI clients
dotnet add package Azure.Identity
# or for local
dotnet add package OllamaSharp

Microsoft.Agents.AI 1.26 is the current stable release. Prefer the non-prerelease package unless you need a preview feature.

Before: Semantic Kernel Agent with a Tool

A typical SK agent that can look up weather:

using System.ComponentModel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel;
using Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Agents;

// Values from configuration
string endpoint = "https://.openai.azure.com/";
string deploymentName = "gpt-4o-mini";
string apiKey = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY")!;

public class WeatherPlugin
{
    [KernelFunction, Description("Gets the current weather for a city")]
    public string GetWeather(string city) =>
        $"Weather in {city}: 18°C, partly cloudy";
}

// In Program.cs or a factory
var kernel = Kernel.CreateBuilder()
    .AddAzureOpenAIChatCompletion(deploymentName, endpoint, apiKey)
    .Build();

kernel.Plugins.AddFromType<WeatherPlugin>();

var agent = new ChatCompletionAgent
{
    Name = "WeatherAgent",
    Instructions = "You are a helpful weather assistant. Use the available tools.",
    Kernel = kernel
};

// Invocation
AgentThread thread = new ChatHistoryAgentThread();
await foreach (var item in agent.InvokeAsync("What's the weather in Seattle?", thread))
{
    Console.WriteLine(item.Message);
}

The Kernel is required, the plugin must be registered on it, the thread type is caller-created, and invocation returns an IAsyncEnumerable.

After: Microsoft Agent Framework

The same agent becomes:

using System.ComponentModel;
using Azure.AI.OpenAI;
using Azure.Identity;
using Microsoft.Agents.AI;
using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;

string endpoint = "https://.openai.azure.com/";
string deploymentName = "gpt-4o-mini";

[Description("Gets the current weather for a city")]
static string GetWeather(string city) =>
    $"Weather in {city}: 18°C, partly cloudy";

// Create the chat client (Azure OpenAI example)
var azureClient = new AzureOpenAIClient(new Uri(endpoint), new DefaultAzureCredential());
IChatClient chatClient = azureClient.GetChatClient(deploymentName).AsIChatClient();

// Turn it into an agent and register the tool in one call
AIAgent agent = chatClient.AsAIAgent(
    name: "WeatherAgent",
    instructions: "You are a helpful weather assistant. Use the available tools when needed.",
    tools: [AIFunctionFactory.Create(GetWeather)]);

// Session is created by the agent
AgentSession session = await agent.CreateSessionAsync();

// Non-streaming invocation returns a single AgentResponse
AgentResponse response = await agent.RunAsync("What's the weather in Seattle?", session);
Console.WriteLine(response.Text);

No Kernel, no plugin class required (a static method or instance method works), no [KernelFunction] attribute, and the session is owned by the agent. Streaming uses RunStreamingAsync and yields AgentResponseUpdate objects.

For a local model the client creation changes but the rest of the API stays identical:

using OllamaSharp;

var ollama = new OllamaApiClient(new Uri("http://localhost:11434"), "llama3.2");

AIAgent localAgent = ollama.AsAIAgent(
    instructions: "You are a helpful local assistant.",
    tools: [AIFunctionFactory.Create(GetWeather)]);

Use a model that supports tool calling (llama3.2, qwen2.5, etc.).

Dependency Injection in ASP.NET Core

Register the chat client and the agent as services. Prefer a keyed singleton when the agent configuration is static:

// Program.cs
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IChatClient>(sp =>
{
    var azureClient = new AzureOpenAIClient(
        new Uri(builder.Configuration["AzureOpenAI:Endpoint"]!),
        new DefaultAzureCredential());

    return azureClient.GetChatClient(
        builder.Configuration["AzureOpenAI:Deployment"]!).AsIChatClient();
});

builder.Services.AddKeyedSingleton<AIAgent>("WeatherAgent", (sp, key) =>
{
    var chatClient = sp.GetRequiredService<IChatClient>();

    return chatClient.AsAIAgent(
        name: "WeatherAgent",
        instructions: "You are a helpful weather assistant. Use tools when appropriate.",
        tools: [AIFunctionFactory.Create(GetWeather)]);
});

Inject it where needed:

public class WeatherController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly AIAgent _agent;

    public WeatherController([FromKeyedServices("WeatherAgent")] AIAgent agent)
    {
        _agent = agent;
    }

    [HttpPost("ask")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Ask([FromBody] string question)
    {
        var session = await _agent.CreateSessionAsync();
        var response = await _agent.RunAsync(question, session);
        return Ok(new { answer = response.Text });
    }
}

If you need per-request state or different tool instances (for example a tool that depends on a scoped DbContext), register the agent as scoped instead.

Sessions, Streaming, and Options

Create a session once per conversation and reuse it for multi-turn chats. For hosted providers that support conversation deletion you still manage cleanup through the underlying client when required.

Streaming is straightforward:

await foreach (var update in agent.RunStreamingAsync(question, session))
{
    if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(update.Text))
        Console.Write(update.Text);
}

Token limits and other inference options move to ChatClientAgentRunOptions:

var options = new ChatClientAgentRunOptions(
    new ChatOptions { MaxOutputTokens = 800 });
var response = await agent.RunAsync(question, session, options);
Incremental Migration Checklist
  1. Add the MAF packages and the Microsoft.Extensions.AI client for your provider.
  2. Extract pure functions that were previously [KernelFunction] methods. They usually need only a [Description] attribute.
  3. Replace Kernel + ChatCompletionAgent construction with IChatClient.AsAIAgent(...) and pass the functions via AIFunctionFactory.Create.
  4. Change thread creation to await agent.CreateSessionAsync().
  5. Switch InvokeAsync / InvokeStreamingAsync to RunAsync / RunStreamingAsync.
  6. Update DI registration from AddKernel + keyed Agent to keyed AIAgent.
  7. Run your existing evaluation suite (or add one) against the new agent before removing the SK code path.
  8. Only after the agent layer is stable, consider adopting MAF workflows for multi-agent orchestration if you need them.

You can keep non-agent Semantic Kernel usage (prompt templates, pure function calling via Microsoft.Extensions.AI) running in parallel during the transition. The model-access layer is already shared. If you are weighing which AI layer to standardize on for an existing system, this is the kind of decision I cover in my AI integration work for .NET teams.

When to Stay on Semantic Kernel a Little Longer

If the existing SK agent is stable, has no need for new orchestration features, and the team is mid-release, there is no emergency. Semantic Kernel still receives critical fixes and security patches, so check Microsoft's current support statement and plan around it. Plan the migration for the next feature cycle rather than forcing it into a hotfix window.

Conclusion

Migrating a Semantic Kernel agent to Microsoft Agent Framework removes the Kernel as the center of gravity, simplifies tool registration, and puts you on the package that receives all new investment. The surface area is smaller than many teams expect: most of the work is mechanical once the chat client is in place. Start with one agent (a support-reply agent like the one in my open-source SupportAgent.NET project is a good candidate), keep the old path behind a feature flag if needed, and move the rest when the first migration is proven in production.
