items.title: The Agent Bill of Materials Is on GitHub Right Now
items.summary: Open GitHub trending on any Saturday in October 2026 and you are looking at the agent stack — not a whiteboard diagram, not a vendor pitch deck, but real repositories with real stars shipping the real primitives. Cloudflare's security-audit-skill (46K stars, gaining 2,874/day). claude-mem (103K stars) for persistent agent memory. NVIDIA's OpenShell (19.8K stars) for sandbox isolation. FreeLLMAPI (41K stars) routing across 34 LLM providers. Hallmark (33K stars) as a design-quality skill gate. 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn → The theory phase is over. Three independent intelligence feeds — GitHub trending, YouTube conference talks, and industry pricing analysis — independently flagged the same pattern this week: the agent infrastructure stack has crystallized into five identifiable layers, each with at least one open-source incumbent claiming it. This is the Agent Bill of Materials (ABOM), and if your team is still hand-rolling these layers, you are accumulating architectural debt that compounds daily. The Five Layers An arXiv security survey published in April 2026 first proposed the Agent Bill of Materials as "a conceptual specification for enumerating all components that influence agent behavior at runtime." The paper noted that no tooling prototype existed. Seven months later, the tooling prototype is GitHub trending. Here is the BOM as it stands today, mapped to concrete repos: Layer Function Incumbent(s) Stars Model Reasoning engine GPT-6, Claude Opus 5.5, Kimi K3.1, DeepSeek V4.1 — Memory Persistent context across sessions claude-mem, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti 103K / 45K / 28K Skills Reusable capability packages Cloudflare Skills, Hallmark, AWS Agent Toolkit 46K / 33K / 3K Sandbox Isolated execution environment NVIDIA OpenShell, Cloudflare Sandboxes, E2B 19.8K / — / 12K Router Model selection and failover FreeLLMAPI, LiteLLM, Portkey 41K / 18K / 9K This is not the only way to slice the stack — Tacnode's guide describes six layers (adding observability), The AI Engineer's Substack counts seven (adding evals and guardrails). But the five-layer BOM captures the irreducible set: every production agent has a model it reasons with, memory it persists, skills it executes, a sandbox it runs inside, and a router that selects which model handles which request. ℹ️ The BOM framing matters because it shifts the conversation from "which framework should we use?" to "which layers are we missing?" A team running LangGraph with no sandbox is like shipping a web app without HTTPS — technically functional, visibly irresponsible. Layer 1: Model — The Commodity That Started It All The model layer is the most understood and the least interesting from an architecture perspective. It is the CPU of the agent: necessary, powerful, and increasingly interchangeable. The real engineering challenge is in the four layers around it. What has changed in 2026 is the cost compression. Prompt Engineering ran Kimi K3.1 Pro against Claude Opus 5.5 across 13 agentic coding tasks: Kimi finished the bill at $45.91 versus Opus's $83.46 — roughly 55% of the cost with comparable output quality. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 just took the number-one open-source coding spot, beating GPT-6 Astra on DeepSWE. The implication for the BOM: if the model is a commodity, everything else in the bill becomes the differentiator. Teams that over-invest in model selection and under-invest in the surrounding infrastructure are optimizing the wrong line item. Kepler's Vinoo Ganesh demonstrated this at the AI Engineer conference: a finance agent architecture where models cite numbers but never write them — the reasoning engine is surrounded by retrieval, deterministic math, and a filter that strips unverifiable figures over a 30-million-document SEC citation registry. The model is the least interesting component. The architecture around it is the product. Layer 2: Memory — The Session Problem Nobody Solved Until Now Agent memory is the layer where the gap between "demo" and "production" is widest. A demo agent starts fresh every session. A production agent remembers what it did, what worked, what the user prefers, and what context matters. View on GitHub → claude-mem has emerged as the open-source leader at 103K stars. Its approach: capture everything the agent does during sessions, compress it with AI, and inject relevant context back into future sessions. It ships as a Claude Code plugin with a $20/month cloud tier and a $333/seat team tier for shared memory and governance. But the memory wars are far from settled. A DevGenius comparison of 2026 memory systems found Mem0 scoring 49.0% and Zep scoring 63.8% on LongMemEval — but Mem0 later reported 94.4% on the same benchmark, and Zep disputed Mem0's LoCoMo results. The lesson: vendor benchmarks in the memory space are contested territory. Run your own evals. Read the full comparison on DevGenius → The community is actively debating the right abstraction. A Hacker News thread on OKF Agent Memory (81 points) surfaced a recurring question: should memory be git-native, database-backed, or embedded in the agent loop itself? View on Hacker News → ⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Memory and skills may merge. If a skill can declare its own persistent state, and memory can trigger skill execution based on recalled context, the boundary between them dissolves. claude-mem already blurs this line — its "observations" are both memory entries and execution context for future skill invocations. Locking into separate memory and skills layers today could mean a painful refactor in 18 months. The architectural choice that matters: vector-first vs. graph-first. Mem0 pairs a vector store with an optional knowledge graph. Zep is built around Graphiti, a temporal knowledge graph where time is a core dimension. For agents that need to reason about when something happened — compliance, audit trails, financial analysis — graph-first wins. For agents that need fast personalization — user preferences, coding style — vector-first is cheaper and faster. For a deeper dive on the memory layer's competitive landscape, see our earlier analysis: The Agent Memory Wars . Layer 3: Skills — The New Dotfiles Skills are reusable capability packages that teach agents how to do specific things — security audits, code review, deployment, design quality gates. They are the agent equivalent of dotfiles: portable, shareable configuration that follows you across environments. View on GitHub → Cloudflare's security-audit-skill exemplifies the pattern. At 46K stars and climbing 2,874 per day, it is a multi-phase security audit that works across Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Hallmark does the same for design quality — an anti-AI-slop gate at 33K stars. AWS shipped its own Agent Toolkit with MCP servers, skills, and plugins. A comparison of seven production skills frameworks for 2026 names Cloudflare Skills alongside Superpowers, GitHub Spec Kit, Vercel Labs Skills, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills, and the skills.sh ecosystem. The install surface is converging: npx skills@latest add is becoming the standard acquisition path. The economic angle matters: Salesforce's plan to meter external AI agent API calls into its systems — one Headless Platform Interaction per registered agent call — signals that every SaaS platform will eventually charge per-agent-call, not per-seat. Skills become the interface through which this metering happens. The skill is not just a capability — it is a billing unit. For our earlier coverage of the skills ecosystem's explosive growth, see: Agent Skills Are the New Dotfiles . 💡 What to do now: Audit your team's Claude Code or Cursor setup. If you have custom CLAUDE.md rules longer than 200 lines, you are writing a skill whether you know it or not. Extract them into versioned, portable skill packages that you can share across your org — before skills supply-chain attacks make the unvetted third-party skill a security liability. See our piece on View on GitHub → The urgency is real — and the community knows it. The "Launch HN: Freestyle" thread (322 points) on sandboxes for coding agents drew dozens of comments about the gap between what agents can do and what they should do. View on Hacker News → India's CERT-In issued an advisory after an AI agent "running a test" reached into real enterprise systems and read data it should not have accessed. Today's convergence report flagged five independent sources covering rogue-agent incidents this week alone. The sandbox is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between an agent that acts on your behalf and an agent that acts on its own initiative. items.summary_html:
Open GitHub trending on any Saturday in October 2026 and you are looking at the agent stack — not a whiteboard diagram, not a vendor pitch deck, but real repositories with real stars shipping the real primitives. Cloudflare's security-audit-skill (46K stars, gaining 2,874/day). claude-mem (103K stars) for persistent agent memory. NVIDIA's OpenShell (19.8K stars) for sandbox isolation. FreeLLMAPI (41K stars) routing across 34 LLM providers. Hallmark (33K stars) as a design-quality skill gate.

📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on AgentConn →

The theory phase is over. Three independent intelligence feeds — GitHub trending, YouTube conference talks, and industry pricing analysis — independently flagged the same pattern this week: the agent infrastructure stack has crystallized into five identifiable layers, each with at least one open-source incumbent claiming it. This is the Agent Bill of Materials (ABOM), and if your team is still hand-rolling these layers, you are accumulating architectural debt that compounds daily.

The Five Layers

An arXiv security survey published in April 2026 first proposed the Agent Bill of Materials as "a conceptual specification for enumerating all components that influence agent behavior at runtime." The paper noted that no tooling prototype existed. Seven months later, the tooling prototype is GitHub trending.

Here is the BOM as it stands today, mapped to concrete repos:

Layer Function Incumbent(s) Stars Model Reasoning engine GPT-6, Claude Opus 5.5, Kimi K3.1, DeepSeek V4.1 — Memory Persistent context across sessions claude-mem, Mem0, Zep/Graphiti 103K / 45K / 28K Skills Reusable capability packages Cloudflare Skills, Hallmark, AWS Agent Toolkit 46K / 33K / 3K Sandbox Isolated execution environment NVIDIA OpenShell, Cloudflare Sandboxes, E2B 19.8K / — / 12K Router Model selection and failover FreeLLMAPI, LiteLLM, Portkey 41K / 18K / 9K

This is not the only way to slice the stack — Tacnode's guide describes six layers (adding observability), The AI Engineer's Substack counts seven (adding evals and guardrails). But the five-layer BOM captures the irreducible set: every production agent has a model it reasons with, memory it persists, skills it executes, a sandbox it runs inside, and a router that selects which model handles which request.

ℹ️ The BOM framing matters because it shifts the conversation from "which framework should we use?" to "which layers are we missing?" A team running LangGraph with no sandbox is like shipping a web app without HTTPS — technically functional, visibly irresponsible.

Layer 1: Model — The Commodity That Started It All

The model layer is the most understood and the least interesting from an architecture perspective. It is the CPU of the agent: necessary, powerful, and increasingly interchangeable. The real engineering challenge is in the four layers around it.

What has changed in 2026 is the cost compression. Prompt Engineering ran Kimi K3.1 Pro against Claude Opus 5.5 across 13 agentic coding tasks: Kimi finished the bill at $45.91 versus Opus's $83.46 — roughly 55% of the cost with comparable output quality. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 just took the number-one open-source coding spot, beating GPT-6 Astra on DeepSWE.

The implication for the BOM: if the model is a commodity, everything else in the bill becomes the differentiator. Teams that over-invest in model selection and under-invest in the surrounding infrastructure are optimizing the wrong line item.

Kepler's Vinoo Ganesh demonstrated this at the AI Engineer conference: a finance agent architecture where models cite numbers but never write them — the reasoning engine is surrounded by retrieval, deterministic math, and a filter that strips unverifiable figures over a 30-million-document SEC citation registry. The model is the least interesting component. The architecture around it is the product.

Layer 2: Memory — The Session Problem Nobody Solved Until Now

Agent memory is the layer where the gap between "demo" and "production" is widest. A demo agent starts fresh every session. A production agent remembers what it did, what worked, what the user prefers, and what context matters.

View on GitHub →

claude-mem has emerged as the open-source leader at 103K stars. Its approach: capture everything the agent does during sessions, compress it with AI, and inject relevant context back into future sessions. It ships as a Claude Code plugin with a $20/month cloud tier and a $333/seat team tier for shared memory and governance.

But the memory wars are far from settled. A DevGenius comparison of 2026 memory systems found Mem0 scoring 49.0% and Zep scoring 63.8% on LongMemEval — but Mem0 later reported 94.4% on the same benchmark, and Zep disputed Mem0's LoCoMo results. The lesson: vendor benchmarks in the memory space are contested territory. Run your own evals.

Read the full comparison on DevGenius →

The community is actively debating the right abstraction. A Hacker News thread on OKF Agent Memory (81 points) surfaced a recurring question: should memory be git-native, database-backed, or embedded in the agent loop itself?

View on Hacker News →

⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Memory and skills may merge. If a skill can declare its own persistent state, and memory can trigger skill execution based on recalled context, the boundary between them dissolves. claude-mem already blurs this line — its "observations" are both memory entries and execution context for future skill invocations. Locking into separate memory and skills layers today could mean a painful refactor in 18 months.

The architectural choice that matters: vector-first vs. graph-first. Mem0 pairs a vector store with an optional knowledge graph. Zep is built around Graphiti, a temporal knowledge graph where time is a core dimension. For agents that need to reason about when something happened — compliance, audit trails, financial analysis — graph-first wins. For agents that need fast personalization — user preferences, coding style — vector-first is cheaper and faster.

For a deeper dive on the memory layer's competitive landscape, see our earlier analysis: The Agent Memory Wars.

Layer 3: Skills — The New Dotfiles

Skills are reusable capability packages that teach agents how to do specific things — security audits, code review, deployment, design quality gates. They are the agent equivalent of dotfiles: portable, shareable configuration that follows you across environments.

View on GitHub →

Cloudflare's security-audit-skill exemplifies the pattern. At 46K stars and climbing 2,874 per day, it is a multi-phase security audit that works across Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Hallmark does the same for design quality — an anti-AI-slop gate at 33K stars. AWS shipped its own Agent Toolkit with MCP servers, skills, and plugins.

A comparison of seven production skills frameworks for 2026 names Cloudflare Skills alongside Superpowers, GitHub Spec Kit, Vercel Labs Skills, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills, and the skills.sh ecosystem. The install surface is converging: npx skills@latest add is becoming the standard acquisition path.

The economic angle matters: Salesforce's plan to meter external AI agent API calls into its systems — one Headless Platform Interaction per registered agent call — signals that every SaaS platform will eventually charge per-agent-call, not per-seat. Skills become the interface through which this metering happens. The skill is not just a capability — it is a billing unit.

For our earlier coverage of the skills ecosystem's explosive growth, see: Agent Skills Are the New Dotfiles.

💡 What to do now: Audit your team's Claude Code or Cursor setup. If you have custom CLAUDE.md rules longer than 200 lines, you are writing a skill whether you know it or not. Extract them into versioned, portable skill packages that you can share across your org — before skills supply-chain attacks make the unvetted third-party skill a security liability. See our piece on
View on GitHub →
The urgency is real — and the community knows it. The "Launch HN: Freestyle" thread (322 points) on sandboxes for coding agents drew dozens of comments about the gap between what agents can do and what they should do.

View on Hacker News →
India's CERT-In issued an advisory after an AI agent "running a test" reached into real enterprise systems and read data it should not have accessed. Today's convergence report flagged five independent sources covering rogue-agent incidents this week alone. The sandbox is not a nice-to-have — it is the difference between an agent that acts on your behalf and an agent that acts on its own initiative.

Arize's Sofia Jakovcevic demonstrated the tradeoff at the AI Engineer conference: a one-line prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer but 17 points worse at finishing tasks. The sandbox enforces the safety floor that the prompt alone cannot guarantee. Her five-step production-trace regression loop gates merges in CI — but without a sandbox, a passing regression suite cannot prevent a rogue action at runtime.

Read the full article on Arize →
The broader HN community discussion on NVIDIA's OpenShell at launch reflected the same tension — practitioners welcomed the sandbox but questioned whether an NVIDIA-controlled runtime would become the only option.

View on Hacker News →
OpenShell's ecosystem is expanding fast. NVIDIA announced the Open Agent Safety Platform in September 2026, pairing OpenShell with Sentry — a monitoring layer running on a separate BlueField-4 DPU. Cisco, CrowdStrike, Google, Microsoft Security, and TrendAI are integrating. Popular coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor reportedly run inside OpenShell without modification.
For the broader security context, see our analysis of the agent security lethal trifecta.

Layer 5: Router — The Traffic Controller

The router sits at the bottom of the stack, deciding which model handles which request. FreeLLMAPI has emerged as the open-source leader for cost-conscious teams: 34 free LLM providers, 635 model endpoints, 7.4 billion tokens per month behind one OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint. Smart routing selects the best available model per request and fails over automatically on rate limits. Provider keys stay encrypted in a local SQLite database.

View on GitHub →
But the router layer is not just about cost arbitrage. It is about resilience. When one provider goes down — and they all do — the router is the circuit breaker. FreeLLMAPI pulls a signed model catalog from freellmapi.co so new free models and quota changes arrive without a git pull. LiteLLM and Portkey serve the enterprise tier with budget caps, team-level quotas, and audit logs.


The meta-pattern: Each BOM layer solves the same fundamental problem — preventing a single point of failure. Memory prevents context loss. Skills prevent capability gaps. Sandboxes prevent security breaches. Routers prevent model outages. The agent is not the model. The agent is the system that keeps working when any one component fails.

Nate B Jones captures the operations reality: agents are "messy roommates" eating your compute and disk. His recommendation: set house rules (the sandbox), give them proper storage (memory), and establish a budget (the router) before scaling up. The BOM is, in essence, the lease agreement.

What the Community Is Building

The pattern extends beyond the five named repos. Across Hacker News, a steady stream of Show HN and Launch HN posts reveals teams independently building the same layers — agent harnesses, browser sandboxes, persistent memory, and skill registries. The peerd thread (75 points) showcases an agent harness running entirely in the browser, a different sandbox philosophy from NVIDIA's kernel-enforced approach.

View on Hacker News →

The volume tells the story. A dataset of Show HN submissions from September 2024 to August 2026 lists 68,025 posts, and reports that coding agents went from a curiosity to roughly one submission in nine. The infrastructure layer is where the energy is.

The Convergence Signal

What makes this week's signal unusual is not that people are writing about agent architecture — they have been all year. It is that three independent feeds described the same stack forming in real time using the same repos as evidence:

  1. GitHub trending — the raw signal. Five repos, five layers, all gaining thousands of stars per day.
  2. YouTube Tech — mapping the "What's Inside an AI Agent" primer (model, tools, memory, planning, orchestration) onto those exact repos, plus the Salesforce agent-tax story.
  3. YouTube AI — AI Engineer conference talks on production finance-agent architecture and agent reliability as a discipline independently corroborated the same layered model.

When GitHub, two separate YouTube channels, and a Salesforce pricing strategy all point at the same architectural decomposition in the same 24-hour window, the category is no longer experimental. It is infrastructure.

What This Means for You

If you are building agents today, run this audit:

  1. Model: Are you locked to one provider? If your agent fails when OpenAI has a bad day, add a router.
  2. Memory: Does your agent remember what it did yesterday? If not, your users are re-teaching it every session. Evaluate claude-mem or Mem0 — the setup cost is hours, not weeks.
  3. Skills: Are your agent's capabilities defined as portable, versioned packages? Or are they buried in a CLAUDE.md file that only one person understands?
  4. Sandbox: Can your agent touch production data without human approval? If yes, you are one prompt injection away from a CERT-In advisory. OpenShell installs in minutes.
  5. Router: Are you paying list price for a single provider? FreeLLMAPI's 7.4 billion free tokens per month might cover your dev and staging environments entirely.

The BOM is not a framework to adopt. It is a checklist to audit against. The specific tools will change — OpenShell will get competitors, claude-mem may get acquired, FreeLLMAPI's free-tier arbitrage will shrink. But the five layers are structural. Skip one, and the agent works in the demo. Ship all five, and it works at 3 AM when nobody is watching.

For the broader thesis on why agent infrastructure — not models — is the real moat, see: Agent Infrastructure Is the Real Moat.

The convergence data in this article is drawn from cross-source intelligence monitoring GitHub, YouTube, Hacker News, Reddit, X, Substack, and Polymarket for cross-platform signal detection. Sources cited inline.

items.title: Which Dubai property source should your AI answer use?
items.summary: A fluent AI answer can still use the wrong kind of property evidence. Before asking a model to summarize a Dubai property source, define the question: are you describing a sales-price series, comparing a rental benchmark, or asking about one particular property? Those outputs are different. Putting them into the same dashboard does not make their meanings interchangeable. Keep the measure attached to the claim Dubai Land Department's Residential Sales Price Index page separates property segments and reporting periods. Its historical reference periods should stay historical: the date a website was updated is not necessarily the period the observations describe. The linked 2020 methodology explains why the mix of properties sold matters and describes a hedonic approach using recorded characteristics. This is a description of that published methodology, not a claim that every present-day index uses an unchanged model. The same index page includes restrictions on commercial use, including pricing, investment decisions and performance measurement. I am linking to the explanation and notice here, not reproducing its series or deriving a property's price from it. Public visibility alone does not establish permission to redistribute data or build a commercial feature around it. A rental benchmark is another input The Smart Rental Index FAQ describes building-related characteristics and registered rental contracts among its inputs, and specifies coverage limits, including an exclusion for DIFC. A rental benchmark does not, by itself, supply an acquisition price, operating costs, financing or realized occupancy for a particular property. My conclusion is limited: that source alone cannot establish the property's investment return. This is not a determination of anyone's permitted rent increase. DLD also has a separate Property Valuation service , with an application, supporting documents and review before a valuation certificate is issued. A model-generated paragraph linking to the service is not such a certificate. Give the summarizer an evidence card This is my proposed record format, not an official DLD form: { "question" : "What claim am I trying to support?" , "source_and_purpose" : "Which document or service addresses it?" , "observation_period" : null , "coverage_and_exclusions" : null , "measure_and_units" : null , "method_and_use_limits" : null , "access_date" : "2026-10-17" , "unresolved" : [] } The nulls are intentional. Missing fields should remain missing until evidence fills them. An instruction to produce a confident summary should not turn an unknown period into a current observation or a market segment into an inspected apartment. For a product, the useful first output may be a source-selection note with the gaps visible. That gives the next reviewer something to inspect before a number becomes a recommendation. The full source-selection guide includes the distinctions, limits and proposed evidence card. Source review: 17 October 2026. This educational article is not a current market report, property valuation, rent-dispute decision or investment recommendation. AI assisted drafting and source comparison. No personal transaction, customer outcome or tested company system is claimed.

A fluent AI answer can still use the wrong kind of property evidence. Before asking a model to summarize a Dubai property source, define the question: are you describing a sales-price series, comparing a rental benchmark, or asking about one particular property?

Those outputs are different. Putting them into the same dashboard does not make their meanings interchangeable.

Keep the measure attached to the claim

Dubai Land Department's Residential Sales Price Index page separates property segments and reporting periods. Its historical reference periods should stay historical: the date a website was updated is not necessarily the period the observations describe.

The linked 2020 methodology explains why the mix of properties sold matters and describes a hedonic approach using recorded characteristics. This is a description of that published methodology, not a claim that every present-day index uses an unchanged model.

The same index page includes restrictions on commercial use, including pricing, investment decisions and performance measurement. I am linking to the explanation and notice here, not reproducing its series or deriving a property's price from it. Public visibility alone does not establish permission to redistribute data or build a commercial feature around it.

A rental benchmark is another input

The Smart Rental Index FAQ describes building-related characteristics and registered rental contracts among its inputs, and specifies coverage limits, including an exclusion for DIFC.

A rental benchmark does not, by itself, supply an acquisition price, operating costs, financing or realized occupancy for a particular property. My conclusion is limited: that source alone cannot establish the property's investment return. This is not a determination of anyone's permitted rent increase.

DLD also has a separate Property Valuation service, with an application, supporting documents and review before a valuation certificate is issued. A model-generated paragraph linking to the service is not such a certificate.

Give the summarizer an evidence card

This is my proposed record format, not an official DLD form:

{
  "question": "What claim am I trying to support?",
  "source_and_purpose": "Which document or service addresses it?",
  "observation_period": null,
  "coverage_and_exclusions": null,
  "measure_and_units": null,
  "method_and_use_limits": null,
  "access_date": "2026-10-17",
  "unresolved": []
}

The nulls are intentional. Missing fields should remain missing until evidence fills them. An instruction to produce a confident summary should not turn an unknown period into a current observation or a market segment into an inspected apartment.

For a product, the useful first output may be a source-selection note with the gaps visible. That gives the next reviewer something to inspect before a number becomes a recommendation.

items.title: Your AI Model Predicts Risk. But Who Decides When to Act?
items.summary: How a decision threshold turns a reliable probability into an action — and why that choice is yours, not the model’s. Beyond Accuracy · Model Evaluation (#6) Honestly evaluating AI models is a personal project of mine, and I’ve been exploring it on clinical problems — by choice. Health is simply the domain I find most revealing, and the one most people feel in their gut: the cost of a missed cancer, or of an unnecessary biopsy, needs no explanation. But nothing in this piece is really about medicine. Any system that turns a probability into an action faces the same step — fraud scoring, demand forecasting, anomaly detection — those are just harder to feel in the same immediate way. Today the model is a synthetic screening model, where I generate the patients and know the ground truth exactly. That lets me study the step everyone rushes past: a trustworthy probability still isn’t an action — and the number you choose to act on decides everything. Start with a model that does its job well. On 4,000 synthetic patients — about 11% of them truly sick (448 cases) — it ranks sick patients ahead of healthy ones reliably ( AUROC 0.84 — AUROC measures how well a model sorts the sick above the healthy). Its probabilities are also honest: the 11% is the overall rate across everyone, but the model doesn’t hand every patient 11% — it gives each one their own risk, and when it says 30% for a group of patients, close to 30% of those patients really are sick. That last property is called calibration . Those are the first three questions this series asks of a model — can it make the call ( F1 ), can it order cases by risk ( AUROC ), can you believe its confidence ( calibration ) — pulled together most recently in the previous piece . This model clears all three. The model gives each patient a probability. Turning those probabilities into yes/no calls is a separate step, and it’s mine to make, not the model’s. So I did what most pipelines do by default: I treated every patient with a predicted risk above 0.5 — that is, above 50% — as a “positive” worth acting on. At that cutoff, it caught just a quarter of the disease — 25%. Of the 448 truly sick patients, it flagged 110 and missed 338 , while raising only 56 false alarms. The model itself didn’t fail — its ranking is intact, and its probabilities are honest. What failed was the decision rule : a cutoff chosen without weighing the consequences turned good risk estimates into a poor decision. It missed those patients because 0.5 was the wrong place to act, and nobody had chosen it on purpose. That’s the whole subject of this piece: once you trust the number, what do you do with it? The fourth question: Decide This series has been building one question at a time. F1 → can it predict? AUROC → can it rank? Calibration → can it be trusted? Those three are about the model. This one is about you : you now hold a trustworthy probability — what threshold turns it into an action? Call it the fourth verb: Decide. A probability is a statement about the world. A threshold is a statement about what you value. The model can hand you the first; only you can supply the second. Deciding is setting that threshold — the cutoff on the probability above which you act and below which you don’t — and the moment you pick it, you’ve made a value judgment about which mistake you’d rather make. 0.5 is a decision you didn’t know you were making The default cutoff of 0.5 feels neutral. It isn’t. A screening model can make two kinds of mistake: a missed case — a sick patient it waves through (a false negative) — and a false alarm — a healthy patient it flags for nothing (a false positive). Acting only when risk exceeds 50% quietly declares that a missed case and a false alarm cost you exactly the same. Cutting at 50% is the right call only if you’d trade one missed patient for one false alarm and feel you came out even — no worse off either way. That holds only in a simplified picture where those two mistakes are the whole story. Real decisions can carry more — the cost of running the test, the harm of the treatment itself, a patient’s own preferences — and a fuller analysis folds those in too. But the balance between the two errors is the right place to begin, so that’s where we’ll start. In almost no clinical setting are the two errors equal. Missing an early cancer is not the same as calling one more patient back for a scan that turns out clear. And when a disease is uncommon, a 0.5 cutoff is especially punishing. On this model it lands at 0.12 , and the picture changes completely: sensitivity jumps from 25% to 77% , specificity is 76% , and the model now catches 344 of the 448 cases instead of 110 — but the false alarms climb with it, from 56 to 848. But look at what Youden’s index quietly assumes: that a point of sensitivity and a point of specificity are worth the same. (“Cost” here means real-world harm: a missed case can mean a disease caught too late; a false alarm means an unnecessary, sometimes invasive, follow-up.) The arithmetic is just that one formula: If the two errors are equal , R = 1 , then p_t = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.50. That’s exactly why the naive default catches so little. If a missed case is 9× worse, R = 9, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 9) = 0.10. You act at just 10% risk, accepting more false alarms to avoid a miss. If a false alarm is what you fear — say it’s 4× worse than a miss, so R = 1/4, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 0.25) = 0.80. Now you act only when you’re 80% sure. One thing R is not : a promise about headcount. It sets the relative cost of the two errors, not the number of false alarms you’ll actually trade for each extra case caught — that depends on the model and how common the disease is. The nine is a statement of values, not a body count. (And the formula assumes the plain yes/no decision we’re in; capacity limits, costs that differ patient to patient, or actions beyond act / don’t-act would each need more than this one line.) On this model, that one number moves everything: Same model, same probabilities, same patients. The only thing that changed was an honest statement of what the mistakes cost — and that statement, not the algorithm, decided who got caught. The threshold is where medicine, not machine learning, has to speak. The question underneath all of it: does acting even help? Suppose you’ve chosen a threshold. One question remains, and it’s the one that should be asked first and almost never is: does using this model actually beat the obvious alternatives — referring everyone, or referring no one? This is what Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) answers — a method from Vickers & Elkin (2006) , not something I’ve invented, and the first time this series meets it. It rests on a quietly brilliant reframing: the threshold you’d act at is itself a statement of how you weigh the two errors against each other. A clinician who’d act at 10% is telling you a missed case is worth about nine false alarms — so weigh their harms in exactly that proportion. That gives a single number of their devising, net benefit , at any threshold: net benefit = (true positives / N) − (false positives / N) × p_t/(1 − p_t) Here N is the total number of patients evaluated. The true positives are the good the model does; the false positives are penalized in exact proportion to that same trade-off. Compute it across every threshold a reasonable clinician might hold, and plot three lines: the model, refer everyone , and refer no one . (In a screening setting those defaults mean testing or referring every patient versus none — not literally treating anyone.) Across the range of thresholds a clinician might reasonably consider for a screening referral — roughly 5% to 30% — the model delivers at least as much estimated net benefit as either alternative: referring everyone, or referring no one. The trade-off is revealing. At very low thresholds, referring everyone can make sense, because the priority is to miss as few cases as possible. But as the threshold rises, each unnecessary referral carries more weight, and eventually referring everyone produces less net benefit than referring no one at all. Referring no one, meanwhile, always scores exactly zero in Decision Curve Analysis — a mathematical reference point, not a claim that missing every case does no harm. The decision curve makes this trade-off visible. Instead of asking only how accurately the model predicts, it asks whether acting on those predictions offers a better balance of benefit and harm than the alternatives, at thresholds that reflect real clinical priorities. In this synthetic experiment, the model performs at least as well as both alternatives across that clinically relevant range; only at the very lowest thresholds — below about 2%, where acting on almost any suspicion and referring everyone amount to the same thing — do the two draw level. But estimated is the important word: these results describe the model’s potential value under the experiment’s assumptions; they don’t establish that patients would actually benefit in practice. Showing that takes further validation and, ultimately, a prospective clinical study. Use it to explore the trade-offs while you work with domain experts to set an appropriate decision policy. You know one error is worse than the other (almost always): set the threshold from the cost ratio , p_t = 1/(1+R). Depending on the kind of shift, a recalibration or a prevalence correction may be enough; but if the relationship between the features and the outcome has changed, simple recalibration may not be enough — the model may need more extensive validation, updating, or redevelopment. A trustworthy AI-assisted decision is held to the same standard: it doesn’t come from the model alone, but from pairing an honest probability with a decision policy that reflects what’s at stake. The model estimates the risk. The policy decides what to do with it. And whether that policy makes sense stays our responsibility — not the machine’s. items.summary_html:
How a decision threshold turns a reliable probability into an action — and why that choice is yours, not the model’s.

Beyond Accuracy · Model Evaluation (#6)

Honestly evaluating AI models is a personal project of mine, and I’ve been exploring it on clinical problems — by choice. Health is simply the domain I find most revealing, and the one most people feel in their gut: the cost of a missed cancer, or of an unnecessary biopsy, needs no explanation. But nothing in this piece is really about medicine. Any system that turns a probability into an action faces the same step — fraud scoring, demand forecasting, anomaly detection — those are just harder to feel in the same immediate way. Today the model is a synthetic screening model, where I generate the patients and know the ground truth exactly. That lets me study the step everyone rushes past: a trustworthy probability still isn’t an action — and the number you choose to act on decides everything.

Start with a model that does its job well. On 4,000 synthetic patients — about 11% of them truly sick (448 cases) — it ranks sick patients ahead of healthy ones reliably (AUROC 0.84 — AUROC measures how well a model sorts the sick above the healthy). Its probabilities are also honest: the 11% is the overall rate across everyone, but the model doesn’t hand every patient 11% — it gives each one their own risk, and when it says 30% for a group of patients, close to 30% of those patients really are sick. That last property is called calibration. Those are the first three questions this series asks of a model — can it make the call (F1), can it order cases by risk (AUROC), can you believe its confidence (calibration) — pulled together most recently in the previous piece. This model clears all three.

The model gives each patient a probability. Turning those probabilities into yes/no calls is a separate step, and it’s mine to make, not the model’s. So I did what most pipelines do by default: I treated every patient with a predicted risk above 0.5 — that is, above 50% — as a “positive” worth acting on.

At that cutoff, it caught just a quarter of the disease — 25%.

Of the 448 truly sick patients, it flagged 110 and missed 338, while raising only 56 false alarms.

The model itself didn’t fail — its ranking is intact, and its probabilities are honest. What failed was the decision rule: a cutoff chosen without weighing the consequences turned good risk estimates into a poor decision. It missed those patients because 0.5 was the wrong place to act, and nobody had chosen it on purpose. That’s the whole subject of this piece: once you trust the number, what do you do with it?

The fourth question: Decide

This series has been building one question at a time. F1 → can it predict? AUROC → can it rank? Calibration → can it be trusted? Those three are about the model. This one is about you: you now hold a trustworthy probability — what threshold turns it into an action?

Call it the fourth verb: Decide.

A probability is a statement about the world. A threshold is a statement about what you value.

The model can hand you the first; only you can supply the second. Deciding is setting that threshold — the cutoff on the probability above which you act and below which you don’t — and the moment you pick it, you’ve made a value judgment about which mistake you’d rather make.

0.5 is a decision you didn’t know you were making

The default cutoff of 0.5 feels neutral. It isn’t. A screening model can make two kinds of mistake: a missed case — a sick patient it waves through (a false negative) — and a false alarm — a healthy patient it flags for nothing (a false positive). Acting only when risk exceeds 50% quietly declares that a missed case and a false alarm cost you exactly the same. Cutting at 50% is the right call only if you’d trade one missed patient for one false alarm and feel you came out even — no worse off either way.

That holds only in a simplified picture where those two mistakes are the whole story. Real decisions can carry more — the cost of running the test, the harm of the treatment itself, a patient’s own preferences — and a fuller analysis folds those in too. But the balance between the two errors is the right place to begin, so that’s where we’ll start.

In almost no clinical setting are the two errors equal. Missing an early cancer is not the same as calling one more patient back for a scan that turns out clear. And when a disease is uncommon, a 0.5 cutoff is especially punishing. Low prevalence doesn’t guarantee this, but when the features give only moderate discrimination, even a well-calibrated model lands many genuinely sick patients below 50% — it’s seldom more than half-sure about anyone. A rule that acts only above 50% then flags almost none of them, and most of the disease slips through. That’s exactly what happened above — three-quarters of the sick patients, missed, at a threshold no one deliberately chose.

(This doesn’t contradict the model’s ranking. AUROC is about order — sick scoring higher than healthy — not about where those scores land on the 0-to-1 scale. A sharper model could push many sick patients above 50%; this one, with only moderate discrimination, leaves 338 of the 448 below it — ranked above the healthy, yet short of the halfway mark.)

The first move, then, is simply to make the choice on purpose.

The statistical answer — and why it’s not enough

The classic way to pick a cutoff from the data is Youden’s index. It leans on two numbers: sensitivity (the share of truly sick patients the model catches) and specificity (the share of truly healthy patients it correctly leaves alone). Youden’s index picks the threshold that maximizes J = sensitivity + specificity − 1 — the same as maximizing their sum, since the −1 is just a constant. It gives the two rates equal weight, with no regard for how common the disease is or what either error actually costs (Youden, 1950). On this model it lands at 0.12, and the picture changes completely: sensitivity jumps from 25% to 77%, specificity is 76%, and the model now catches 344 of the 448 cases instead of 110 — but the false alarms climb with it, from 56 to 848.

But look at what Youden’s index quietly assumes: that a point of sensitivity and a point of specificity are worth the same. It’s a statistical balance, blind to what the errors actually cost and to how common the disease is. It’s a reasonable reference point when you genuinely have no cost information — and the wrong anchor the moment you do. Which is almost always.

The honest driver: the cost of the two errors

Here’s the idea that reorganizes everything. The ROC curve shows what different thresholds can achieve, but it can’t, by itself, tell you which trade-off is clinically acceptable. That is set by a single question: how many times worse is a missed case than a false alarm?

Call that number — how many times worse a missed case is than a false alarm — the cost ratio, and write it R. (“Cost” here means real-world harm: a missed case can mean a disease caught too late; a false alarm means an unnecessary, sometimes invasive, follow-up.) For a calibrated risk model, when the only things on the scale are the cost of a false positive and the cost of a false negative, the threshold that minimizes expected cost is

act if predicted risk ≥ p_t,   where   p_t = 1 / (1 + R)

Here p_t is the probability threshold — p for probability, the small t for “threshold.” Read it slowly, because it’s the whole game. The arithmetic is just that one formula:

  • If the two errors are equal, R = 1 , then p_t = 1 / (1 + 1) = 0.50. That’s exactly why the naive default catches so little.
  • If a missed case is 9× worse, R = 9, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 9) = 0.10. You act at just 10% risk, accepting more false alarms to avoid a miss.
  • If a false alarm is what you fear — say it’s 4× worse than a miss, so R = 1/4, then p_t = 1 / (1 + 0.25) = 0.80. Now you act only when you’re 80% sure.

One thing R is not: a promise about headcount. It sets the relative cost of the two errors, not the number of false alarms you’ll actually trade for each extra case caught — that depends on the model and how common the disease is. The nine is a statement of values, not a body count. (And the formula assumes the plain yes/no decision we’re in; capacity limits, costs that differ patient to patient, or actions beyond act / don’t-act would each need more than this one line.)

On this model, that one number moves everything:

Same model, same probabilities, same patients. The only thing that changed was an honest statement of what the mistakes cost — and that statement, not the algorithm, decided who got caught. The threshold is where medicine, not machine learning, has to speak.

The question underneath all of it: does acting even help?

Suppose you’ve chosen a threshold. One question remains, and it’s the one that should be asked first and almost never is: does using this model actually beat the obvious alternatives — referring everyone, or referring no one?

This is what Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) answers — a method from Vickers & Elkin (2006), not something I’ve invented, and the first time this series meets it. It rests on a quietly brilliant reframing: the threshold you’d act at is itself a statement of how you weigh the two errors against each other. A clinician who’d act at 10% is telling you a missed case is worth about nine false alarms — so weigh their harms in exactly that proportion. That gives a single number of their devising, net benefit, at any threshold:

net benefit = (true positives / N) − (false positives / N) × p_t/(1 − p_t)

Here N is the total number of patients evaluated. The true positives are the good the model does; the false positives are penalized in exact proportion to that same trade-off. Compute it across every threshold a reasonable clinician might hold, and plot three lines: the model, refer everyone, and refer no one. (In a screening setting those defaults mean testing or referring every patient versus none — not literally treating anyone.)

Across the range of thresholds a clinician might reasonably consider for a screening referral — roughly 5% to 30% — the model delivers at least as much estimated net benefit as either alternative: referring everyone, or referring no one.

The trade-off is revealing. At very low thresholds, referring everyone can make sense, because the priority is to miss as few cases as possible. But as the threshold rises, each unnecessary referral carries more weight, and eventually referring everyone produces less net benefit than referring no one at all. Referring no one, meanwhile, always scores exactly zero in Decision Curve Analysis — a mathematical reference point, not a claim that missing every case does no harm.

The decision curve makes this trade-off visible. Instead of asking only how accurately the model predicts, it asks whether acting on those predictions offers a better balance of benefit and harm than the alternatives, at thresholds that reflect real clinical priorities.

In this synthetic experiment, the model performs at least as well as both alternatives across that clinically relevant range; only at the very lowest thresholds — below about 2%, where acting on almost any suspicion and referring everyone amount to the same thing — do the two draw level. But estimated is the important word: these results describe the model’s potential value under the experiment’s assumptions; they don’t establish that patients would actually benefit in practice. Showing that takes further validation and, ultimately, a prospective clinical study.

Which threshold when
  • You genuinely don’t know the costs yet: reach for Youden’s index as a statistical reference point — not a clinically justified default. Use it to explore the trade-offs while you work with domain experts to set an appropriate decision policy.
  • You know one error is worse than the other (almost always): set the threshold from the cost ratio, p_t = 1/(1+R). Make the relative costs explicit — "how much worse is missing a true case than triggering an unnecessary referral?" — then look at the actual trade-off the model produces at that threshold, not at 0.5.
  • Before you deploy anything: run a decision curve. If it shows the model doing no better than simply referring everyone, or no one, at the risk levels your clinicians would actually use, then it may offer no decision advantage in its current form — a signal to investigate (recalibrate, improve the model, or rethink the workflow) before deployment, not merely to nudge the cutoff. Either way, you’ve found out before a single patient was affected.
One assumption hiding underneath all of this

Every threshold in this piece rests on one quiet assumption: that the probabilities are calibrated in the population where the decision actually gets made. This model is well calibrated at 11% prevalence — when it says 30%, about 30% of those patients really are sick. Move it to a hospital with a different case mix, or a different disease rate, and that may no longer hold — and a threshold set on the old probabilities would now be aimed at the wrong place. A decision rule is only as trustworthy as the probabilities underneath it.

In practice the first move isn’t to nudge the cutoff — it’s to check whether the model is still calibrated in the new population at all. Depending on the kind of shift, a recalibration or a prevalence correction may be enough; but if the relationship between the features and the outcome has changed, simple recalibration may not be enough — the model may need more extensive validation, updating, or redevelopment. Only once the probabilities are trustworthy there does the threshold mean what you think it means — and that is the next stop on the map. So the real next question is whether those probabilities survive the trip: will it work elsewhere?

The one line to remember

F1 asks whether the model predicted right. AUROC asks whether it can rank. Calibration asks whether you can trust it. Decide asks the question none of them can: at what number do you act, and at what cost?

A trustworthy clinician doesn’t just estimate risk well. They know what to do with the estimate — and they know that the right action depends on what’s at stake, not on a number that happens to sit at one-half. A trustworthy AI-assisted decision is held to the same standard: it doesn’t come from the model alone, but from pairing an honest probability with a decision policy that reflects what’s at stake. The model estimates the risk. The policy decides what to do with it. And whether that policy makes sense stays our responsibility — not the machine’s.

One caution worth keeping: clearing these four verbs is not a certificate of trustworthiness. A model can pass all four and still fail — under a shift in population, a gap between subgroups, or clumsy, unsafe deployment. That’s why the map keeps going.

This is the fourth question in the evaluation journey — the sixth piece in the Beyond Accuracy series. The model has been asked to predict, to rank, to be trusted, and now to inform a decision. Next the journey leaves the model itself and turns to the humans around it — validation, generalization, and whether people should rely on it at all. If this was useful, tell me the worst default-threshold story you’ve seen — I read every reply.

Question assumptions. Build intuition.

A note on the data: the numbers here come from a synthetic screening model (4,000 patients, ~11% prevalence / 448 cases, AUROC 0.84, decile calibration error ≈ 1%) built for an honest-evaluation project — I generate the patients, so every sensitivity, threshold, and net-benefit figure above is computed, not asserted, and reproducible. The generating script lives in the Model Evaluation Handbook repo (code/build_decide_experiment.py); it uses a fixed random seed, so one run rebuilds the dataset, and these exact numbers fall out. The next step is to carry the same decision-curve analysis onto real, multimodal data; that companion is coming.

A note on scope: the worked example is clinical, but the machinery — a probability, a cost ratio, a threshold, a net-benefit check — is domain-neutral. Relabel “sick” as “fraudulent,” “defective,” or “about to churn,” and “refer” as “investigate,” “pull from the line,” or “step in,” and every move in this piece still holds. Rare-event decisions rhyme across domains.

References
  • Youden, Index for Rating Diagnostic Tests, Cancer (1950) — the sensitivity-plus-specificity operating point.
  • Vickers & Elkin, Decision Curve Analysis: A Novel Method for Evaluating Prediction Models, Medical Decision Making (2006) — net benefit vs. treat-all / treat-none.
  • Vickers, van Calster & Steyerberg, A Simple, Step-by-Step Guide to Interpreting Decision Curve Analysis, Diagnostic and Prognostic Research (2019) — the plain-language DCA primer.
  • Steyerberg et al., Assessing the Performance of Prediction Models: A Framework for Traditional and Novel Measures, Epidemiology (2010) — discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness together.
The series so far

Start with the map: The Journey Toward Trustworthy AI — the overview the whole series follows.

  • #1 — Why 90% Accuracy Doesn’t Mean You Should Trust an AI Model: the accuracy trap.
  • #2 — A Fraud Model Can Be 99.9% Accurate and Catch Zero Fraud: F1 — can it predict? Precision and recall under class imbalance.
  • #3 — A Model With 0.96 AUROC Can Still Bury You in False Alarms: AUROC — can it rank? Separating power across every threshold.
  • #4 — Does Your AI Know When It Might Be Wrong?: Calibration — can it be trusted? When it says 90%, is it right 90% of the time?

items.title: Claude Code Mods Explained: What They Can Do That Hooks and Skills Can’t
items.summary: I built one to find the edges. How mods work, what they can reach, and the bugs that taught me the most. “All tests pass.” Claude Code said it at the end of a long turn, and the run was green. In the same turn, it had also edited tests/conftest.py. Nothing in the transcript hid that. It sat on line 31 of 33 lines of reads, edits and test logs. I scroll past line 31 on most days. So when Anthropic shipped mods in Claude Code, the first thing I built was a mod that puts that line where I can’t miss it. This article is what I learned about mods while doing it: what they are, how the pieces fit, what a mod can reach on your machine, and the bugs that taught me the most. Image by the author. What a mod is A mod is a Claude Code plugin that changes how Claude Code looks and behaves. It is a JavaScript or TypeScript file of event handlers. Claude Code calls a handler when something happens: a tool call, a submitted prompt, a part of the screen about to be drawn. The handler can watch the event, change it, or take it over. items.summary_html:
I built one to find the edges. How mods work, what they can reach, and the bugs that taught me the most.

“All tests pass.” Claude Code said it at the end of a long turn, and the run was green. In the same turn, it had also edited tests/conftest.py.

Nothing in the transcript hid that. It sat on line 31 of 33 lines of reads, edits and test logs. I scroll past line 31 on most days. So when Anthropic shipped mods in Claude Code, the first thing I built was a mod that puts that line where I can’t miss it. This article is what I learned about mods while doing it: what they are, how the pieces fit, what a mod can reach on your machine, and the bugs that taught me the most.

Image by the author.What a mod is

A mod is a Claude Code plugin that changes how Claude Code looks and behaves. It is a JavaScript or TypeScript file of event handlers. Claude Code calls a handler when something happens: a tool call, a submitted prompt, a part of the screen about to be drawn. The handler can watch the event, change it, or take it over.

Mods arrived in Claude Code 2.1.287. They run in the terminal CLI, the Code tab of the Desktop app and the VS Code extension. You need no Node.js, bundler or build step: Claude Code loads the .ts file directly.

Mods vs settings hooks, skills and MCP servers

Claude Code already had ways to extend it, so the first question is when a mod is the right tool. The short answer: settings hooks, skills, status lines and MCP servers work from outside Claude Code. A mod runs inside it.

  • Settings hook: a shell command, HTTP call or prompt from a settings file. Good for blocking or logging a tool call, or running a formatter.
  • Skill: text Claude reads. Good for teaching Claude a workflow.
  • MCP server: a separate process. Good for giving Claude new tools and data.
  • Mod: functions inside Claude Code. Good for drawing UI, redrawing Claude Code’s own UI, and stepping into a call or a request.

Being inside buys you five things the others can’t do:

  1. Draw an interface: a pane beside the transcript or a band above the prompt, with tabs, buttons and text fields.
  2. Redraw Claude Code’s own interface: replace a tool call’s row, the spinner, or the question dialog.
  3. Step into a tool call or a model request: hold a call while you ask the user, answer it without running the tool, or send one request to a different model.
  4. Run code on a command: a /command that runs your function at once, with no Claude turn, even while Claude works.
  5. Share data between hooks: one hook counts tool calls, another shows the count beside the spinner.

If a settings hook already does the job, use the settings hook. I needed number 2, so a mod was the only option.

The three parts: events, render sites and $

Everything in a mod is one of three things.

Events decide when your code runs. The ones I used most follow a turn, which is everything Claude does to answer one prompt:

  • turn.start fires when a turn begins and gives you a turnId.
  • turn.step fires before each request to the model. A turn with tool calls has several.
  • turn.complete fires when the turn ends, including one you interrupted. It carries the answer, the duration and the token usage. Return { text } and Claude Code shows a line under the answer.
  • tool.call fires for each tool call. You can pass it on, change it or refuse it.

Render sites are the places in the screen you can draw. A ui.render hook fires each time Claude Code is about to draw one, and you pick the site with a matcher such as { component: 'Spinner' }. Sites include ToolUse, ToolGroup, AssistantMessage, Spinner, TurnDuration, PromptHint, AbovePrompt (the band above the prompt) and Pane. Each site gets e.surface, which says whether the terminal, Desktop or VS Code is drawing.

$ is the mods API. Every hook gets it as its first argument. Its methods sit in namespaces: $.ui (open panes, notify, set the status line), $.session (messages, usage, the project root), $.store (a key-value store every session on the machine shares), $.clock, $.fs, $.process, $.http, $.model and more.

Here is a whole mod in that shape. It adds a line under each answer with the time and the share of context used:

import type { Register } from 'claude-code'

export const register: Register = (on) => {
  on('turn.complete', async ($, e, next) => {
    const r = await next(e)
    if (e.agentId !== undefined) return r  // skip subagent turns
    const { context } = await $.session.usage()
    const secs = Math.round(e.durationMs / 1000)
    return { text: `${secs}s · context ${context.percent}% full` }
  })
}

Two habits from that example carry over to every mod. Call next(e) so the mods after yours still run. And check e.agentId, because subagent turns fire the same events.

The build loop

You can ask Claude to write a mod: describe it in a session, and Claude writes the plugin. To work on one yourself, three commands do most of the work:

claude --plugin-dir .      # run Claude Code with your mod; a save reloads it
claude plugin validate .   # check the manifest and list every hook and call
claude plugin test .       # run the mod's tests

The reload on save is what makes mods fast to build. I change a render hook, save, and the row redraws in the session I already have open.

Anthropic also shares three sample mods in its claude-code-playground repository: token-weather (a forecast of your context window above the prompt), blast-radius (holds a risky command such as rm -rf and shows what it would change) and replay-theater (a /replay command that steps through the last turn's edits). Read them before you write your first one.

What a mod can reach

This part matters more than the API. A mod is not sandboxed. Once it loads, it runs with your permissions. It can read and write your files, start programs, make network requests, read your environment variables, see every prompt and tool call, and approve a tool call before you are asked. Turning on Claude Code’s sandbox does not cover it: the sandbox wraps the Bash commands Claude runs, not processes a mod starts.

So before you install a mod, read what it does. Clone it and run claude plugin validate on the folder. The hooks: and calls: lines list every event it handles and every API it calls, without running it. A mod that only draws rows should not list $.http.fetch or $.process.run. If you want to stop all mods, claude --safe-mode turns them off for one session, and "disableAllHooks": true in ~/.claude/settings.json turns them off everywhere.

A worked example: TL;DR for Claude Code

The mod I built is TL;DR for Claude Code. It folds each turn into one row in Claude Code’s own style: the files Claude changed, the tests before and after, and what to check before you trust the result. Every raw line stays one click away. It is free and open source (MIT), and I’m the only author.

Here is how it maps onto the three parts:

  • Events: tool.call reads each call and its result, then passes it on unchanged. turn.start and turn.complete open and close the row. session.compact keeps rows when you run /compact.
  • Render sites: ToolUse and ToolGroup draw the row in place of the tool rows. Spinner names the current job, such as Reading src/auth.py. AbovePrompt draws a context bar. Three Panes hold the detail, the context and the history.
  • $: $.store keeps finished rows (50 per session) and how long each command took last time. $.session.usage feeds the context bar. $.ui.notify pings you when a turn over 30 seconds ends.

The calls it does not make are the point. It makes no $.http or $.model calls and starts no processes. It reads everything from what Claude Code reports.

The row flags the edits that can fake a green run:

Image by the author.What I learned building it1. A static reader misses more than you expect

TL;DR reads each Bash command as text. It never runs or expands a command to learn what it did. I chose that for privacy and safety. The cost showed up fast. I wrote 30 edge cases, and the first version missed many: quoted paths, sudo tee, a cd before a write, mv into a folder, git restore, find -delete, and echo "npm test", which it counted as a test run.

Then a live turn wrote a script with S=/tmp/x.sh; cat > "$S" and the row showed nothing. Now the reader follows variables the command sets. My rule became: name what the text names, and drop what it can't name. A path built from $OUT drops out, because a row that says $OUT via Bash reads like a real file name.

2. A wrapper can hide a failure

I run a hook that wraps test output and prints its own summary line, such as Go test: 20 passed, 2 failed. The first parser didn't know that line. A failing run showed green. Pipes do the same: in go test | tail, the exit code is tail's. Now a failure in the output counts as a failure, whatever the exit code says. If your mod reports test results, test it against the wrappers you actually use.

3. Real data breaks your layout

A flag once quoted a whole heredoc command. The check line was 6,000 characters. Now each flag is one line, cut at the row’s edge, and it names the act, not the command: force push, skipped hooks. The commands behind it open in a pane.

4. Deleting made it look native

The first version was a seven-row box with labels, buttons, a diff pane and hint lines. On a dark terminal the labels were almost invisible, and a 60-file refactor took nine rows of cut-off file names. Version 0.1.5 removed the box, the buttons, the diff pane and every hint line. A clean turn is now three lines, and the dot’s color is the verdict. It reads as part of Claude Code, which is what a mod that redraws Claude Code’s rows should do.

5. Make your mod easy to audit

To get listed in Claude’s plugin directory, I moved every function that takes $ into the one hooks module. The draw code takes plain values. Now one file holds every call the mod can make, and anyone can check it in a few minutes.

6. Bugs hide in the quiet features

My latest fix was not in the row. The context bar kept the old numbers after /compact, because it measured the transcript before the new one was in place. It looked right until the next request, so I didn't see it for days.

Image by the author.Try it, or build your own

If you want to see a mod that redraws Claude Code’s own rows, install TL;DR inside Claude Code (2.1.301 or later, terminal only):

/plugin install tldr --marketplace kushalBanda/claude-tldr

The source is on GitHub at kushalBanda/claude-tldr. Read the hooks module and run claude plugin validate on it first. That's the habit I'd want for every mod you install, mine included.

If you build your own, start from Anthropic’s mods overview and the three sample mods. Pick one render site and one event, and get a single line on screen. Everything else grows from there.

Resources

  • GitHub: https://github.com/kushalBanda/claude-tldr
  • Mods overview, Claude Code Docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview
  • Create a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/create
  • React to events with a mod: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/events
  • Mods reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/reference
  • TL;DR for Claude Code: https://kushalbanda.com/claude-tldr/?utm_source=medium&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=claude-tldr

What would you build first with a mod? If you found this useful, give it a clap and drop a comment. I’d love to hear your thoughts 🙌

items.title: Claude Code Changed Too Much? Keep the Fix, Cut the Extras
items.summary: A small bug fix can leave you with a lot to review. Learn to separate necessary edits from cleanup without throwing away useful work. Claude Code: Keep the Fix Consider a hypothetical bug: your app exports a zero amount as an empty CSV cell. You ask Claude Code to preserve the zero. The proposed fix also changes a shared formatter, renames functions and replaces a dependency. Which edits should stay? Keep your current work safe first. Then ask what each edit contributes to the original fix. Keep necessary changes, separate unrelated cleanup, and hold unexplained changes out of the shared version. That review matters as Claude gains more room to work. An October 22 update from Anthropic says auto mode will become the default the following week for new sessions in most Claude apps on Pro, Max and Team plans. Fewer approval prompts leave the question of what belongs in the task to be answered separately. 1. Does fixing this bug really require those changes? Keep an edit when its connection to the bug can be explained and checked. Move cleanup into another task. File count is a poor substitute for that decision. For this CSV example, the requirement is narrow: export zero as 0, preserve the existing columns and other value formats, and leave on-screen amounts unchanged. The code and root cause are unspecified. A shared formatter might be responsible; a blank cell alone cannot establish that. Zero Is Not an Empty CSV Cell Use the proposed changes to make the review concrete: Ask for that explanation against the actual differences between versions. “Improves consistency” does not tell you why the zero needs a different export library. Several files may legitimately belong to one repair: the exporter, its helper and its test. A change in one file can still remove unrelated behavior. The useful boundary is the requested behavior and the work needed to preserve it. 2. Why does Claude Code make unrelated changes? Claude may interpret a bug report as a broader improvement task, or it may identify the wrong cause. Those lead to different corrections. In the hypothetical CSV case, it might follow this path: find the blank output, inspect a shared formatter, notice inconsistent formatting elsewhere, then update other callers. Investigating the formatter could be necessary. Standardizing every caller needs its own justification. The fact that one step led to another does not make the whole chain part of your request. Anthropic’s auto mode design explanation describes both overeager initiative and mistakes about an action’s impact. Its documented Claude Code design allows in-project file edits without a classifier call. An edit can therefore be permitted while its relevance to your bug still needs review. Anthropic: In-Project File Edits There is another explanation to check before blaming every changed line on the model: a formatting command or project hook may have rewritten files. Prettier’s CLI documentation says prettier . --write formats supported files in the current directory and its subdirectories. Look at the commands and configuration involved. Whitespace changes can obscure a functional edit, and a large formatting diff does not reveal who chose each change. If the execution history is unavailable, leave the origin uncertain. The October update explains why approval behavior is topical. It does not establish that auto mode caused an earlier unwanted edit, or that changing modes will repair it. Claude: October 22 Rollout Update Clearer instructions help with ambiguous scope. When your request already said to preserve other behavior and the result changed it anyway, the result needs correction. Repeating the same boundary in a longer prompt is no substitute for checking the changes already made. 3. How do you undo unwanted changes without losing your work? Pause further edits, preserve the current state, and identify which changes belong to which piece of work. Then separate the useful repair from the extras. Start with what existed before Claude began. Were there uncommitted edits, another active session, or work from a colleague in the same files? Git’s git-restore reference describes restoring paths to match a source version. That source may not contain your newer work. A whole-file restore can remove those changes along with Claude’s cleanup. If you lack a clean starting point, mark that uncertainty before choosing anything to undo. Save Mixed Work Before Separating It Next, have Claude explain the actual changes in three groups: required for the zero fix, needed only if a shared cause is confirmed, and unrelated cleanup. Each explanation should name the behavior affected and the check that would establish it. A summary saying the code was “optimized” is insufficient. When the edits are separate, keep the supported repair and remove or save the unrelated cleanup for another task. When they are mixed in the same lines, preserve a recoverable copy first. It may be clearer to reapply the smaller repair from a known starting point than to delete selected files from an unfamiliar diff. Check the result again after separating it. Claude Code offers checkpointing and rewind , but check its coverage before relying on it. Files changed only through Bash are not tracked; later shell changes to an already tracked file are a different case. Subagent edits and concurrent changes also have coverage conditions. A rewind point is not proof that every change in the directory can be restored. Claude Docs: Rewind Limitations For the shared formatter, compare the callers it affects with the behavior you agreed to preserve. For formatting noise, establish which command produced it before trying to separate it. Until the necessary edits and your original work are distinguishable, avoid a blanket reset of the working directory. 4. How do you keep the next bug fix focused? State the symptom, the required result, the behavior to preserve and what should happen if the repair needs a wider change. You do not have to predict every file the fix will touch. For the same hypothetical bug, an untested request example is: Fix the CSV export so a zero amount is exported as 0 rather than an empty cell. Preserve the existing export columns, other value formats, and on-screen amounts. Check the cause and list the proposed changes before editing. Include a regression test for zero. Leave unrelated renaming, cleanup, and dependency upgrades out of this task. If the fix requires changing shared behavior or a dependency, explain why and wait for confirmation. Report the changes and the checks actually run. Replace those preservation requirements with the ones that matter in your app. This example permits a necessary shared-code repair; it asks for a decision when the proposed work changes shared behavior or a dependency beyond the original agreement. Once an approach is approved, Claude should carry out the work within it. Ask again when a new finding requires a wider decision. An obvious small correction does not need a lengthy planning ceremony. Investigating first is useful when the cause, impact or proposed approach is unclear. Keep lasting project conventions in CLAUDE.md , and put the particular bug and its acceptance criteria in the current request. Claude’s documentation describes these instruction files as context rather than enforced configuration. They help guide the work; they cannot guarantee that every action follows the intended boundary. Claude Docs: Guidance and Enforcement For something that must be inaccessible, use a restriction the tool or environment can actually enforce, and check its coverage. The permission documentation distinguishes built-in file-tool rules from arbitrary subprocess access. Blocking one editing route does not establish that every way of writing a file is blocked. Configuration details deserve a separate check before anyone relies on them. Claude Docs: File-Rule Coverage 5. How do you know the fix is actually finished? Accept the repair when the original failure is resolved, the agreed existing behavior is preserved, and the remaining edits have an explained purpose. Ask for the evidence behind those conclusions. For this example, start with the zero case. Look for a reproduction or regression check that exercises the real export path. It should demonstrate the old failure and the required 0 output after the repair. A test of a helper in isolation may miss a different problem later in the export. Then check the promises around it: the CSV columns, the other agreed value formats and the on-screen amounts. If a shared function changed, include the relevant callers. Do not invent an empty-value requirement just because zero and blank values appeared in the same discussion; use the behavior the app is meant to preserve. Accept the Fix Against the Agreed Behavior Review changes to the tests too. A green result obtained by deleting an assertion or changing an expected value needs an explanation against the original requirement. Tests can need legitimate updates, but the reason must survive that comparison. The completion note can be short: what changed, what was preserved, which checks actually ran and what remains unchecked. If the execution environment was unavailable, the patch is written but its runtime result is still unverified. For this repair to be complete, the CSV zero must export correctly, with evidence for the surrounding behavior you asked to keep. Unrelated cleanup belongs in another task.
